1:
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## Dīgha Nikāya
## Sīlakkhandhavagga-aṭṭhakathā
## Ganthārambhakathā

I pay homage to the Buddha, whose heart is cooled by great compassion, who has dispelled the darkness of ignorance with the light of wisdom, who is the teacher honored by the world of beings including men, devas, and brahmas, who has fared well (Sugata), and who is specially liberated from the five destinations of rebirth.

I pay homage to that peerless and sublime Dhamma, the ten-fold Dhamma (of Paths, Fruits, and Nibbāna), which the Buddha himself developed within his own continuity and realized, thereby reaching the state of a Buddha free from the stains of defilements.

I pay homage with my head to the community of the eight Noble Saṅgha, the true heart-born sons of the Sugata, who crush the Ruler of Evil (Māra) and his army.

Through the merit arising from this homage to the Triple Gem, may my mind be clear. By the power of that merit, may all obstacles be well dispelled (as I compose this work).

To clarify the meaning of this noble Dīgha Nikāya, which is marked by long discourses, is subtle and profound, is praised and explained by the Buddha and his noble disciples, and possesses the quality of inspiring faith in the Triple Gem,

I shall explain that commentary which was first chanted and rehearsed at the First Council by five hundred Arahants led by the Venerable Mahākassapa, and subsequently rehearsed again at the Second and Third Councils by Arahants such as the Venerable Yasa and the Venerable Moggaliputtatissa.

However, that commentary was brought to the island of Laṅkā by the Venerable Mahā-Mahinda and was established in the Sinhala language for the benefit of the inhabitants of the island.
2:
Removing the Sinhala language from that ancient commentary, I shall present it in the faultless Magadhi language, which is pleasing to the minds of the wise and conforms to the method and style of the Pali scriptures.

This will be done without contradicting the traditions of the Great Elders (Mahātheras) who resided at the Mahāvihāra, who possessed extremely subtle judgment, and who were like lamps in the lineage of the Elders.

Discarding the meanings that appear repeatedly, I shall clarify the meaning for the delight of virtuous people and for the long-lasting endurance of the sublime Sasana.

Discourses on virtue (sīla), the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), all subjects of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna), the details of the meditative attainments (jhāna-samāpatti) along with the various temperaments (carita), all the higher powers (abhiññā), the decisions concerning the sphere of wisdom (paññā), the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), sense bases (āyatana), faculties (indriya), and the Four Noble Truths, the teaching on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) with its extremely pure and subtle methods, and the practice of insight meditation (vipassanā-bhāvana) which is not divorced from the path of the scriptures—

since I have already explained all these very clearly in the Visuddhimagga, I shall not treat them here again in detail.

"The Visuddhimagga stands in the midst of the four Nikāyas and will clarify the meaning as spoken therein." With this intention, it was composed.

Therefore, taking that Visuddhimagga together with this commentary, understand the meaning contained in the Dīgha Nikāya.

## Nidānakathā

Regarding the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīghāgama), it consists of three divisions (vagga): the Sīlakkhandhavagga, the Mahāvagga, and the Pāthikavagga. In terms of discourses, it contains a collection of thirty-four suttas. Among these divisions, the Sīlakkhandhavagga is the first; among the suttas, the Brahmajāla Sutta is the first. The beginning of the Brahmajāla Sutta is the introduction starting with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ," which was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council.
3: The words beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" are the start of the introduction spoken by the Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council. ## Paṭhamamahāsaṅgītikathā Although this First Great Council has been included as scripture in the Vinaya Piṭaka, it should also be understood here in this commentary for the sake of proficiency in the introduction. The Blessed One, having performed the Buddha's duties starting from the turning of the Wheel of Dhamma until the conversion of the wandering ascetic Subhadda, attained Parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) at dawn on the full moon day of Visākha, between the twin Sal trees in the Sal grove of the Malla princes at Kusināra. On the day the relics of the Blessed One, the Refuge of the World, were distributed, among the seven hundred thousand monks who had assembled, the Elder of the Saṅgha, Venerable Mahākassapa, recalled the words spoken by the monk Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, on the seventh day after the Blessed One's Parinibbāna: "Enough, friends! Do not sorrow, do not lament. We are well rid of that Great Ascetic. We were oppressed by him saying, 'This is allowable for you, this is not allowable for you.' But now we shall do whatever we wish, and we shall not do what we do not wish." Considering that such an assembly of the Saṅgha would be difficult to obtain again, he thought: "It is possible that evil monks, thinking 'The Teacher's word is a thing of the past,' will gain a following and before long cause the True Dhamma to disappear. As long as the Dhamma and Vinaya endure, the Teacher's word is not a thing of the past." For it was said by the Blessed One: "Ānanda, the Dhamma I have taught and the Vinaya I have prescribed for you shall be your Teacher after my passing." He then thought: "It would be well if I were to rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya so that this Sasana may be long-lasting and endure for a long time." Furthermore, Venerable Mahākassapa reflected on how the Blessed One had honored him by placing him on an equal footing regarding the nine successive attainments (anupubbavihāra-samāpatti) and the six higher powers (abhiññā), which are superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), and by allowing him to share his robes, saying: "Kassapa, will you wear my worn-out hempen rag-robes?" and "Monks, for as long as I wish, I can enter and dwell in the first jhāna... and likewise, monks, Kassapa too, for as long as he wishes, can enter and dwell in the first jhāna..."
4:
'Monks, for as long as I wish, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, I enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion. Monks, Kassapa also, for as long as he wishes, secluded from sensual pleasures, secluded from unwholesome states, can enter and dwell in the first jhāna, which is accompanied by thought and examination, with rapture and happiness born of seclusion' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.152). In this manner, he was favored by the Buddha by being placed on an equal footing with Himself in the superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma), consisting of the nine successive attainments and the six higher powers. Furthermore, he was praised by the Buddha as having a mind as unattached as a hand moving in the sky and for his moon-like practice. Thinking, 'What other task could be my debt-clearance to the Buddha, who has favored and praised me so, other than performing the rehearsal (Saṅgāyana) of the Dhamma and Vinaya?', he inspired the monks to strive for the rehearsal of the Dhamma and Vinaya. 

As it is said: 'Then the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks—Friends, once I was traveling on the long road from Pāvā to Kusinārā with a large Saṅgha of about five hundred monks' (Cūḷavagga 437). The entire section on Subhadda (Subhadda-kaṇḍa) should be understood in detail as stated there. However, we shall explain the meaning of that Subhadda-kaṇḍa in the place where it occurs at the end of the Mahāparinibbāna Sutta. 

Thereafter, he said: 'Come, friends, let us rehearse the Dhamma and the Vinaya. In the future, what is not Dhamma will shine and Dhamma will be pushed aside; what is not Vinaya will shine and Vinaya will be pushed aside. In the future, those who speak what is not Dhamma will be strong and those who speak Dhamma will be weak; those who speak what is not Vinaya will be strong and those who speak Vinaya will be weak.' 

The monks said: 'If that is so, Bhante, let the Elder select the monks.' Then the Elder [selected] many hundreds and thousands of monks who were worldlings (puthujjana), stream-enterers (sotāpanna), once-returners (sakadāgāmi), non-returners (anāgāmi), dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka), and Arahats, all of whom were bearers of the ninefold teaching (pariyatti) of the Teacher's Dispensation...
5:
The Elder Mahākassapa, excluding worldlings, stream-enterers, once-returners, non-returners, and dry-insight Arahats, selected only four hundred and ninety-nine Arahats who were masters of the entire three-fold Piṭaka, who had attained analytical insights (paṭisambhidā), possessed great psychic power, were mostly designated as foremost (etadagga) by the Blessed One, and possessed the three knowledges (tevijjā) and other such qualities. Referring to those monks, it was said: 'Then the Venerable Mahākassapa selected five hundred Arahats less one' (Cūḷavagga 437).

Why did the Elder select one less than five hundred? It was to make room for the Venerable Ānanda. For it was impossible to conduct the rehearsal of the Dhamma either with him or without him. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda was a trainee (sekha) with work still to be done (sakaraṇīya); therefore, it was not possible to include him [as he was]. However, there was not a single discourse, such as Sutta or Geyya, taught by the Possessor of Ten Powers (Dasabala) that he had not personally witnessed. As he himself said:

'I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha, and two thousand from the monks; thus, eighty-four thousand teachings are familiar to me' (Theragāthā 1027).

Therefore, it was also impossible to conduct the rehearsal without him.

If so, even though he was a trainee, since he was of great benefit to the rehearsal of the Dhamma, why did the Elder not select him at the beginning? It was to avoid the criticism of others. For the Elder was extremely intimate with the Venerable Ānanda. Indeed, even when grey hairs had appeared on Ānanda's head, the Elder would still admonish him using the term 'boy' (kumāraka), saying, 'This boy does not know his measure' (Saṃ. Ni. 2.154). Furthermore, the Venerable Ānanda was born of the Sakyan clan and was the younger brother (cousin) of the Tathāgata, being the son of His paternal uncle. In that case, some monks might think the Elder was acting out of favoritism (agati) and criticize him, saying, 'The Elder has set aside many Arahats who have attained analytical insights and selected Ānanda, who is but a trainee.' To avoid such criticism from others, and thinking, 'It is impossible to rehearse the Dhamma without Ānanda; I will take him only with the consent of the monks,' he did not select him initially.

Then the monks themselves, of their own accord, requested the Elder on behalf of Ānanda. As it is said: 'The monks said this to the Venerable Mahākassapa—Bhante, this Venerable Ānanda, although a trainee, is incapable of going to a wrong course through desire, hatred, delusion, or fear. Moreover, he has mastered much Dhamma and Vinaya in the presence of the Blessed One. Therefore, Bhante, let the Elder...'
6:
"Please select the Venerable Ānanda as well," they requested. Then, the Venerable Mahākassapa selected the Venerable Ānanda as well.

Thus, with the consent of the monks, there were five hundred elders including the selected Venerable Ānanda.

Then, the elder monks thought: "Where should we recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya?" Then, the elder monks thought: "The city of Rājagaha has a wide area for alms-resort and plenty of lodgings. What if we spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya? No other monks should enter the rains retreat in Rājagaha."

Why did they think so? Because they thought: "This is our long-term task; a person of differing views like Subhadda might enter the midst of the Saṅgha and cause disruption." Then, the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha with a formal motion and a second announcement (ñattidutiya-kammavācā):

"Venerables, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is timely for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha authorize these five hundred monks to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and no other monks are to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha. This is the motion (ñatti).

"Venerables, let the Saṅgha listen to me. The Saṅgha authorizes these five hundred monks to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and no other monks are to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha. Whichever venerable approves of the authorization of these five hundred monks to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and that no other monks are to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha, let him be silent. Whichever venerable does not approve, let him speak.

"These five hundred monks have been authorized by the Saṅgha to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya, and no other monks are to spend the rains retreat in Rājagaha. The Saṅgha approves, therefore it is silent. Thus I record this decision."
7:
This formal act (kammavācā) was performed on the 21st day after the Parinibbāna of the Blessed One. The Blessed One attained Parinibbāna at dawn on the full moon day of Kasone (Vesākha). For seven days thereafter, they honored the golden-hued body with scents, garlands, and so on. Thus, there were seven days of celebration (sādhukīḷana). Then, within seven days, the body was cremated on a pyre of sandalwood. For another seven days, they constructed a cage-like enclosure with spears and performed a relic-worship ceremony at the Santhāgāra hall. Thus, twenty-one days passed. On the 5th waxing day of Nayone (Jeṭṭha), the relics were distributed. On that day of relic distribution, having informed the assembled Saṅgha of the improper conduct of Subhadda, who had gone forth in old age, and having selected the monks according to the aforementioned method, this formal act (kammavācā) was performed.

After performing this formal act, the Elder Mahākassapa addressed the monks: "Venerables, you are now given a period of forty days. After that period, you will not be allowed to say, 'I still have such-and-such an impediment (palibodha).' Therefore, within this period, if anyone has an impediment of illness, or matters concerning teachers or preceptors, or matters concerning parents, or if there is a bowl to be fired or robes to be sewn, let them cut off those impediments and perform those duties."

Having spoken thus, the Elder Mahākassapa, surrounded by his retinue of five hundred, departed for Rājagaha. Other great elders also took their respective retinues and departed for various directions, wishing to console the people who were pierced by the arrows of grief. The Elder Puṇṇa, however, remained in Kusinārā with a retinue of seven hundred monks, thinking, "I will console the people who come to the place where the Tathāgata attained Parinibbāna."

The Venerable Ānanda, just as he did before the Parinibbāna, personally took the bowl and robes of the Blessed One who had attained Parinibbāna and set out on a journey toward Sāvatthī with five hundred monks. As he traveled, the monks in the Venerable Ānanda's retinue became too numerous to count. In every place the Venerable arrived, there was great lamentation. When they eventually reached Sāvatthī, the people of Sāvatthī, hearing that "the Elder has arrived," came out to meet him with scents, garlands, and so on, and wept bitterly, saying, "Venerable Ānanda, in the past you came with the Blessed One; where have you left the Blessed One today that you come alone?" and so forth.
8:
They wept bitterly, saying things such as, "Have you come leaving the Blessed One behind?" There was a great lamentation, just as on the day of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna.

Then, the Venerable Ānanda comforted the multitude with a Dhamma discourse related to impermanence and other such themes. He then entered the Jetavana monastery, paid homage to the Gandhakuṭī (scented chamber) where the One of Ten Powers had resided, opened the door, took out the couch and chair, dusted them, swept the Gandhakuṭī, discarded the withered flowers and refuse, brought the couch and chair back in, and placed them in their original positions. He performed all the major and minor duties that were customarily done while the Blessed One was alive. While performing these duties, such as sweeping the bathroom and preparing the bathwater, he paid homage to the Gandhakuṭī and wept, saying, "Blessed One, is this not the time for Your bath? Is this not the time for Your Dhamma teaching? Is this not the time for Your giving exhortation to the monks? Is this not the time for Your lion-like sleep? Is this not the time for Your washing of the face?"

The Venerable Ānanda acted thus, weeping, because he was one who knew the nectar-like essence of the Blessed One's multitude of virtues, possessed steadfast affection, had not yet exhausted the taints (āsavas), and had a heart softened by mutual help rendered over many hundreds of thousands of births. Then, a certain deity, wishing to stir his sense of urgency (saṃvega), said, "Venerable Ānanda, if you are weeping in this manner, how will you be able to comfort others?"

Stirred by the deity's words, the Venerable Ānanda steadied his heart. Because he had spent much time standing and sitting since the day of the Tathāgata's Parinibbāna, his physical humors (phlegm, bile, and wind) were disturbed. To soothe his body, he took a milk-purgative on the second day and remained within the monastery. With reference to that taking of medicine, he said to the young man sent by Subha the youth: "Young man, it is not the right time; today I have taken a dose of medicine. Perhaps we may visit tomorrow."

On the second day, taking the Elder Cetaka as his attendant monk, he went and, being questioned by Subha the youth, preached the Subha Sutta, which is the tenth sutta in this Dīgha Nikāya.

Then, the Elder Ānanda, having had the broken and dilapidated parts of the Jetavana Mahāvihāra repaired, left the community of monks as the time for the rains retreat (Vassa) approached and went to Rājagaha...
9:
Just like the Elder Ānanda, the other monks who were to participate in the Council also proceeded to Rājagaha. With reference to their going, the Elders who conducted the Council said: "Then the Elder monks went to Rājagaha to recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya." Those venerable ones performed the Uposatha on the full moon day of Āsāḷha and, having assembled on the first day of the waning moon, entered the rains retreat (Vassa).

At that time, there were eighteen great monasteries surrounding the city of Rājagaha, all of which were dirty with refuse, having been abandoned and fallen into disrepair. This was because, at the time of the Blessed One's Parinibbāna, all the monks had taken their own bowls and robes and departed, abandoning the monastery grounds and buildings. The Elders, wishing to make a commitment to these monasteries, thought: "In the first month, let us repair the broken and dilapidated buildings," both as an act of worship to the Blessed One's words and to free themselves from the criticism of heretics. For if they did not repair them, the heretics might say: "The disciples of the Ascetic Gotama looked after the monasteries only while their Teacher was alive; now that he has attained Parinibbāna, they have abandoned them. The great wealth sacrificed by the families has gone to waste." It is meant that they thought thus to be free from such criticism. Having thought so, they made a formal commitment. With reference to that commitment, it was said:

"Then this thought occurred to the Elder monks: 'Friends, the Blessed One praised the repair of broken and dilapidated buildings. Come, friends, let us repair the buildings in the first month; in the middle month, let us assemble and recite the Dhamma and the Vinaya.'"

On the second day, they went and stood at the palace gate. King Ajātasattu came, paid homage, and asked about his duty: "Venerable sirs, for what purpose have you come?" The Elders informed him that they needed manual laborers to repair the eighteen great monasteries. The King provided men skilled in manual labor. The Elders had all the monasteries repaired during the first month and then informed the King: "Great King, the repair of the monasteries is finished. Now we shall conduct the Council (recitation) of the Dhamma and Vinaya." The King replied, "Very well, venerable sirs, perform it with confidence. Let my wheel of authority and your wheel of Dhamma proceed together. Command me, venerable sirs, what should I do?" "Great King, a meeting place is needed for the monks who will conduct the Council," they said. "Where shall I prepare it, venerable sirs?" he asked. "Great King, it is appropriate to prepare it at the entrance of the Sattapaṇṇi Cave on the side of Mount Vebhāra," they replied. "Very well, venerable sirs," said King Ajātasattu...
10:
King Ajātasattu had a pavilion constructed, as beautiful as if created by the celestial architect Vissakamma, with well-proportioned walls, pillars, and staircases, and adorned with various floral and creeper designs. This pavilion appeared to surpass the splendor of a royal palace and mock the glory of a celestial mansion. It was like a single landing-stage where the birds—the eyes of gods and humans—could rest together, a concentrated essence of all the world's beauty. He adorned it with a beautiful ceiling from which various flower garlands hung, and a floor as exquisite as a jeweled pavement inlaid with various gems. Inside this great pavilion, which resembled a mansion of the Brahmas, he had five hundred priceless and allowable rugs spread for the five hundred monks. On the southern side, he prepared the seat for the Elders facing north, and in the center of the pavilion, he prepared a Dhamma-seat (dhammāsana) facing east, worthy of the Blessed Buddha's presence. Having placed an ivory-inlaid fan there, he informed the Saṅgha of monks: "Venerable sirs, my task is completed."

On that very day, some monks, referring to the Venerable Ānanda, said: "In this Saṅgha of monks, there is one monk wandering about who gives off a foul odor (of defilements)." When the Elder heard this, he reflected: "In this Saṅgha, there is no other monk who wanders about giving off a foul odor except me. Surely, these people are referring to me," and he was moved by a sense of spiritual urgency (saṃvega). Some monks even told him directly: "Friend Ānanda, tomorrow is the assembly day. You are still a 'learner' (sekha) with tasks yet to be done. Therefore, it is not fitting for you to go to the assembly as a sekha; be diligent!"

Then the Venerable Ānanda thought: "Tomorrow is the assembly. It is not proper for me to go to the assembly while still being a sekha." He spent much of the night in mindfulness immersed in the body (kāyagatāsati). At dawn, he descended from the walking path (caṅkama) and entered his chamber, thinking, "I will lie down for a moment." As he was reclining his body, his two feet were already off the ground and his head had not yet reached the pillow; in that very interval, his mind was liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging, and he became an Arahant. Indeed, while the Venerable Ānanda was striving on the walking path and unable to attain distinction, he reflected: "Did not the Blessed One tell me, 'Ānanda, you have performed merit in the past; exert yourself in striving, and you will soon be free from the taints'? The words of the Buddhas cannot be false. However, my energy (vīriya) is too excessive, and thus my mind tends toward restlessness (uddhacca). Now, I shall balance my energy and concentration." Having so reflected, he descended from the walking path, stood at the place for washing feet, and after washing his feet, he entered the chamber. He sat on the couch and thought, "I will rest for a moment." As he reclined his body, his two feet left the ground, and before his head reached the pillow, in that very moment, he became an Arahant, free from the taints.

Because he attained the Fruit of Arahantship while free from all four postures, if it is asked in this Dispensation, "Which monk became an Arahant while neither lying, sitting, standing, nor walking?" it should be answered, "The Venerable Elder Ānanda."
11:
After washing his feet, the Venerable Ānanda entered the chamber and sat on the small couch, thinking, "I will rest for a while," and reclined his body onto the couch. His two feet were off the ground, and his head had not yet reached the pillow; in that interval, his mind was liberated from the taints (āsavas) without clinging to anything through craving or views. The Elder's Arahantship occurred while being free from the four postures. Therefore, when it is said, "In this Dispensation, which monk reached Arahantship without lying down, without sitting, without standing, and without walking?" it is proper to say, "The Elder Ānanda."

Then, on the second day after the Elder became an Arahant (the fifth day of the waning moon of Sāvaṇa), the elder monks, having finished their meal and put away their bowls and robes, assembled in the Dhamma Hall. Then the Venerable Ānanda, being an Arahant, went to the assembly. How did he go? With a heart exceedingly joyful and glad, thinking, "Now I am worthy to enter the midst of the assembly," he placed his robe over one shoulder and approached. He appeared like a ripe palm fruit fallen from its stalk, like a genuine ruby placed on a pale yellow blanket, like the full moon rising in a sky free of clouds, or like a lotus blossomed by the touch of the morning sun's rays and filled with golden pollen. He went as if announcing his attainment of Arahantship with a most pure, bright, radiant, and glorious countenance. Upon seeing him, the Venerable Mahākassapa thought: "How beautiful is the Venerable Ānanda who has attained Arahantship! If the Teacher were still alive, he would surely give Ānanda a 'Sādhu' (Well done!) today. Come, I shall now give him the 'Sādhu' that should be given by the Teacher." Thus, he gave the 'Sādhu' call three times.

However, the Reciters of the Majjhima Nikāya (Majjhima-bhāṇakas) say: "The Elder Ānanda, wishing to make known his attainment of Arahantship, did not go together with the other monks. When the monks sat in their respective seats according to seniority, they left a seat for the Elder Ānanda. Then some asked, 'Whose seat is this?' and were told, 'It is Ānanda's.' When they asked, 'Where has Ānanda gone?', at that moment the Elder thought, 'Now is the time for me to go.' Then, wishing to demonstrate his psychic power, he dived into the earth and manifested himself right in his own seat." Others say he went through the air and sat down. Be that as it may, seeing him arrive in such a manner, it was indeed fitting for the Venerable Mahākassapa to give the 'Sādhu' call.

When the Venerable Ānanda had thus arrived, the Venerable Mahākassapa addressed the monks: "Friends, what shall we recite first in council, the Dhamma or the Vinaya?"
12:
The monks said, "Venerable Mahākassapa, the Vinaya is the life of the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana). As long as the Vinaya endures, the Dispensation is said to endure. Therefore, let us first recite the Vinaya." When asked, "Whom shall we make the leader?" they replied, "Let us make the Venerable Upāli the leader." When asked, "Is the Venerable Ānanda not capable?" they replied, "It is not that he is not capable; he is capable. However, while the Fully Enlightened One was still alive, he placed the Venerable Upāli in the foremost position (etadagga) regarding the mastery of the Vinaya, saying: 'Monks, among my disciples who are bearers of the Vinaya, this Upāli is the foremost.' Therefore, let us recite the Vinaya by questioning the Elder Upāli."

Then, the Elder Mahākassapa formally authorized himself to question the Vinaya. The Elder Upāli also formally authorized himself to answer. In that authorization, it proceeded according to this Pali: Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha—

"Let the Saṅgha hear me, friends. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I would question the Venerable Upāli on the Vinaya."

The Venerable Upāli also informed the Saṅgha—

"Let the Saṅgha hear me, venerable sirs. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I would answer the Vinaya when questioned by the Venerable Mahākassapa."

Having thus authorized themselves, the Venerable Upāli rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the senior elders, and sat on the Dhamma-seat holding an ivory-inlaid fan. Then, the Elder Mahākassapa sat on the elders' seat and questioned the Venerable Upāli on the Vinaya. "Friend Upāli, where was the first Pārājika promulgated?" he asked. "Venerable sir, it was promulgated in Vesālī," he replied. "Concerning whom?" he asked. "Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalanda," he replied. "On what matter?" he asked. "On the matter of sexual intercourse," he replied.

"Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Upāli on the basis (vatthu), the origin (nidāna), the person (puggala), the regulation (paññatti), the supplementary regulation (anupaññatti), the offense (āpatti), and the non-offense (anāpatti) of the first Pārājika. The Venerable Upāli answered each question as it was asked."

In this first Pārājika, is there anything to be removed or anything to be added? There is nothing to be removed. In the words spoken by the Blessed Buddha, there is nothing to be removed. For the Tathāgatas do not speak even a single syllable that is without purpose. For the disciples'...
13:
In the words spoken by deities, there may be things to be removed; those things to be removed were indeed removed by the Elders who were the Reciters of the Dhamma (Dhamma-saṅgāhaka). However, there are things to be added in all the teachings (of the Buddha, disciples, and deities). Therefore, whatever word was appropriate to be added in a particular place, they indeed added it. What are those added words? They are merely connecting words such as "At that time" (tena samayena), "Now at that time" (tena kho pana samayena), "Then" (atha kho), "When this was said" (evaṃ vutte), "He said this" (etadavoca), and so on. Having thus added the words that were appropriate to be added, they established, "This is the first Pārājika." When the first Pārājika was included in the recitation, the five hundred Arahants performed a group chanting in the same manner as it was included in the recitation: "At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was staying at Verañjā." At the very moment they began the chanting, the great earth shook violently as far as the water's edge, as if giving a cry of "Sādhu."

In this same manner, having included the remaining three Pārājikas in the recitation, they established, "This is the Pārājika-kaṇḍa." They established the thirteen Saṅghādisesas as "Terassaka." They established the two Aniyata rules as "Aniyata." They established the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules as "Nissaggiya Pācittiya." They established the ninety-two Pācittiya rules as "Pācittiya." They established the four Pāṭidesanīya rules as "Pāṭidesanīya." They established the seventy-five Sekhiya rules as "Sekhiya." They established the seven principles as "Adhikaraṇasamatha." Thus, they designated and established the two hundred and twenty-seven rules as the "Mahāvibhaṅga." At the conclusion of the Mahāvibhaṅga recitation, the great earth shook just as before.

Then, in the Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga, they established the eight Pārājika rules as "This is the Pārājika-kaṇḍa." They established the seventeen Saṅghādisesas as "Sattarasaka." They established the thirty Nissaggiya Pācittiya rules as "Nissaggiya Pācittiya." They established the one hundred and sixty-six Pācittiya rules as "Pācittiya." They established the eight Pāṭidesanīya rules as "Pāṭidesanīya." They established the seventy-five Sekhiya rules as "Sekhiya." They established the seven principles as "Adhikaraṇasamatha." Thus, having designated the three hundred and four rules as the "Bhikkhunīvibhaṅga," they established, "This Ubhatovibhaṅga consists of sixty-four recital sections (bhāṇavāra)." At the conclusion of the Ubhatovibhaṅga recitation, the shaking of the great earth occurred just as mentioned before.

In this same way, having included the Khandhaka, which consists of eighty recital sections, and the Parivāra, which consists of twenty-five recital sections, in the recitation, they established, "This is the Vinaya Piṭaka."
14:
(The recitation of the Vinaya Piṭaka was completed) and it was established. At the conclusion of the Vinaya Piṭaka, a great earthquake occurred in the same manner as previously described. They entrusted that Vinaya Piṭaka to the Venerable Upāli, saying, "Friend, teach this to your pupils." At the conclusion of the Vinaya Piṭaka recitation, the Elder Upāli laid down the ivory-handled fan, descended from the Dhamma seat, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat in his own assigned seat.

Having recited the Vinaya, the Venerable Mahākassapa, wishing to recite the Dhamma (Sutta and Abhidhamma), asked the monks: "In reciting the Dhamma, which person should be made the leader for the recitation?" The monks replied, "The Elder Ānanda should be made the leader."

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa informed the Saṅgha: "Friends, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I would like to question Ānanda regarding the Dhamma."

Then the Venerable Ānanda also informed the Saṅgha: "Venerable Sirs, let the Saṅgha listen to me. If it is suitable for the Saṅgha, I would like to answer the Dhamma when questioned by the Venerable Mahākassapa."

Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, arranged his robe over one shoulder, paid homage to the elder monks, and sat on the Dhamma seat, holding the ivory-handled fan. Then the Venerable Mahākassapa asked the monks: "Friends, which Piṭaka shall we recite first?" The monks replied, "Venerable Sir, let us recite the Suttanta Piṭaka."

"In the Suttanta Piṭaka, there are four Nikāyas; among them, which Nikāya shall we recite first?" When asked, they replied, "Venerable Sir, let us recite the Dīgha Nikāya."

"In the Dīgha Nikāya, there are thirty-four suttas and three vaggas; among them, which vagga shall we recite first?" When asked, they replied, "Venerable Sir, let us recite the Sīlakkhandhavagga."

"In the Sīlakkhandhavagga, there are thirteen suttas; among them, which sutta shall we recite first?" When asked, they replied, "Venerable Sir, let us first recite the Brahmajāla Sutta, which is adorned with the three types of virtue, which destroys various forms of wrong livelihood such as scheming and talk, which untangles the net of sixty-two types of wrong views, and which is the cause of the shaking of the ten thousand world systems."

Then the Venerable Mahākassapa said this to the Venerable Ānanda: "Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla Sutta spoken?" "Venerable Sir, it was spoken at the royal rest-house in Ambalaṭṭhikā, between Rājagaha and Nālandā." "Concerning whom..."
15:
"...concerning whom was it spoken?" When asked, he replied, "It was spoken concerning Suppiya the wanderer and the youth Brahmadatta." "On what subject was it spoken?" When asked, he replied, "On the subject of praise and dispraise (vaṇṇāvaṇṇa)." Then the Venerable Mahākassapa questioned the Venerable Ānanda regarding the origin, the persons, and the subject matter of the Brahmajāla Sutta (Cūḷavagga, 440). The Venerable Ānanda answered. At the conclusion of the answers, the five hundred Arahants performed a group recitation. In the manner already described, the earth shook.

Having thus recited the Brahmajāla Sutta, they proceeded to recite all thirteen suttas together with the Brahmajāla Sutta in the order of questioning and answering, starting with, "Friend Ānanda, where was the Sāmaññaphala Sutta spoken?" and so on. They then designated it, saying, "This is called the Sīlakkhandhavagga."

Immediately after the Sīlakkhandhavagga, they recited the Mahāvagga, and immediately after that, the Pāthikavagga. Thus, having recited the text composed of three vaggas, adorned with thirty-four suttas, and measuring sixty-four bhāṇavāras (recital sections), they declared, "This is called the Dīgha Nikāya," and entrusted it to the Venerable Ānanda, saying, "Friend, teach this to your pupils."

Immediately after the Dīgha Nikāya, they recited the Majjhima Nikāya, which measures eighty bhāṇavāras, and entrusted it to the pupils of the General of the Dhamma, the Venerable Sāriputta, saying, "You should maintain this Majjhima Nikāya."

Immediately after the Majjhima Nikāya, they recited the Saṃyutta Nikāya, which measures one hundred bhāṇavāras, and entrusted it to the Venerable Mahākassapa, saying, "Venerable Sir, please teach this Saṃyutta Nikāya to your pupils."

Immediately after the Saṃyutta Nikāya, they recited the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which measures one hundred and twenty bhāṇavāras, and entrusted it to the Venerable Anuruddha, saying, "Please teach this Aṅguttara Nikāya to your pupils."

Immediately after the Aṅguttara Nikāya, the Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna are called the Abhidhamma. Having recited the text thus explained, which is the domain of subtle knowledge, they declared, "This is called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka," and the five hundred Arahants performed the recitation. In the manner already described, the earth shook.

After that, the Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Suttanipāta, Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu...
16:
The elders who recite the Dīgha Nikāya (Dīghabhāṇakas) say that after chanting this text beginning with the Theragāthā and Therīgāthā, they named it "Khuddaka Gantha" and included it only within the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. However, the elders who recite the Majjhima Nikāya (Majjhimabhāṇakas) say that all this Khuddaka Gantha, along with the Cariyāpiṭaka and Buddhavaṃsa, is included within the Suttanta Piṭaka.

Thus, all these words of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) should be understood as one-fold by way of essence (rasa), two-fold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya, three-fold by way of the first, middle, and last [words]. Similarly, it is three-fold by way of Piṭaka, five-fold by way of Nikāya, nine-fold by way of Aṅga, and eighty-four thousand-fold by way of the units of Dhamma (dhammakkhandha).

How is it one-fold by way of essence? From the time the Blessed One realized the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until he attained parinibbāna through the element of Nibbāna without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu), all the words spoken while teaching or reflecting for the benefit of devas, humans, nāgas, yakkhas, and others during these forty-five years have only one essence: the essence of liberation (vimuttirasa). Thus, it is one-fold by way of essence.

How is it two-fold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya? All these words of the Buddha are designated as Dhamma and Vinaya. Therein, the Vinaya Piṭaka is called Vinaya, and the remaining words of the Buddha are called Dhamma. Therefore, [Venerable Mahākassapa] said, "Let us chant the Dhamma and the Vinaya," and "I shall ask Venerable Upāli about the Vinaya and Venerable Ānanda about the Dhamma." Thus, it is two-fold by way of Dhamma and Vinaya.

How is it three-fold by way of the first, middle, and last? All these words of the Buddha are divided into three: the first words of the Buddha, the middle words of the Buddha, and the last words of the Buddha. Therein:

Through many a birth in saṃsāra have I wandered, seeking but not finding the builder of this house (craving). Sorrowful is birth again and again.
O house-builder, you are seen! You shall not build the house again.
All your rafters (defilements) are broken, the ridge-pole (ignorance) is shattered.
My mind has reached the unconditioned (Nibbāna); it has attained the destruction of cravings (arahantship).

These are the first words of the Buddha. Some teachers say the Udāna verse from the Mahāvagga Khandhaka beginning with "Yadā have pātubhavanti dhammā" is the first words of the Buddha. However, it should be understood that this Udāna verse arose while reflecting on dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) with knowledge accompanied by joy on the day he attained omniscience.
17:
The words spoken at the time of his parinibbāna: "Come now, monks, I exhort you: all conditioned things are subject to decay; strive on with diligence (appamāda)"—these are the last words of the Buddha (pacchimabuddhavacana). Whatever was spoken between these two [the first and the last] is called the middle words of the Buddha (majjhimabuddhavacana). Thus, it is three-fold by way of the first, middle, and last words of the Buddha.

How is it three-fold by way of Piṭaka? All these words of the Buddha are divided into three: the Vinaya Piṭaka, the Suttanta Piṭaka, and the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Among these, the collection of everything chanted or not chanted at the First Council—namely, the two Pātimokkhas, the two Vibhaṅgas, the twenty-two Khandhakas, and the sixteen Parivāras—is called the Vinaya Piṭaka. The Dīgha Nikāya, which contains 34 suttas beginning with the Brahmajāla Sutta; the Majjhima Nikāya, which contains 152 suttas beginning with the Mūlapariyāya Sutta; the Saṃyutta Nikāya, which contains 7,762 suttas beginning with the Oghataraṇa Sutta; the Aṅguttara Nikāya, which contains 9,557 suttas beginning with the Cittapariyādāna Sutta; and the Khuddaka Nikāya, which is fifteen-fold consisting of Khuddakapāṭha, Dhammapada, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Suttanipāta, Vimānavatthu, Petavatthu, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, Jātaka, Niddesa, Paṭisambhidāmagga, Apadāna, Buddhavaṃsa, and Cariyāpiṭaka—these words of the Buddha are called the Suttanta Piṭaka. The Dhammasaṅgaṇī, Vibhaṅga, Dhātukathā, Puggalapaññatti, Kathāvatthu, Yamaka, and Paṭṭhāna—these words of the Buddha are called the Abhidhamma Piṭaka. Among these three Piṭakas:

"Because it has diverse and special methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, those wise ones who know the meaning of 'Vinaya' call this Piṭaka 'Vinaya'."

Indeed, in this Vinaya Piṭaka, there are diverse methods such as the fivefold recitation of the Pātimokkha, the seven groups of offenses beginning with Pārājika, the Mātikā, and the Vibhaṅga. The methods of supplementary regulations (anupaññatti), which serve the purpose of strengthening or relaxing the original regulations, are the special methods. It disciplines the body and speech by prohibiting transgressions of body and speech. Therefore, because of its diverse methods, special methods, and the disciplining of body and speech, it is called Vinaya. Thus, it is said for the sake of proficiency in the meaning of the word 'Vinaya':

"Because it has diverse and special methods, and because it disciplines body and speech, those wise ones who know the meaning of 'Vinaya' call this Piṭaka 'Vinaya'."
18:
As for the other, the Suttanta Piṭaka:

"It is called 'Sutta' because it indicates meanings, because it is well-spoken, because it produces benefits (like fruit), because it pours out benefits, because it protects well, and because it is similar to a carpenter's thread or a string for flowers."

Indeed, that Sutta indicates various meanings such as one's own benefit and the benefit of others. Because it is taught in accordance with the inclinations of those to be taught (veneyya), the meanings in this Sutta are well-spoken. This Sutta produces benefits just as a crop produces fruit; this means it brings them forth. This Sutta pours out benefits just as a cow yields milk; this means it causes them to flow. It also protects those benefits well; this means it guards them. This Sutta is also similar to a carpenter's thread or a string for flowers. Just as a carpenter's thread is a measure for carpenters, so too is this Sutta a measure for the wise. And just as flowers strung together with a thread do not scatter or perish, so too the meanings collected by this Sutta do not scatter or perish. For that reason, in order to be skillful in the derivation of this word 'Sutta', it is said:

"It is called 'Sutta' because it indicates meanings, is well-spoken, produces benefits, pours out benefits, protects well, and is similar to a carpenter's thread."

As for the other, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka:

"It is called 'Abhidhamma' because in it are taught dhammas that are increasing, possessed of specific characteristics, revered, distinguished, and surpassing."

Indeed, this word 'Abhi' is seen in the senses of growth (vuddhi), specific characteristic (salakkhaṇa), revered (pūjita), distinguished (paricchinna), and surpassing (adhika). That is true; this word 'Abhi' appears in the sense of growth (vuddhi) in such Pali passages as: "My painful feelings increase (abhikkamanti), they do not recede." It appears in the sense of specific characteristic (salakkhaṇa) in such passages as: "Those nights that are known (abhijñātā) and marked (abhilakkhitā)." It appears in the sense of revered (pūjita) in such passages as: "The king of kings (rājābhirājā), the lord of men." It appears in the sense of distinguished (paricchinna) in such passages as: "He is capable of training in Abhidhamma and Abhivinaya," which means in the Dhamma and Vinaya that are free from mutual confusion. It appears in the sense of surpassing (adhika) in such passages as: "With surpassing beauty (abhikkantena vaṇṇena)."

In this Abhidhamma, dhammas that are increasing are also taught by such methods as: "He develops the path for the sake of arising in the fine-material sphere (rūpūpapatti)," and "He dwells pervading one direction with a mind imbued with loving-kindness." Dhammas that are possessed of specific characteristics are also taught because they are marked by such things as objects, by such methods as: "Whether it is a visible-form object or a sound object."
19:
Dhammas that are possessed of specific characteristics are also taught because they are to be characterized by objects and so forth. Dhammas that are revered are also taught by such methods as: "Dhammas of the trainee (sekkhā dhammā), dhammas of the non-trainee (asekkhā dhammā), supramundane dhammas (lokuttarā dhammā)"; 'revered' here means they are worthy of reverence. Dhammas that are distinguished are also taught because they are distinguished by their own nature by such methods as: "There is contact (phasso hoti), there is feeling (vedanā hoti)." Dhammas that are surpassing are also taught by such methods as: "Lofty dhammas (mahaggatā dhammā), immeasurable dhammas (appamāṇā dhammā), unsurpassed dhammas (anuttarā dhammā)." For the sake of skill in the derivation of this word 'Abhidhamma' due to those reasons such as growth (vuddhimanto), this verse is said:

"It is called 'Abhidhamma' because in it are taught dhammas that are increasing, possessed of specific characteristics, revered, distinguished, and surpassing."

As for the word 'Piṭaka', which is not different in meaning here:

"Scholars who know the meaning of Piṭaka say it is called 'Piṭaka' because of the meaning of learning (pariyatti) and the meaning of a vessel (bhājana). By combining it with that word, the three such as Vinaya should be known."

Learning (pariyatti) is called 'Piṭaka' in such Pali passages as: "Do not go by the authority of the scriptures (mā piṭakasampadānena)." Any kind of vessel is also called 'Piṭaka' in such passages as: "Then a man might come carrying a hoe and a basket (kudālapiṭaka)." Therefore, scholars who know the meaning of Piṭaka say it is called 'Piṭaka' because of the meaning of learning and the meaning of a vessel.

Now, regarding "By combining it with that word, the three such as Vinaya should be known," it means that by forming a compound with that word 'Piṭaka' which has these two meanings: it is the Vinaya and it is also a Piṭaka because it is learning to be studied and because it is a vessel for various meanings; thus it is called 'Vinaya Piṭaka'. In the same manner already mentioned, it is the Sutta and it is also a Piṭaka; thus it is called 'Suttanta Piṭaka'. It is the Abhidhamma and it is also a Piṭaka; thus it is called 'Abhidhamma Piṭaka'. In this way, these three such as Vinaya should be known.

Having known this, for the sake of skill in various ways regarding these three Piṭakas:

"In those Piṭakas, one should explain the distinctions of teaching (desanā), instruction (sāsanā), and discourse (kathā) as appropriate, as well as the training (sikkhā), abandonment (pahāna), and the quality of depth (gambhīra).
One should also clarify all of how a monk reaches the distinctions of learning, the success (sampatti), and the failure (vipatti) in whichever Piṭaka."

In those verses, the following explanation is called 'paridīpanā' (detailed explanation) and 'vibhāvanā' (clarification). These three Piṭakas are called, in order: the Teaching of Authority (āṇā-desanā), the Teaching of Convention (vohāra-desanā), and the Teaching of Ultimate Truth (paramattha-desanā); also, the Instruction according to the Offense (yathāparādha-sāsanā), the Instruction according to the Inclination (yathānuloma-sāsanā), and the Instruction according to the Dhamma (yathādhamma-sāsanā); and also, the Discourse on Restraint and Non-restraint (saṃvarāsaṃvara-kathā), the Discourse on the Disentangling of Views (diṭṭhiviniveṭhana-kathā), and the Discourse on the Analysis of Mind and Matter (nāmarūpapariccheda-kathā).
20:
Among these three Piṭakas, the Vinaya Piṭaka is called 'the Teaching of Authority' (Āṇādesanā) because it was taught with many authoritative instructions by the Blessed One who is worthy of exercising authority. The Sutta Piṭaka is called 'the Teaching of Conventional Usage' (Vohāradesanā) because it was taught with many worldly conventions by the Blessed One who is skilled in conventional usage. The Abhidhamma Piṭaka is called 'the Teaching of Ultimate Reality' (Paramatthadesanā) because it was taught with many ultimate realities by the Blessed One who is skilled in ultimate reality.

Likewise, the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, is called 'the Instruction according to Offence' (Yathāparādhasāsana) because it is said: "Herein, beings who have committed many offences are disciplined according to their offences." The second, the Sutta Piṭaka, is called 'the Instruction according to Inclination' (Yathānulomasāsana) because it is said: "Herein, beings who have various inclinations, latent tendencies, temperaments, and dispositions are disciplined according to their inclinations." The third, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, is called 'the Instruction according to Dhamma' (Yathādhammasāsana) because it is said: "Herein, beings who perceive 'I' and 'mine' in a mere heap of mental and physical phenomena are disciplined according to the nature of things (Dhamma)."

Likewise, the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, is called 'the Discourse on Restraint and Non-restraint' (Saṃvarāsaṃvarakathā) because it is said: "Herein, the lesser and greater restraints (saṃvara), which are the opposites of bodily and verbal transgressions, are taught." 'Restraint and non-restraint' refers to lesser and greater restraint, just as in the terms kammākamma (greater and lesser actions) and phalāphala (greater and lesser fruits). The second, the Sutta Piṭaka, is called 'the Discourse on the Unravelling of Views' (Diṭṭhiviniveṭhanakathā) because it is said: "Herein, the unravelling of views, which is the opposite of the sixty-two types of wrong views, is taught." The third, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, is called 'the Discourse on the Delimitation of Mind and Matter' (Nāmarūpaparicchedakathā) because it is said: "Herein, the delimitation of mind and matter, which is the opposite of lust and so forth, is taught."

In these three Piṭakas, the three trainings, the three abandonings, and the fourfold depth (gambhīrabhāva) should be understood. Indeed, in the Vinaya Piṭaka, the training in higher virtue (adhisīlasikkhā) is specifically taught; in the Sutta Piṭaka, the training in higher mind (adhicittasikkhā); and in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the training in higher wisdom (adhipaññāsikkhā).

In the Vinaya Piṭaka, the abandoning of transgression (vītikkamappahāna) is taught because virtue is the opposite of the transgression of defilements. In the Sutta Piṭaka, the abandoning of obsession (pariyuṭṭhānappahāna) is taught because concentration is the opposite of the obsession of defilements. In the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, the abandoning of latent tendencies (anusayappahāna) is taught because wisdom is the opposite of the latent tendencies of defilements. In the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, abandoning by substitution of opposites (tadaṅgappahāna) is taught; in the other two Piṭakas, abandoning by suppression (vikkhambhanappahāna) and abandoning by eradication (samucchedappahāna) are taught. In the first, the Vinaya Piṭaka, the abandoning of the defilement of misconduct is taught; in the other two Piṭakas, the abandoning of the defilements of craving and views is taught.

In each of these Piṭakas, the fourfold depth (gambhīrabhāva) consisting of Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha should be understood. Therein, 'Dhamma' refers to the Pāḷi text (tanti). 'Attha' refers to the meaning of that very text. 'Desanā' refers to the exposition of that text as determined by the [Buddha's] mind. 'Paṭivedha' refers to the penetration and understanding of the text and its meaning as they truly are. In these three Piṭakas, these [four depths of] Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha are, for small creatures such as hares...
21:
Just as the great ocean is deep because it is difficult for those of dull wisdom to enter and find a footing, so too these three Piṭakas are deep because they are difficult for those of dull wisdom to enter and find a footing. Thus, in each of these three Piṭakas, the fourfold depth should be understood.

In another way, Dhamma means cause. Thus it is said: "Knowledge of the cause is the Discrimination of Dhamma (Dhammapaṭisambhidā)." Attha means the result of the cause. Thus it is said: "Knowledge of the result of the cause is the Discrimination of Meaning (Atthapaṭisambhidā)." Desanā means designation (paññatti); it is intended as the ultimate reality (paramattha) sounds correctly recited in accordance with causes and effects. Or, it is the teaching by way of direct order, reverse order, brevity, detail, and so forth. Paṭivedha means penetration (abhisamaya). That penetration is of two kinds, mundane and supramundane; it is the knowledge that penetrates causes in accordance with effects, effects in accordance with causes, and designations in accordance with the reasons for designation, both by way of object and by way of non-delusion. Or, Paṭivedha is the unerring nature, known as the individual characteristic (salakkhaṇa), which is to be penetrated in the phenomena such as mind, matter, and Nibbāna taught in those respective Piṭakas.

Now, in these Piṭakas, there exists whatever cause or effect, and the exposition (desanā) that illuminates that meaning as it appears before the wisdom of the listeners, and the penetration (paṭivedha) known as the unerring knowledge of penetration, or the unerring nature known as the individual characteristic of those respective phenomena which is to be penetrated. All these combined—Dhamma, Attha, Desanā, and Paṭivedha—are deep, like the great ocean to small hares, because they are difficult to enter and find a footing for those of poor wisdom who have not accumulated the requisites of merit. Thus, in each of these three Piṭakas, the fourfold depth should be understood.

By this much of the discourse:
"The teaching (desanā), the instruction (sāsana), the discourse (kathā), and their distinctions in those [Piṭakas] as appropriate;
The training (sikkhā), the abandoning (pahāna), and the depth (gambhīrabhāva) should be explained."
This verse has its meaning already explained.

"The distinctions of learning (pariyatti), the success (sampatti), and the failure (vipatti);
And how a bhikkhu attains them—all that should be clarified."
In this verse, the meaning should be understood as follows: In the three Piṭakas, the threefold distinction of learning (pariyatti) should be noted. There are three types of learning: the learning like the simile of the water-snake (alagaddūpama), the learning for the sake of liberation (nissaraṇattha), and the treasurer's learning (bhaṇḍāgārika).

Among those three, that learning which is wrongly grasped, which is studied for the sake of criticizing others and so forth, is called the learning like the simile of the water-snake. Referring to such wrong grasping, it was said: "Monks, just as a man who wants a water-snake..."
22:
"Bhikkhus, for example, suppose a man needing a water-snake, seeking a water-snake, wandering in search of a water-snake, should see a large water-snake. He would grasp it by its coils or by its tail. That water-snake would turn back and bite him on his hand, his arm, or some other limb. On that account, he would suffer death or deadly pain. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, of the water-snake being wrongly grasped.

In the same way, bhikkhus, here some misguided men (mogha-purisā) learn the Dhamma—the Sutta... Vedalla. Having learned that Dhamma, they do not examine the meaning of those teachings with wisdom. Not examining the meaning with wisdom, those teachings do not gain their reflective acceptance. They learn the Dhamma for the sake of criticizing others and for the sake of rebutting accusations. They do not experience the purpose for which they learn the Dhamma. Those teachings, being wrongly grasped by them, lead to their harm and suffering for a long time. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, of the teachings being wrongly grasped."

That learning (pariyatti) which is well-grasped, being studied only with the desire for the fulfillment of the aggregate of virtue and so on, and not for the sake of criticizing others, is called the learning for the sake of deliverance (nissaraṇattha-pariyatti). Referring to such well-grasped learning, it was said: "Those teachings, being well-grasped by them, lead to their benefit and happiness for a long time. Why is that? Because, bhikkhus, of the teachings being well-grasped."

When a person who has fully understood the aggregates, abandoned the defilements, developed the path, realized the fruit of Arahantship, and witnessed the truth of cessation—such a Khīṇāsava (one whose taints are exhausted)—learns the Dhamma solely for the sake of preserving the tradition and maintaining the lineage, this is called the treasurer's learning (bhaṇḍāgārika-pariyatti).

A bhikkhu who practices well in the Vinaya Piṭaka attains the Threefold Knowledge (vijjā) based on the perfection of virtue, because the distinctions of those three knowledges are taught therein. A bhikkhu who practices well in the Sutta Piṭaka attains the Six Higher Powers (abhiññā) based on the perfection of concentration, because the distinctions of those higher powers are taught therein. A bhikkhu who practices well in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka attains the Four Analytical Insights (paṭisambhidā) based on the perfection of wisdom, because the distinctions of those analytical insights are taught in that very Piṭaka. Thus, a bhikkhu who practices well in these three Piṭakas attains, in due order, this fulfillment (sampatti) consisting of the Threefold Knowledge, the Six Higher Powers, and the Four Analytical Insights.

A bhikkhu who practices wrongly in the Vinaya Piṭaka, thinking that the touch of forbidden 'clung-to' objects (upādinnaka-phassa, such as the touch of a woman) is similar to the touch of permitted comfortable rugs and robes, considers it to be faultless.
23:
This was also spoken by the Blessed One: "As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructions' by the Blessed One are not actually obstructions for one who indulges in them" (as said by the monk Ariṭṭha). Due to such a perception of faultlessness, he falls into the state of immorality (dussīla) by committing transgressions.

One who practices wrongly in the Sutta Piṭaka, not knowing the intention of the Blessed One in such passages as "Bhikkhus, these four persons are found existing in the world," grasps it wrongly. Referring to such wrong grasping, it was said: "By his own wrong grasp, he misrepresents us, injures himself, and stores up much demerit." Due to such wrong grasping, he falls into wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi).

One who practices wrongly in the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, by over-thinking about the nature of things, thinks about the unthinkable (acinteyya). Due to such thinking, he falls into mental distraction and madness. It was said: "Bhikkhus, these four unthinkables are not to be thought about; one who thinks about them would reach madness and vexation." Thus, one who practices wrongly in these three Piṭakas falls, in due order, into this failure (vipatti) consisting of immorality, wrong view, and mental distraction.

By this sequence of words:
"The distinctions of learning, the fulfillment (sampatti),
And the failure (vipatti) which a bhikkhu reaches in whichever Piṭaka,
All that should be clearly explained."
This verse also has the meaning already explained. Having known the Piṭakas in various ways, the Word of the Buddha should be understood as threefold by means of those Piṭakas.

## How is it fivefold by means of Nikāya?

All this Word of the Buddha is fivefold: Dīgha Nikāya, Majjhima Nikāya, Saṃyutta Nikāya, Aṅguttara Nikāya, and Khuddaka Nikāya. Among them, what is the Dīgha Nikāya? It consists of thirty-four suttas, such as the Brahmajāla Sutta, collected into three divisions (vaggas).

"The collection of exactly thirty-four suttas,
Gathered into three divisions,
This first Nikāya is named Dīgha Nikāya,
According to its meaning."

Why is this Nikāya called Dīgha Nikāya? It is called Dīgha Nikāya because it is a collection (samūha) and an abode (nivāsa) of suttas of long (dīgha) length. For a collection and an abode are called 'Nikāya'. In the passage, "Bhikkhus, I do not see any other single group (nikāya) so diverse as the animal kingdom," and in worldly usage such as 'Poṇika-nikāya' (abode of the Poṇikas) and 'Cikkhallika-nikāya' (abode of the Cikkhallikas), the word 'Nikāya' denotes both collection and place. The meaning of 'Nikāya' in the remaining Nikāyas should be understood in the same way.

What is the Majjhima Nikāya? It consists of one hundred and fifty-two suttas of middle length, such as the Mūlapariyāya Sutta, collected into fifteen divisions. It should be noted that the Nikāya which has one hundred and fifty-two suttas and is gathered into fifteen divisions is the Majjhima Nikāya.

What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? It consists of seven thousand, seven hundred and sixty-two suttas, such as the Oghataraṇa Sutta, taught by way of the Devatā Saṃyutta and so on...
24:
“Monks, just as these animals [are diverse]” (Saṃ. Ni. 2.100). This scripture and examples such as the Poṇika-nikāya and Cikkhallika-nikāya serve as evidence from both the Dispensation (Sāsana) and worldly texts that the word 'Nikāya' refers to a collection or a group, as well as a dwelling place. In the same way, the meaning of the term 'Nikāya' for the remaining Nikāyas should also be understood.

What is the Majjhima Nikāya? It consists of one hundred and fifty-two (152) suttas, including the Mūlapariyāya Sutta and others, which are of medium length and are categorized into fifteen vaggas (chapters).

“The Nikāya in which there are one hundred and fifty suttas plus two suttas, and which is comprised of fifteen vaggas, is called the Majjhima Nikāya.”

What is the Saṃyutta Nikāya? It consists of seven thousand seven hundred and sixty-two (7,762) suttas, such as the Oghataraṇa Sutta, preached by way of the Devatā-saṃyutta and so forth.

“Seven thousand suttas, seven hundred suttas, and sixty-two suttas; this is the collection of the Saṃyutta Nikāya.”

What is the Aṅguttara Nikāya? It consists of nine thousand five hundred and fifty-seven (9,557) suttas, such as the Cittapariyādāna Sutta, preached by way of increasing by one limb (numerical unit) at a time.

“Nine thousand suttas, five hundred suttas, and fifty-seven suttas; this is the count in the Aṅguttara Nikāya.”

What is the Khuddaka Nikāya? It includes the entire Vinaya Piṭaka, the Abhidhamma Piṭaka, and the fifteen divisions previously mentioned such as the Khuddakapāṭha. Excluding the four great Nikāyas, all other words of the Buddha are to be understood as the Khuddaka Nikāya.

“Excluding these four Nikāyas starting with the Dīgha, the remaining words of the Buddha are known as the Khuddaka Nikāya.”

Thus, there are five divisions by way of Nikāya.

How are there nine divisions by way of Aṅga (limbs)? All these words of the Buddha are divided into nine types: Sutta, Geyya, Veyyākaraṇa, Gāthā, Udāna, Itivuttaka, Jātaka, Abbhutadhamma, and Vedalla. Among these, the Ubhatovibhaṅga, Niddesa, Khandhaka, Parivāra, and the Maṅgala Sutta, Ratana Sutta, Nālaka Sutta, and Tuvaṭṭaka Sutta in the Sutta Nipāta, as well as other discourses named Sutta...
25:
...the words of the Tathāgata should be known as Sutta. All suttas containing verses should be known as Geyya. Specifically, the entire Sagāthā-vagga in the Saṃyutta Nikāya, the entire Abhidhamma Piṭaka, suttas without verses, and any other words of the Buddha not included in the other eight limbs should be known as Veyyākaraṇa. The Dhammapada, Theragāthā, Therīgāthā, and the pure verses in the Sutta Nipāta not bearing the name 'Sutta' should be known as Gāthā. The eighty-two suttas associated with verses born of joy and wisdom should be known as Udāna. The one hundred and ten suttas beginning with the method “Vuttaṃ hetaṃ Bhagavatā” (Thus it was said by the Blessed One) should be known as Itivuttaka. The five hundred and fifty birth stories, such as the Apaṇṇaka Jātaka, should be known as Jātaka. All suttas associated with marvelous and extraordinary qualities, such as those beginning with “Monks, these four wonderful and marvelous qualities are found in Ānanda,” should be known as Abbhutadhamma. All suttas asked and answered after gaining wisdom and satisfaction, such as the Cūḷavedalla, Mahāvedalla, Sammādiṭṭhi, Sakkapañha, Saṅkhārabhājanīya, and Mahāpuṇṇama Suttas, should be known as Vedalla. Thus, there are nine divisions by way of Aṅga.

How are there eighty-four thousand divisions by way of Dhammakkhandha (Dhamma aggregates)? All these words of the Buddha are as follows:
“I received eighty-two thousand from the Buddha,
And two thousand from the monks;
Thus, the Dhamma that are present in me
Are eighty-four thousand.” (Thus said Venerable Ānanda).
In this way, there are eighty-four thousand divisions by way of the Dhamma aggregates shown. Among them, a sutta with a single connection (topic) is one Dhamma aggregate. In a sutta with multiple connections, the Dhamma aggregates are counted by the number of connections. In verse compositions, a question asked is one Dhamma aggregate, and the answer is another. In the Abhidhamma, each analysis of a Triad (Tika) or Dyad (Duka), and each analysis of a thought-process (Cittavāra), is one Dhamma aggregate. In the Vinaya, there are the Basis (Vatthu), the Matrix (Mātikā), the Word-analysis (Padabhājanīya), the Intermediate Offense (Antarāpatti), the Offense (Āpatti), the Non-offense (Anāpatti), and the Triad-sections (Tikaccheda). There, each portion should be known as one Dhamma aggregate. Thus, there are eighty-four thousand divisions by way of Dhammakkhandha.

In this way, the words of the Buddha, which are of one kind by way of the single taste (rasa) of liberation, and of two or more kinds by way of Dhamma, Vinaya, etc., were categorized by the group of masters of the senses led by Venerable Mahākassapa during the Council. They defined the distinctions, saying: “This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya, this is the first word of the Buddha, this is the middle word, this is the last word; this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Suttanta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīgha Nikāya... this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these are the nine limbs such as Sutta; these are the eighty-four thousand Dhamma aggregates.” Not only that, they also defined various methods of collection found in the three Piṭakas, such as the Uddāna-saṅgaha, Vagga-saṅgaha, Peyyāla-saṅgaha, and Paṇṇāsa-saṅgaha, and completed the Council in seven months. At the conclusion of the Council, Venerable Mahākassapa [ensured] this Dispensation of the Buddha would last for five thousand years...
26:
"This is the Dhamma, this is the Vinaya; this is the first word of the Buddha, this is the middle word of the Buddha, this is the last word of the Buddha; this is the Vinaya Piṭaka, this is the Suttanta Piṭaka, this is the Abhidhamma Piṭaka; this is the Dīgha Nikāya ... this is the Khuddaka Nikāya; these are the nine limbs such as the Suttas; these are the eighty-four thousand aggregates of Dhamma." Having defined these distinctions in this manner, they conducted the Council.

They did not only conduct the Council for these distinctions alone; they also defined and conducted the Council for seven months regarding various other categories of compilation found in the three Piṭakas, such as the Uddānasaṅgaha, Vaggasaṅgaha, Peyyālasaṅgaha, the Nipātasaṅgaha including the Ekanipāta and Dukanipāta, the Saṃyuttasaṅgaha, and the Paṇṇāsasaṅgaha.

At the conclusion of the Council, with the thought, "Venerable Mahākassapa has made this Dispensation of the Ten-Powered One capable of lasting for a period of five thousand years," this great earth, as if giving a cry of 'Sādhu' in great joy, shook, trembled, and quaked in many ways up to the water's edge; it quaked violently, rising up again and again; it quaked, sinking and rising; it quaked violently in various ways, swaying towards the four directions. Many wonders also became manifest. This is known as the First Great Council.

Regarding that First Council, it is said in the world:
"Because it was performed by five hundred Arahants, it is called 'Pañcasatā' (The Five Hundred);
And because it was performed only by Elders, it is called 'Therikā' (The Elders')."
27:
## 1. Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta
## Commentary on the Discussion of the Wanderers
While this First Great Council was being held, at the conclusion of the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka, Venerable Mahākassapa, inquiring about the Brahmajāla Sutta—the first sutta of the Dīgha Nikāya, which is the first Nikāya in the Suttanta Piṭaka—asked: "Friend Ānanda, where was the Brahmajāla Sutta spoken?" At the end of such words, Venerable Ānanda, wishing to make clear everything—where it was spoken and on whose account it was spoken—said: "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard), and so forth. Therefore, it is said: "The beginning of the prologue of the Brahmajāla Sutta, starting with 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', was spoken by Venerable Ānanda at the time of the First Great Council."

In that phrase, "Evaṃ" is an indeclinable (nipāta). "Me" and the others are nouns (nāma). In the phrase "Paṭipanno hoti," "paṭi" is a prefix (upasarga) and "hoti" is a verb (ākhyāta). In this manner, the division of words should first be understood.

As for the meaning, the word "Evaṃ" has many distinctions of meaning, such as simile (upamā), instruction (upadesa), approval (sampahaṃsana), blame (garahaṇa), acceptance of words (vacanasampaṭiggaha), manner (ākāra), indication (nidassana), and emphasis (avadhāraṇa).

This is true. In passages such as "A mortal thus born should do much good," it occurs in the sense of a simile. In passages such as "Thus you should advance, thus you should retreat," it occurs in the sense of instruction (upadesa). In passages such as "So it is, Blessed One; so it is, Sugata," it occurs in the sense of approval (sampahaṃsana). In passages such as "This wretch speaks thus and in this manner of the virtue of that shaven-headed monkling," it occurs in the sense of blame (garahaṇa). In passages such as "'Yes, Bhante,' those monks replied to the Blessed One," it occurs in the sense of acceptance of words (vacanasampaṭiggaha). In passages such as "Bhante, I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a manner," it occurs in the sense of manner (ākāra). "Come, young man, go to where the Venerable Ānanda is, and having approached, ask in my name whether Venerable Ānanda is free from illness, free from disease, light in body, strong, and living comfortably. Ask: 'The young man Subha, son of Todeyya, asks whether Venerable Ānanda is free from illness, free from disease, light in body, strong, and living comfortably.' And speak thus: 'It would be good if the Venerable Ānanda [would come] to where...'
28:
In the sense of illustration (nidassana), it is found in such passages as: "Out of compassion, may you go to the house of the young man Subha, the son of the Brahmin Todeyya." In the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa), it is found in such passages as: "What do you think, Kālāmas? Are these things wholesome or unwholesome?" "Unwholesome, Bhante." "Are they blameworthy or blameless?" "Blameworthy, Bhante." "Are they censured or praised by the wise?" "Censured by the wise, Bhante." "When undertaken and followed to completion, do they lead to harm and suffering, or not? What is your view on this?" "Bhante, when undertaken and followed to completion, they lead to harm and suffering; such is our view on this." In this phrase 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ,' this word 'evaṃ' should be understood in the senses of manner (ākāra), illustration (nidassana), and emphasis (avadhāraṇa).

Among these three senses, through the sense of manner (ākāra), the word 'evaṃ' clarifies this meaning: Who is capable of knowing in every aspect the words of the Blessed One—which are subtle and profound through various methods, arisen from many dispositions, endowed with meaning and phrasing, possessing diverse miracles, and deep in terms of Dhamma, meaning, teaching, and penetration—which reach the ear-path of all beings according to their respective languages? Indeed, even though one generates the desire to hear with all one's strength, 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' shows that 'I, too, have heard it in only this one manner.'

Through the sense of illustration (nidassana): Freeing himself from being a 'thief of Dhamma' by saying, 'I am not self-enlightened, I have not realized this myself,' he indicates the entire sutta to be spoken now by saying, 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ'—'I, too, have heard it thus.'

Through the sense of emphasis (avadhāraṇa): The Blessed One said, 'Monks, among my monk disciples who are of great learning, Ānanda is the foremost; among those who possess mindfulness, who possess a clear course of mind, who possess energy, and who are attendants, Ānanda is the foremost.' Likewise, the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, praised him saying, 'Venerable Ānanda is skilled in meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in phrasing, skilled in linguistics, and skilled in the sequence of what precedes and follows.' In accordance with being so praised, showing his own power of retention, he generates the desire to hear in beings: 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ'—'I have heard it in this way only.' It should be understood that the sutta heard is neither deficient nor excessive in meaning or phrasing; it is exactly like this and not otherwise.

The word 'me' is seen in three senses. Indeed: In passages such as 'Food chanted over with verses is not to be eaten by me (me),' it is used in the sense of 'mayā' (by me). In passages such as 'Bhante, may the Blessed One teach me (me) the Dhamma in brief,' it is used in the sense of 'mayhaṃ' (to/for me). In passages such as 'Monks, be heirs of my (me) Dhamma,' it is used in the sense of 'mama' (of my/mine).
29:
In the passage 'Monks, be [heirs] of my (me) [Dhamma]' and so forth (Majjhima Nikāya 1.29), 'me' has the sense of 'of mine' (mama). In this context, however, both meanings—'it was heard by me' (mayā) and 'my (mama) hearing [occurred]'—are appropriate.

The word 'sutaṃ,' whether with a prefix or without, has many various meanings such as going, renown, wetness, accumulation, devotion, cognizable by the ear, and cognized through the ear-door. Indeed: In 'senāya pasuto' (one who has gone to the army), it means 'one who goes.' In 'sutadhammassa passato' (one who sees the renowned Dhamma), it means 'renowned.' In 'avassutā avassutassa' (the wet one for the wet one), it means 'wetness.' In 'tumhehi puññaṃ pasutaṃ anappakaṃ' (much merit has been accumulated by you), it means 'accumulated.' In 'ye jhānapasutā dhီrā' (those wise ones who are devoted to jhāna), it means 'devoted to.' In 'diṭṭhaṃ sutaṃ mutaṃ' (seen, heard, sensed), it means 'cognized by the ear.' In 'sutadharo sutasannicayo' (one who remembers what has been heard, a storer of what has been heard), it means 'one who remembers the Dhamma cognized through the ear-door.' In this context, the word 'sutaṃ' means 'retained through the ear-door' or 'the act of retaining.' If the word 'me' has the sense of 'by me' (mayā), it is appropriate as 'Thus it was retained by me through the ear-door.' If it has the sense of 'of mine' (mama), it is appropriate as 'Thus my retaining through the ear-door [occurred].'

Thus, among these three words, 'evaṃ' is an indication of the function of consciousness such as ear-consciousness. 'Me' is an indication of the person endowed with the aforementioned consciousness. 'Sutaṃ' is an indication of reception that is neither deficient, nor excessive, nor distorted, by way of rejecting non-hearing. Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is an expression of the occurrence of that cognitive process (viññāṇavīthi), which proceeds through the ear-door, upon the object in various manners. 'Me' is an expression of the self. 'Sutaṃ' is an expression of the Dhamma. The summary here is: 'By the cognitive process occurring upon the object in various manners, I have performed no other task but this; I have heard this Dhamma.'

Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is an expression of the Dhamma to be indicated. 'Me' is an expression of the person. 'Sutaṃ' is an expression of the person's task. The meaning is: 'The sutta which I shall indicate, I have heard it thus.'

Furthermore, 'evaṃ' is an indication of the various manners of that mental continuum (cittasantāna) by which the various meanings and phrasings are grasped. 'Evaṃ' is a designation of manner (ākārapaññatti). 'Me' is an indication of the agent (kattā). 'Sutaṃ' is an indication of the object (visaya). By this much...
30:
By means of the mental continuum occurring in various modes, the determination in grasping the object is made by the agent who possesses that mental continuum.

Alternatively, the word 'Evaṃ' (Thus) is an indication of the person's function. The word 'Sutaṃ' (Heard) is an indication of the function of consciousness. The word 'Me' (By me) is an indication of the person associated with both functions. The summary here is: 'I, the person endowed with the consciousness that has the function of hearing, and who has acquired the designation of the function of hearing by means of consciousness, have heard.'

Among those terms, the designations 'Evaṃ' and 'Me' are 'designations of the non-existent' (avijjamāna-paññatti) in terms of the ultimate sense (paramattha).
