For what is there in these ultimate realities that could receive the designation 'Evaṃ' or 'Me'? 'Sutaṃ', however, is a 'designation of the existent' (vijjamāna-paññatti). This is because the thing (sound) acquired here through the ear-door is clearly existent in the ultimate sense. Similarly, 'Evaṃ' and 'Me' are 'derivative designations' (upādā-paññatti) because they are spoken of in dependence on various phenomena. 'Sutaṃ' is a 'comparative designation' (upanidhā-paññatti) because it is spoken of in relation to things seen (diṭṭha) and so forth. Furthermore, by the word 'Evaṃ', non-delusion (asammoha) is shown. Indeed, one who is deluded is not capable of penetration in various ways. By the word 'Sutaṃ', the non-forgetfulness (asammosa) of what has been heard is shown. For one who has forgotten what was heard cannot later profess, 'I have heard.' Thus, through non-delusion, the perfection of wisdom (paññā) is achieved, and through non-forgetfulness, the perfection of mindfulness (sati) is achieved. Between them, through mindfulness preceded by wisdom, one is capable of retaining the phrasing (byañjana); through wisdom preceded by mindfulness, one is capable of penetrating the meaning (attha). Through being endowed with both capabilities, one is able to preserve the treasury of the Dhamma, which is complete in meaning and phrasing, thereby achieving the status of 'Treasurer of the Dhamma' (Dhamma-bhaṇḍāgārika).

Another method: By the word 'Evaṃ', wise attention (yoniso manasikāra) is shown. For one who applies unwise attention lacks penetration in various ways. By the word 'Sutaṃ', non-distraction (avikkhepa) is shown. For one with a distracted mind does not truly hear. This is true; a person with a distracted mind, even when being told something with full perfection, says, 'I did not hear, please say it again.' Here, through wise attention, one accomplishes right self-direction (attasammāpaṇidhi) and the state of having performed merit in the past (pubbe ca katapuññatā). This is because these are absent in one who has wrong self-direction or has not performed merit in the past. Through non-distraction, one accomplishes the hearing of the True Dhamma (saddhammassavana) and reliance on virtuous people (sappurisūpanissaya). For just as a distracted person cannot hear, so too there is no hearing for one who does not rely on virtuous people.
31:
In another way, because the word 'Evaṃ' (Thus) describes the various modes of the mental continuum through which the grasping of various meanings and phrasings occurs, it is called the 'description of various modes.' Such a noble mode is not possible for one who has not directed himself rightly or who has not performed merit in the past. Therefore, by this noble mode 'Evaṃ', he shows his own endowment with the last two 'wheels' (attasammāpaṇidhi and pubbe ca katapuññatā). By the word 'Sutaṃ' (Heard), in conjunction with the act of hearing, he shows his endowment with the first two 'wheels' (patirūpadesavāsa and sappurisūpanissaya). This is because hearing is not possible for one living in an unsuitable locality or for one devoid of reliance on virtuous people. Thus, by the accomplishment of the last two wheels, the purity of disposition (āsaya-suddhi) is achieved. By the accomplishment of the first two wheels, the purity of application (payoga-suddhi) is achieved. Through that purity of disposition, proficiency in realization (adhigama-byatti) is achieved; through purity of application, proficiency in the scriptures (āgama-byatti) is achieved. Thus, the words of the Venerable Ānanda, who is pure in application and disposition and endowed with scripture and realization, are like the dawn before the rising of the sun, or like wise attention before the arising of wholesome kamma. Desiring to place the introduction in its proper place as the precursor to the words of the Blessed One, he said, 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ' and so forth.

In another way, by the word 'Evaṃ', which shows various kinds of penetration, he shows his own endowment with the analytical knowledge of meanings (attha-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of expressions (paṭibhāna-paṭisambhidā). By the word 'Sutaṃ', which shows the penetration of the various types of things to be heard, he shows his endowment with the analytical knowledge of the Dhamma (dhamma-paṭisambhidā) and the analytical knowledge of language (nirutti-paṭisambhidā). Furthermore, by uttering the word 'Evaṃ', which shows wise attention, he shows: 'These teachings have been reflected upon by my mind and well-penetrated by view.' By uttering the word 'Sutaṃ', which shows the conjunction with hearing, he shows: 'Many teachings have been heard by me, retained, and practiced by speech.' By both of these, showing the completeness of meaning and phrasing, he inspires respect in the hearing. Because a person who does not listen respectfully to the Dhamma that is complete in meaning and phrasing remains outside of great benefit, he inspires respect and urges: 'This Dhamma should be heard with reverence.'

By the entire phrase 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', the Venerable Ānanda, not claiming the Dhamma proclaimed by the Tathāgata as his own, transcends the ground of the ignoble (asappurisa-bhūmi). By professing the status of a disciple, he enters the ground of the virtuous (sappurisa-bhūmi). Likewise, he raises his mind from the false Dhamma and establishes it in the True Dhamma. By showing, 'This was only heard by me; it is the word of that Blessed One alone,' he releases himself (from the charge of ignoble speech), points to the Teacher, attributes the words to the Victor (Jina), and establishes the Guide of the Dhamma (dhamma-netti).
32: Alternatively, by the words "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" (Thus have I heard), [the speaker] admits that this is not his own invention but reveals the words of the Buddha that already existed previously—"I myself heard and received this teaching in the presence of the Blessed One, who is courageous through the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa), who possesses the ten powers (dasabala), who stands in the supreme position, who utters the courageous sound of the Dhamma like the roar of a lion, who is the most excellent among all beings, the Lord of Dhamma, the King of Dhamma, the Sovereign of Dhamma, the Lamp of Dhamma, the Refuge of Dhamma, and who turns the noble Wheel of the True Dhamma, the Perfectly Self-Enlightened One. No doubt, hesitation, or uncertainty should be entertained regarding the meaning (attha), the text (dhamma), the word (pada), or the phrasing (byañjana) of this teaching." Thus, he destroys the lack of faith in this Dhamma among all devas and humans and produces the fulfillment of faith. Therefore, it is said: "Destroying lack of faith, increasing faith in the Dispensation; thus saying 'Evaṃ me sutaṃ', the disciple of Gotama (Venerable Ānanda) speaks." "Ekaṃ" refers to a numerical distinction. "Samayaṃ" refers to a designated time. "Ekaṃ samayaṃ" indicates an indefinite time. Among these words, the term samaya is found in the senses of: "concordance (samavāya), occasion (khaṇa), time (kāla), assembly (samūha), cause (hetu), view (diṭṭhi), attainment (paṭilābha), abandonment (pahāna), and penetration (paṭivedha)." This is true. In passages such as "Perhaps we might come tomorrow, depending on the time and concordance," it expresses the sense of concordance (samavāya). In passages such as "Monks, there is only one occasion and time (khaṇa) for living the holy life," it expresses the sense of occasion (khaṇa). In "hot time, sweltering time," it expresses the sense of time (kāla). In "There is a great assembly (samūha) in the forest," it expresses the sense of assembly (samūha). In "Bhaddāli, you did not penetrate the cause (samaya)..." it expresses the sense of cause (hetu). In "At that time, the wanderer Uggahamāna... lived in the Mallikā park... where views are discussed," it expresses the sense of view (diṭṭhi). "The benefit obtained in the present life and the benefit in the life to come; because of attaining both benefits, the wise one is called a Paṇḍita."
33: In such phrases, it means attainment (paṭilābha). In phrases such as "By the complete abandonment of conceit, he has made an end of suffering," it means abandonment (pahāna). In phrases such as "the sense of oppression of suffering, the sense of being conditioned, the sense of burning, the sense of change, and the sense of penetration," it means penetration (paṭivedha). However, in this Pali phrase (ekaṃ samayaṃ), the meaning of the word samaya is time (kāla). By this word samaya meaning time, it indicates one particular time among various divisions of time such as year, season, month, fortnight (pakkha), night, day, morning, midday, evening, the first watch, the middle watch, the last watch, and a moment (muhutta). In this context of ekaṃ samayaṃ, whichever Sutta was taught in whichever year, season, month, fortnight, part of the night, or part of the day—all of that was well known and well distinguished by the wisdom of the Elder Ānanda. However, if he were to say, "Thus have I heard: in such a year, in such a season, in such a month, in such a fortnight, in such a part of the night, or in such a part of the day," it would not be easy to maintain or memorize, nor to recite oneself, nor to have others recite; and the words spoken would be too numerous. Therefore, summarizing that meaning with just one phrase, he said "ekaṃ samayaṃ" (at one time). Alternatively, there are many distinct times of the Blessed One that are very well known among devas and humans, such as the time of conception, the time of birth, the time of spiritual urgency (saṃvega), the time of the great renunciation, the time of practicing austerities, the time of the victory over Māra, the time of enlightenment, the time of dwelling in the happiness of the present life, the time of teaching the Dhamma, and the time of final Nibbāna. Among these times, it indicates one particular time known as the time of teaching. Between the times of the function of wisdom and the function of compassion, it refers to the time of performing the function of compassion; between the times of practicing for one's own benefit and the benefit of others, it refers to the time of practicing for the benefit of others; between the two duties of those assembled, it refers to the time of Dhamma talk; between the times of teaching and practice, it refers to the time of teaching. Referring to one of these times, he said "ekaṃ samayaṃ." Why is it that in this phrase (ekaṃ samayaṃ), the accusative case (upayoga-vacana) is used, unlike in the Abhidhamma where the locative case (bhumma-vacana) is used as in "At which time (yasmiṃ samaye) the sense-sphere...", or in other Sutta passages as in "At which time, monks, a monk secluded from sensual pleasures...", or in the Vinaya where the instrumental case (karaṇa-vacana) is used as in "At that time (tena samayena) the Blessed One..."? It is because just as those cases (locative and instrumental) are appropriate in those contexts, this case (accusative) is appropriate for the meaning here.
34:
Because of the appropriateness of the meaning (it is said thus). In that Abhidhamma and in other Sutta passages besides this, the locative sense (adhikaraṇattha) and the sense of defining a state by another state (bhāvena bhāvalakkhaṇattha) are appropriate. The term 'samaya' (occasion), which has the meaning of time and the meaning of a group, is the locative sense. By the occurrence of the 'samaya'—known as the moment (khaṇa), the conjunction of conditions (samavāya), and the cause (hetu)—of the phenomena such as contact (phassa) and others taught in those various Abhidhamma and Suttas, the occurrence of those phenomena is marked. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the designation is made there with the locative case (sattamī-vibhatti).

In the Vinaya Piṭaka, however, the causal sense (hetuattha) and the instrumental sense (karaṇattha) are appropriate. Even individuals such as the Venerable Sāriputta and others find it difficult to know the occasion when a training rule (sikkhāpada) was prescribed. While prescribing the training rules by means of that occasion, which serves as the cause and the instrument, and while looking towards the reason for the prescription of the training rules, the Blessed One dwelt in various places. Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the designation is made in that Vinaya with the instrumental case (karaṇa-vibhatti).

In this phrase 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' and in other phrases of such nature, the sense of continuous duration (accantasaṃyogattha) is appropriate. For as long as the Blessed One taught this Sutta or another, for that entire duration, He dwelt without interruption in the 'dwelling of compassion' (karuṇāvihāra). Therefore, to illuminate that meaning, the designation is made here with the accusative case (dutiyā-vibhatti).

For that reason, it is said:
'Looking towards those respective meanings, the word samaya is stated in other places (Abhidhamma and Vinaya) in the locative and instrumental cases; but here (in the Sutta), it is stated in the accusative case.'

However, the ancient teachers explain: whether it is said as 'tasmiṃ samaye', 'tena samayena', or 'ekaṃ samayaṃ', these are merely differences in expression; in all instances, only the locative sense (adhikaraṇattha) is intended. Therefore, even when 'ekaṃ samayaṃ' is said, the meaning should be understood only as 'ekasmiṃ samaye'.

'Bhagavā' means a venerable person (garu). In the world, a venerable person is called 'Bhagavā'. And this Blessed One, because He is distinguished by all qualities, is the venerable one of all beings; therefore, He should be known as 'Bhagavā'. The ancient teachers also said:
'The word Bhagavā is the most noble; the word Bhagavā is supreme.
He is the Teacher (garu) endowed with qualities deserving of reverence; therefore He is called Bhagavā.'

Furthermore:
'He is called Bhagavā because He is fortunate (bhāgyavā), He has broken the defilements (bhaggavā), He is endowed with qualities (yutto), He is a possessor of analytical divisions (vibhattavā), He is a partaker of the Dhamma (bhattavā), He has renounced going to the three worlds (vantagamano), and He has destroyed the causes of existence (bhavesu).'
35:
By virtue of this verse, the detailed meaning of the word 'Bhagavā' should be understood. That meaning has already been stated in the 'Buddhānussati-niddesa' of the Visuddhimagga.

In this introductory passage, by the words 'evaṃ me sutaṃ' (thus have I heard), showing the Dhamma as it was heard, the Dhamma-body (dhamma-kāya) of the Blessed One is made manifest. By showing this, he comforts those people who are distressed by not seeing the Teacher, saying: 'This Dispensation is not one whose Teacher has passed away; this very Dhamma is your Teacher.'

By the words 'ekaṃ samayaṃ Bhagavā', showing that the Blessed One was no longer present at that time, he establishes the final passing away (parinibbāna) of the form-body (rūpa-kāya). By showing this, he causes spiritual urgency (saṃvega) in those people who are intoxicated with the pride of life, saying: 'Even that Blessed One, who taught such Noble Dhamma, who possessed the Ten Powers, and whose body was like a mass of diamond, has passed away; what hope for life can others have?' and he generates effort in the True Dhamma (saddhamma).

By reciting 'evaṃ', he indicates the accomplishment of the teaching (desanā-sampatti). By 'me sutaṃ', he indicates the accomplishment of the disciple (sāvaka-sampatti). By 'ekaṃ samayaṃ', he indicates the accomplishment of time (kāla-sampatti). By 'Bhagavā', he indicates the accomplishment of the teacher (desaka-sampatti).

In the phrase 'antarā ca Rājagahaṃ antarā ca Nāḷandaṃ', the word 'antarā' is found in the senses of cause, moment, mind, middle, interval, and so on. In the passages such as 'Who besides the Tathāgata could know that cause?' and 'People gather and consult, what is the cause between me and you?', the word 'antarā' is used in the sense of cause. In the passage 'Venerable sir, I saw a certain woman washing dishes at the moment (khaṇa) of a lightning flash', it is in the sense of a moment. In the passage 'In whose mind (citta) there are no angers', it is in the sense of the mind. In the passage 'He reached completion in the middle (vemajjha) between the beginning and the end', it is in the sense of the middle. In the passage 'Monks, this Tapodā river flows from the interval (vivara) between two great hells', it is in the sense of an interval. Here, however, it is used in the sense of an interval; therefore, the meaning should be understood as 'in the interval between Rājagaha and Nāḷandā'. Because it is associated with the word 'antarā', the accusative case (dutiyā-vibhatti) is used. In such places, grammarians usually use the word 'antarā' only once, as in 'antarā gāmañca nadiñca yāti' (he goes between the village and the river), and that word must also be connected with the second term; if not connected, the accusative case cannot be attained. Here, however, (Venerable Ānanda) spoke by directly connecting it twice.
36:
"Addhānamaggappaṭipanno hoti" means he had entered upon a journey known as a long road; it means a "long journey." Because it is stated in the Vibhaṅga of the Addhānagamanasamaya (the time of traveling a long distance), "One should eat intending to travel half a league (yojana)," etc., even a journey of half a league is called addhānamagga. From Rājagaha to Nāḷandā, however, it is only one league.

In the phrase "mahatā bhikkhusaṅghena saddhiṃ," "mahatā" means great either because of the greatness of qualities or because of the greatness of number. That community of monks was great in quality because they were endowed with qualities such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā), etc. It was also great in number because it consisted of five hundred. A community of monks is called "bhikkhusaṅgho"; [he was] together with that community of monks. It means together with the group of recluses (samaṇagaṇa) who are united by the commonality of view (diṭṭhi) and virtue (sīla). "Saddhiṃ" means together.

In the phrase "pañcamattehi bhikkhusatehi," they are called "pañcamattāni" because they have a measure of five. "Mattā" means measure (pamāṇa). Therefore, just as it is said, "one who knows the measure in food (bhojane mattaññū)," here too, the meaning should be understood as "the measure of five of those hundreds of monks." Hundreds of monks are "bhikkhusatāni"; [he was] together with those five hundred monks.

In the phrase "suppiyo pi kho paribbājako," "Suppiya" is his name. The word "pi" (also) expresses the inclusion of a person who shares the same nature of traveling on the road. The word "kho" is a particle used for euphonic connection of words. "Paribbājaka" refers to a wandering ascetic who wears clothes, a disciple of the teacher Sañjaya. This means: "When the Blessed One entered upon that long journey, the wanderer Suppiya also entered upon it." Here, the word "hoti" (is) expresses the past tense.

In the phrase "saddhiṃ antevāsinā brahmadattena māṇavena," he is called "antevāsī" because he dwells near. It means a disciple who moves about and stays in the vicinity. "Brahmadatta" is his name. "Māṇava" can mean a being, a thief, or a young man.

Those young men (beings) who, urged by the divine messengers (devadūta), are negligent,
They, as humans who have reached a low state of existence, sorrow for a long time.
37:
In the preceding [verses] etc., a being is called 'māṇava.' In such passages as 'They meet with youths (māṇavehi), both those who have done their work and those who have not,' a thief is called 'māṇava.' In such passages as 'Ambaṭṭha the youth (māṇava), Aṅgaka the youth (māṇava),' a young man is called 'māṇava.' Here too, this very meaning [of young man] applies. This is what is meant: together with the young pupil named Brahmadatta. 'Tatra' means on that long journey, or else between those two people. 'Sudaṃ' is a mere particle. In the phrase 'anekapariyāyena,' the word 'pariyāya' occurs in the senses of turn, the Dhamma that is taught, and cause. In such passages as 'Ananda, whose turn (pariyāyo) is it today to exhort the nuns?' it occurs in the sense of turn. In such passages as 'Remember it as the Honey-ball Discourse (pariyāyo),' it occurs in the sense of the Dhamma that is taught. In such passages as 'By this reason (pariyāyena) too, Prince, let it be so,' it occurs in the sense of cause. This word 'pariyāya' here also occurs in the sense of cause; therefore, the meaning here is 'by more than one various cause,' which means 'by many reasons.'

'Buddhassa avaṇṇaṃ bhāsati' means speaking in dispraise of the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is free from fault and endowed with immeasurable virtues. [He says:] 'In the world, the act of showing respect such as saluting those who are great by birth is called "the essence of harmony" (sāmaggirasa); that act does not exist in the recluse Gotama. Therefore, the recluse Gotama is one without the essence of harmony, one without enjoyment (nibbhoga), a teacher of non-action (akiriyavāda), an annihilationist (ucchedavāda), one who is loathsome (jegucchī), a subverter (venayika), an ascetic (tapassī), and one who is free from rebirth (apagabbha). The recluse Gotama does not have any superhuman state (uttarimanussadhamma), any distinction in knowledge and vision worthy of the noble ones (alamariyañāṇadassana-visesa). The recluse Gotama teaches a Dhamma that is hammered out by logic (takkapariyāhata), followed by investigation (vīmaṃsānucarita), and self-intuition (sayaṃpaṭibhāna). The recluse Gotama is not omniscient (sabbaññū), not a knower of worlds (lokavidū), not unsurpassed (anuttara), and not the supreme person (aggapuggala).' Thus, speaking of various improper reasons as if they were reasons, he speaks dispraise, fault, and blame in various ways.

Just as he speaks dispraise of the Buddha, so too of the Dhamma, by taking various improper reasons as reasons: 'The Dhamma of the recluse Gotama is badly proclaimed (durakkhāta), badly understood (duppaṭivedita), not leading out [of suffering] (aniyyānika), and not leading to peace (anupasamasamvattanika).' Thus he speaks dispraise in various ways.
38:
Just as he disparaged the Dhamma, he also spoke dispraise of the Saṅgha in various ways, citing whatever baseless reasons as if they were reasons: "The community of disciples of the ascetic Gotama practices wrongly, practices crookedly, practices a way that is contrary [to the truth], a way that is not in accordance [with the Dhamma], a way that is inconsistent with the Dhamma."

However, his student, the youth Brahmadatta, thought: "Our teacher offends the Noble Ones who should not be offended; he treads upon those who should not be trodden upon. This teacher of ours, like one swallowing fire, like one grasping the blade of a sword with his hand, like one wishing to break Mount Sineru with his fist, like one playing on a row of saw teeth, or like one grasping a fierce elephant in rut with his hand, will come to ruin and destruction because he speaks dispraise of the Triple Gem, which is worthy of praise. Even if the teacher treads upon excrement, fire, thorns, or a cobra, or climbs onto a stake, or eats deadly poison, or falls into a stream of salty and bitter water, or leaps into the abyss of hell, the student should not follow and do all those things. Beings are owners of their kamma; they go to a destination according to their own kamma. A father does not go [to a destination] because of the kamma of his son, nor a son because of the kamma of his father; a mother not because of the son, nor a son because of the mother; a brother not because of the sister, nor a sister because of the brother; a teacher not because of the student, nor a student because of the teacher's kamma. My teacher speaks dispraise of the Triple Gem; indeed, the reviling of Noble Ones (ariyūpavāda) is a grave offense." Thus, reflecting wisely, extricating himself from the kamma of reviling Noble Ones, and refuting his teacher's doctrine, he pointed out only the true reasons and began to speak the praise of the Triple Gem in many ways, just as a wise man of good family would do. Therefore, it was said: "But the youth Brahmadatta, the student of Suppiya the wanderer, spoke in many ways in praise of the Buddha, in praise of the Dhamma, and in praise of the Saṅgha."

In that context, the word "vaṇṇa" is seen in the senses of shape (saṇṭhāna), caste (jāti), visual object (rūpāyatana), cause (kāraṇa), measure (pamāṇa), quality (guṇa), praise (pasaṃsā), and so on. Among these, in passages such as "having created a great shape of a king of snakes," it is called "vaṇṇa" in the sense of shape. In passages such as "Only the Brahmin is the superior caste (vaṇṇa), other castes are inferior," it is called "vaṇṇa" in the sense of caste. In passages such as "endowed with the highest beauty of complexion (vaṇṇa-pokkharatā)," it is called "vaṇṇa" in the sense of visual object.
39:
In passages such as: "I do not carry it away, nor do I break it; I only smell the lotus from afar. Why then am I called a 'scent-thief' (gandhattheno)?" the word vaṇṇa means cause (kāraṇa). In passages such as: "There are three measures (vaṇṇa) for a bowl," it means measure (pamāṇa). In passages such as: "O householder, when were these qualities (vaṇṇa) of the ascetic Gotama composed by you?" it means quality (guṇa). In passages such as: "He speaks the praise (vaṇṇa) of one worthy of praise," it means praise (pasaṃsā). Here, however, both quality and praise should be taken. This youth Brahmadatta, pointing out various true reasons, spoke praise associated with the qualities of the Triple Gem in many ways.

Therein, the praise of the Buddha should be understood by such methods as: "That Blessed One is such: he is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One..." and "Monks, whatever persons have confidence in the Buddha, they have confidence in the foremost," and "Monks, one person arising in the world arises... peerless, the equal of the unequaled." The praise of the Dhamma should be understood by such methods as: "The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One," and "The uprooting of attachment, the cutting off of the round of suffering," and "Monks, whatever persons have confidence in the Noble Eightfold Path, they have confidence in the foremost Dhamma." The praise of the Saṅgha should be understood by such methods as: "The community of disciples of the Blessed One has practiced well," and "Monks, whatever persons have confidence in the Saṅgha, they have confidence in the foremost Saṅgha."

A capable Dhamma-preacher should manifest the praise of the Buddha and others by delving with wisdom into the five Nikāyas, the ninefold teaching of the Teacher, and the eighty-four thousand units of Dhamma. In manifesting the qualities of the Triple Gem in this way, such a Dhamma-preacher cannot be said to be one who plunges into a place that is not a landing-place. Indeed, in such matters, the intellectual power of a Dhamma-preacher is to be known. The youth Brahmadatta, however, spoke the praise of the Triple Gem according to his own capacity, which was connected merely to what he had heard.

"Thus these two, teacher and student" means those two, the teacher and the student. "Of one another" means of each other (the teacher of the student, and the student of the teacher). "Speaking in direct opposition" means that without avoiding each other even slightly, they directly spoke various opposing views many times. When the teacher spoke dispraise of the Triple Gem, the student spoke praise; when the former spoke dispraise again, the latter spoke praise again. In this way, the teacher repeatedly spoke dispraise of the Triple Gem, like one driving a poisonous wooden peg into a heartwood plank. The student, however, repeatedly spoke the praise of the Triple Gem, like one driving out that peg with a peg made of gold, silver, and rubies. Therefore, it is said, "speaking in direct opposition." "Following closely behind the Blessed One and the community of monks" means following right behind them without letting the Blessed One and the community of monks out of their sight.
40:
The teacher repeatedly spoke in dispraise of the Triple Gem, as if repeatedly striking a poisonous wooden peg into a piece of heartwood. The student, however, repeatedly spoke in praise of the Triple Gem, as if removing that peg with one made of gold, silver, and gems. Therefore, it is said, "they spoke in direct opposition to each other."

"Following close behind the Blessed One, following close behind the Saṅgha of monks" means following without losing sight of the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks, following by way of their physical postures, and following while looking up with their heads raised.

Why did the Blessed One set out on that journey? Why did Suppiya follow? And why did he speak in dispraise of the Triple Gem? At that time, the Blessed One, having stayed in one of the eighteen great monasteries around the city of Rājagaha, performed his morning bodily ablutions and, surrounded by the Saṅgha of monks, entered Rājagaha for alms at the time of the alms round. On that day, after ensuring that the Saṅgha of monks obtained alms easily, and having returned from the alms round after the meal, he had the monks take their bowls and robes and, saying, "I will go to Nāḷandā," he departed from Rājagaha and set out on that journey. Suppiya also, at that time, was staying in a certain park of the wanderers around Rājagaha and, surrounded by a group of wanderers, went for alms in Rājagaha. He too, on that day, after ensuring that his group of wanderers obtained alms easily and having finished his morning meal, had the wanderers take their requisites and, saying, "I will go to Nāḷandā," followed behind, unaware that the Blessed One had set out on that same path. Had he known, he would not have followed. As he was going along unknowingly, he raised his neck and looked, and he saw the Blessed One, magnificent with the glory of a Buddha, like a moving golden mountain peak wrapped in red blankets.

At that time, it is said, the six-colored rays (chabbaṇṇaraṃsi) emanating from the body of the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) raced to and fro in the surrounding area of about eighty cubits, like scattered jewels, jeweled garlands, and jeweled powder; like a golden cloth beautiful with spread-out jewels; like being poured with molten red gold; like a place crowded with falling meteors; like Kaṇikāra flowers scattered without interval; like cinnabar powder tossed by the force of the wind; and like the spreading and flashing brilliance of rainbows, lightning, and clusters of stars, so did that forest interior become.
41:
Furthermore, the body of the Blessed One, being repeatedly adorned with the eighty minor marks (anubyañjana), was more beautiful than—as if mocking with its own splendor—a pond with blooming paduma, uppala, and white lotuses; a Parijatta tree in full bloom; or the sky brightened by the radiance of the stars. The sequence of the thirty-two major marks (lakkhaṇa), magnificent with the circle of the fathom-wide aura, was as if it surpassed with its own glory the glory of thirty-two moons arranged in a garland, thirty-two suns in a garland, or thirty-two Cakkavatti kings, thirty-two Sakkas, and thirty-two Mahābrahmās placed in a row.

And the monks who stood surrounding the Blessed One were all of few desires, contented, secluded, not mingling with crowds, admonishers of evil, despisers of evil, givers of advice, patient of speech, and endowed with virtue, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation. In the midst of those monks, the Blessed One was like a golden pillar surrounded by a red blanket wall, like a golden boat in the midst of a cluster of red lotuses, like a mass of fire surrounded by coral railings, or like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars; he delighted the eyes of even beasts and birds, let alone those of gods and humans.

On that day, for the most part, eighty great elders (Mahātheras), draping their cloud-colored rag-robes over one shoulder and carrying their walking staffs, surrounded the Blessed One like scent-elephants well-armored, being those whose faults were gone, who had vomited out faults, who had destroyed the defilements, who had disentangled the tangle, and who had cut the bonds. The Blessed One, being himself free from lust, was surrounded by those free from lust; being himself free from hatred, by those free from hatred; being himself free from delusion, by those free from delusion; being himself free from craving, by those free from craving; being himself free from defilements, by those free from defilements; and being himself the Awakened One, he was surrounded by those who had awakened after him (Anubuddhas).

Like the stamen surrounded by petals, like the pericarp surrounded by stamens, like the Chaddanta elephant king surrounded by eight thousand elephants, like the Dhataraṭṭha swan king surrounded by ninety thousand swans, like a Cakkavatti king surrounded by his fourfold army, like Sakka the king of gods surrounded by the host of gods, or like Hārita Mahābrahmā surrounded by the host of Brahmas—with the inconceivable and incomparable Buddha-grace (Buddha-līlā) born of the power of merit accumulated over immeasurable time, he set out on that path like the moon across the sky.

Then, as soon as he saw the Blessed One walking with such incomparable Buddha-grace, and the monks with downcast eyes, serene faculties, and serene minds, who were venerating only the Blessed One who was like the full moon stationed in the upper sky, the wanderer looked at his own followers. They were hanging [their loads] on carrying poles...
42:
The followers of that Suppiya the Wanderer carried many burdens of requisites such as small benches, three-legged stools, peacock-feather fans, clay bowls, small bags, and water pots, which were broken or damaged in various ways. They spoke useless words such as, "This one's hands are beautiful, that one's feet are beautiful." They were loud-mouthed and spoke in a scattered manner. They were unseemly and not inspiring. Seeing his own followers, Suppiya the Wanderer felt remorse (vippaṭisāra).

Now, that wanderer should have spoken the praises of the Blessed One. However, he was always envious of the Blessed One because of the loss of gains and honors, as well as the loss of his following. Indeed, for other sectarians, gains and honors arose only as long as a Buddha had not appeared in the world. But from the time of the Buddha's appearance, their gains and honors declined. They became devoid of glory, like fireflies when the sun rises. Only when Upatissa and Kolita were ordained under the teacher Sañjaya did the wanderers have a large following; but when they left, that following was broken. Thus, for these two reasons, because this wanderer was always envious of the Blessed One, it should be understood that he spoke only dispraise of the Triple Gem, vomiting the poison of envy.

Then the Blessed One, together with the Saṅgha of monks, went to the King’s rest-house (Rājāgāraka) in the Ambalaṭṭhikā garden to stay for one night. As the Blessed One traveled with such Buddha-grace, he reached the gate of the Ambalaṭṭhikā garden in due course. Looking at the sun, he thought, "Now is not the time to go further; the sun is near setting," and he entered the King’s rest-house in the Ambalaṭṭhikā garden to stay for one night.

There, "Ambalaṭṭhikā" refers to the King’s garden. It is said that there was a young mango tree near its gate, and they called that tree "Ambalaṭṭhikā." Because it was not far from that mango tree, the garden also came to be known as "Ambalaṭṭhikā." That garden was well-endowed with shade and water, enclosed by a wall, with a well-fitted gate, and was as well-secured as a casket. In that garden, they had built a house decorated with various imaginative designs for the King’s amusement. That house is called the "Rājāgāraka."

Suppiya the Wanderer also looked at the sun at that place and thought, "Now is not the time to go; the wanderers, both young and old, are many, and this road is full of dangers from robbers, fierce spirits (yakkhas), and wild beasts. This Ascetic Gotama has entered the garden; of Ascetic Gotama..."
43:
...deities protect the place of residence. Let me also stay here for one night and go only tomorrow." Thus, he entered that very garden. After entering, the Saṅgha of monks performed their duties toward the Blessed One and then noted their respective places of residence. Suppiya the Wanderer also set down his wanderer’s requisites at one side of the garden and stayed there with his following. However, according to the sequence of words presented in the Pali text, it is said, "together with his pupil, the youth Brahmadatta."

While staying thus, that wanderer looked toward the Ten-Powered One (Dasabala) during the night. At that time, lamps were shining all around like scattered stars. The Blessed One sat in the middle, and the Saṅgha of monks surrounded the Blessed One. Among those monks, there was not even the movement of a hand or a foot, nor the sound of coughing or sneezing. This was because that assembly, for two reasons—due to their own well-trained discipline and out of reverence for the Teacher—sat as motionless as a lamp flame in a windless place. 

Suppiya the Wanderer, seeing that splendor of the Buddha’s assembly, looked back at his own following. Among his followers, some were tossing their hands, some their feet; some were talking incoherently in their sleep; some lay with tongues lolling out, drooling, grinding their teeth, making sounds like crows, and snoring loudly. Although that Suppiya the Wanderer should have spoken the praises of the Triple Gem, out of envy (issā) he again began only to disparage. The youth Brahmadatta, however, spoke praise in the manner already mentioned. Therefore, the entire passage beginning with "There too, Suppiya the Wanderer" should be understood. In that Pali, "tatrāpi" means "in that garden called Ambalaṭṭhikā as well."

"Sambahulānaṃ" means "many." In that context, according to the Vinaya method, three persons are called "sambahula." Beyond that, it is a "Saṅgha." According to the Sutta method, however, three are just called "three," and only from four onwards is it called "sambahula." Here, it should be understood as "sambahula" according to the Sutta method. "Maṇ膽alamāḷe": in some places, a gabled hall built with two peaks and a roof like a hamsa’s curve is called a "maṇ膽alamāḷa." In other places, an assembly hall built by surrounding a row of pillars with a single peak is also called a "maṇ膽alamāḷa." Here, however, it should be understood as a sitting hall. "Sannisinnānaṃ" is said in the sense of sitting down. "Sannipatitānaṃ" is said in the sense of having assembled (gathered together). In the phrase "ayaṃ saṅkhiyadhammo," speech is called "saṅkhiyā."
44:
## Talk (kathā) means the nature of talk. 'Arose' (udapādi) means it came to be. What is that talk? It is the talk beginning with, "Friends, it is wonderful!" In that context, 'wonderful' (acchariya) refers to something that does not happen constantly, like a blind person climbing a mountain. This is the method according to the science of grammar (sadda). According to the method of the Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), it is called 'acchariya' because it is worthy of snapping one's fingers. It means it is appropriate to snap one's fingers [in amazement]. Something that has never happened before but has now occurred is called 'marvelous' (abbhuta). Both of these are synonyms for astonishment. By the phrase "yāvañcidaṃ", the immeasurable nature [of the Dhamma] is shown because it is so well-penetrated.

Regarding "The Blessed One, knowing... they are well-penetrated," the summary of the meaning is as follows: That Blessed One, having fulfilled the thirty perfections, destroyed all defilements, and fully awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment (sammāsambodhi), knows the inclinations (āsaya) and underlying tendencies (anusaya) of various beings, seeing all knowable things (ñeyyadhamma) as if they were an emblic myrobalan (āmalaka) fruit placed in the palm of his hand.

Furthermore, he knows through the knowledge of recollecting past lives and so forth, and sees with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). He knows through the three true knowledges (vijjā) or the six direct knowledges (abhiññā), and sees with the "all-seeing eye" (samantacakkhu) which is unobstructed in all things. Or, he knows with the wisdom capable of knowing all things, and sees even those forms (rūpa) beyond the range of the eyes of beings, such as those behind walls, with his exceedingly pure physical eye (maṃsacakkhu). Or, he knows with the wisdom of penetration (paṭivedha-paññā) which accomplishes his own benefit and has concentration as its proximate cause, and sees with the wisdom of teaching (desanā-paññā) which accomplishes the benefit of others and has compassion as its proximate cause.

He is called 'Arahant' because he has slain the enemies of defilements and because he is worthy of receiving the four requisites and so forth. The Blessed One, called 'Sammāsambuddha' because he has rightly and by himself known all things, knows the obstructive states (antarāyika-dhamma) and sees the states leading to liberation (niyyānika-dhamma). He is called 'Arahant' because he has slain the enemies of defilements, and 'Sammāsambuddha' because he has rightly and by himself known all things. Thus, praised in four ways by the power of the four kinds of intrepidity (vesārajja-ñāṇa), the Blessed One has well-penetrated and known the various inclinations and various dispositions of beings.

Now, to show how he has thus well-penetrated [this knowledge], he said "ayañhi" and so forth. The meaning is: The Blessed One said, "Monks, beings come together and associate according to their elements (dhātu). Those of low inclinations come together and associate with those of low inclinations; those of good inclinations come together and associate with those of good inclinations. Monks, in the past too, beings came together and associated according to their elements..."
45:
...beings of low inclinations associated and came together only with those of low inclinations. ... beings of good inclinations associated and came together only with those of good inclinations. Monks, in the future too, beings will associate and come together only according to their dispositional elements. Monks, now in the present too, beings associate and come together only according to their dispositional elements. Those of low inclinations with those of low inclinations ... those of good inclinations with those of good inclinations associate and come together. Thus, the fact of beings having various inclinations, various dispositions, various views, various types of patience, and various preferences, has been known by the Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa)—the knowledge that knows various inclinations—just as if measuring with a measuring cup or weighing with a scale. This fact has been very well-penetrated and known. In the world, it is rare to find even two beings with the same disposition. When one wants to go, the other wants to stay; when one wants to drink, the other wants to eat. Regarding these two persons, the teacher and the pupil, it is said: "The wanderer Suppiya ... followed closely behind the Blessed One and the Saṅgha of monks." In that Pali text, "itihameti" should be resolved as "iti ha ime", meaning "thus these [people]". The remaining words are as previously explained.

Then, regarding "the Blessed One, having known this talk of those monks," here "having known" means knowing with the Omniscient Knowledge. In some places, the Blessed One knows by seeing with the physical eye (maṃsacakkhu). This is as in such passages as: "The Blessed One saw a large log being carried along by the current of the River Ganges." In some places, he knows by seeing with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu). This is as in such passages as: "The Blessed One, with the divine eye, purified and surpassing that of humans, saw those deities taking possession of sites in Pāṭali village." In some places, he knows by hearing with the natural ear (pakati-sota). This is as in such passages as: "The Blessed One heard this conversation between the Venerable Ānanda and the wanderer Subhadda." In some places, he knows by hearing with the divine ear (dibba-sota). This is as in such passages as: "The Blessed One, with the divine ear-element, purified and surpassing that of humans, heard this conversation between the householder Sandhāna and the wanderer Nigrodha." In this instance, however, he knew by hearing with the Omniscient Knowledge. While doing what did he know? He knew while performing the duties of the last watch [of the night]. Duties (kicca) are of two kinds: purposeful duties (sātthaka) and purposeless duties (niratthaka). Among them, the Blessed One had already completely uprooted purposeless duties by the Path of Arahantship at the very foot of the Bodhi tree. Only purposeful duties...
46: Furthermore, the Blessed One has duties. These duties are of five kinds: the duty before the meal, the duty after the meal, the duty in the first watch, the duty in the middle watch, and the duty in the last watch. Among these five, this is the duty before the meal (purebhatta-kicca): The Blessed One, having risen early in the morning, performs his personal duties such as washing his face for the sake of his attendant's service and for his own physical comfort. He then spends the time in a secluded place until it is time for the alms-round. When it is time for the alms-round, he adjusts his undergarment, fastens his waistband, puts on his upper robe, takes his bowl, and enters a village or a market town for alms, sometimes alone and sometimes accompanied by the community of monks. Sometimes he enters in his natural manner, and sometimes accompanied by many miracles. These miracles are as follows: As the Lord of the World (Lokanātha) enters for alms, gentle winds go before him to sweep the ground. Clouds release drops of water to settle the dust on the path and then remain above like a canopy. Other winds bring flowers and scatter them on the path. High places on the ground sink down, and low places rise up. At the moment he steps, the ground becomes level. Soft-to-the-touch lotus flowers also receive his feet. As soon as he places his right foot inside the city threshold, six-colored rays (chabbaṇṇaraṃsi) emanate from his body, adorning palaces, gabled houses, and so on, like streams of liquid gold or as if surrounded by exquisite cloths, darting here and there. Animals such as elephants, horses, and birds, while remaining in their respective places, make sweet sounds. Similarly, musical instruments like drums and lutes, as well as the ornaments worn by people, produce pleasant sounds. By these signs, people know: "Today the Blessed One has entered here for alms." These people, well-dressed and well-groomed, take scents, flowers, and so on, leave their houses, go to the main street, and after respectfully worshipping the Blessed One with scents and flowers, they request: "Venerable Sir, please give us ten monks, twenty, fifty... a hundred." They then take the Blessed One's bowl, prepare seats, and respectfully serve him with alms-food. When the meal is finished, the Blessed One looks into the mental dispositions of those beings and teaches the Dhamma in such a way that some are established in the Refuges, some in the Five Precepts, some in one of the fruits of Stream-entry, Once-returning, or Non-returning, and some, having gone forth, in the fruit of Arahantship, which is the highest fruit. Having thus benefited the great multitude, he rises from his seat and goes to the monastery. Arriving there, he sits on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāla). For the monks...
47: (The Blessed One) sits waiting for the monks to finish their meal. Then, when the monks' meal is finished, the attendant monk informs the Blessed One. At that time, the Blessed One enters the Gandhakuṭi. This is the duty before the meal (purebhatta-kicca). Then, having performed the duty before the meal, the Blessed One sits near the Gandhakuṭi, washes his feet, and standing on the foot-stool, exhorts the community of monks: "Bhikkhus, strive to attain [the three trainings] with diligence. Rare is the appearance of a Buddha in the world. Rare is the attainment of human birth. Rare is the attainment of favorable conditions (sampatti). Rare is the opportunity to go forth as a monk. Rare is the hearing of the True Dhamma." Among those monks, some ask the Blessed One for a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna). The Blessed One gives them a meditation subject suitable for their temperaments. Then all the monks worship the Blessed One and go to their respective night and day quarters. Some go to the forest, some to the foot of a tree, some to a certain place among the mountains, some to the realm of the Four Great Kings... some to the realm of the Paranimmita-vasavatti devas. Then the Blessed One enters the Gandhakuṭi and, if he so desires, lies down on his right side and rests for a moment in the Lion's Posture (sīhaseyya), mindful and clearly comprehending. When he has rested and his body is refreshed, he rises and, in the second part [of the afternoon], surveys the world. In the third part [of the afternoon], the great multitude in the village or market town where the Blessed One is residing, having given alms in the morning, dress well in the evening, take scents, flowers, and so on, and gather at the monastery. Then the Blessed One, proceeding with miracles suitable for the assembled audience, sits on the noble Buddha-seat prepared in the Dhamma hall and teaches the Dhamma appropriate for the time and occasion. Having thus preached, and knowing the time is right, he dismisses the assembly. The people worship the Blessed One and depart. This is the duty after the meal (pacchābhatta-kicca). Having thus finished the duty after the meal, if the Blessed One wishes to bathe his body, he rises from the Buddha-seat, enters the bathroom, and refreshes his body with water prepared by the attendant monk. The attendant monk then brings the Buddha-seat and prepares it in the courtyard of the Gandhakuṭi. The Blessed One puts on a well-dyed double robe, fastens his waistband, places his upper robe over his left shoulder, goes to that place, and sits there alone in seclusion for a moment. Then the monks come from various places...
48:
The monks come to attend upon the Blessed One. Among those monks, some ask questions, some ask for meditation subjects, and some request to hear the Dhamma. The Blessed One, fulfilling their desires, spends the first watch of the night (purimayāma). This is the duty to be performed in the first watch.

At the conclusion of the duties of the first watch, when the monks have paid homage to the Blessed One and departed, the deities from the entire ten thousand world systems, obtaining the opportunity, approach the Blessed One and ask questions, even if they are as short as four syllables, according to what they have prepared. The Blessed One, answering the questions of those deities, spends the middle watch of the night (majjhimayāma). This is the duty to be performed in the middle watch.

As for the last watch (pacchimayāma), he divides it into three parts. He spends one part in walking meditation (caṅkama) to relieve the physical fatigue caused by sitting since before the meal. In the second part, he enters the Perfumed Chamber (gandhakuṭi) and, mindful and clearly comprehending, takes up the lion's posture (sīhaseyya) on his right side. In the third part, having risen and sat down, he surveys the world with the Buddha-eye (buddhacakkhu) to see those individuals who have performed meritorious deeds (adhikāra) such as giving and virtue in the presence of previous Buddhas. This is the duty to be performed in the last watch.

On that day, the Blessed One, having finished his pre-meal duties in the city of Rājagaha, set out on his journey in the afternoon. Having taught meditation subjects to the monks in the first watch and answered the deities' questions in the middle watch, he ascended the walking path in the last watch. While walking, he heard and knew through his omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) this conversation of the five hundred monks which had arisen concerning his omniscience. Therefore, it is said: "He knew while performing the duties of the last watch."

Having known this, the following thought occurred to the Blessed One: "These monks are speaking of the virtues concerning my omniscience. The function of omniscience is not clear to these monks; it is clear only to me. When I go there, these monks will continuously relate their conversation. Then, taking that conversation as the starting point, I will teach the Brahmajāla Sutta—which shakes the ten thousand world systems—by analyzing the threefold virtue, by roaring an irreversible lion's roar (sīhanāda) in sixty-two instances, by combining the factors of the Law of Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda), and by making the Buddha's virtues manifest, as if lifting Mount Sineru or striking the sky with a golden peak, concluding it with the pinnacle of Arahantship. That teaching of mine, even after I have attained Parinibbāna, will lead beings to the Great Deathless Nibbāna for five thousand years." Having thought thus, he went towards the Maṇḍalamāḷa pavilion...
49:
"Tenupasaṅkami" means he approached that direction which was to be approached. Or, this instrumental case is used in the sense of the locative; it means he went to that place where the Maṇḍalamāḷa pavilion was located.

"He sat on the prepared seat" (paññatte āsane nisīdi) means that during the time of the Buddha, it is said that a seat was always prepared for the Buddha in every place where even a single monk resided. Why? It is because the Blessed One would reflect on the monks who, having taken a meditation subject from him, were living in a suitable place: "This monk has gone after taking a meditation subject from me; will he be able to attain distinction or not?" Then he sees that monk having abandoned his meditation subject and thinking unwholesome thoughts. Thereupon, thinking, "How is it that unwholesome thoughts overcome this son of good family who is living after taking a meditation subject from a teacher like me, and cause him to sink in the beginningless suffering of the round of rebirths (saṃsāra)?", he would manifest himself right there to assist that monk, and after admonishing that son of good family, he would fly into the air and return to his own dwelling place. Then, those monks who were thus admonished thought: "The Teacher, knowing our minds, comes and manifests himself standing right near us." At that moment, they considered the search for a seat, saying "Venerable Sir, sit here, sit here," to be a burden. Thus, they lived having always prepared a seat. He who had a bench prepared that bench. He who had none prepared a couch, a plank, a piece of wood, a stone slab, or a pile of sand. Not obtaining those, they would even gather old leaves and spread a rag-robe (paṃsukūla) over them. In this instance, however, the King's own seat was present; having dusted and prepared it, those monks sat surrounding it, praising the virtues of the Blessed One concerning his knowledge of the inclinations of beings (adhimuttika-ñāṇa). With reference to that prepared seat, it is said: "He sat on the prepared seat."

When he had thus sat down, although he already knew, he questioned the monks in order to start the conversation. And they told him everything. Therefore, it is said: "The Blessed One, having sat down," and so forth. Therein, "Kāya nuttha" means "With what talk are you sitting together?" There is also a Pali reading "Kāya nettha," which means "With what [talk] here [are you sitting]?" There is also a Pali variant "Kāya nottha," which has the same meaning as the first one.
50:
"Antarākathā" refers to another kind of talk that occurs in the midst of reflecting on the meditation subjects, reciting the Pali text, inquiring into the meaning, and so forth. "Vippakatā" refers to a talk that is unfinished or has not reached its climax because of my arrival. What is shown by this? It means: "I have not come to interrupt your talk; rather, I have come with the intention of completing your talk with my omniscience and bringing it to its climax." Thus, while seated, he made an offer of his omniscience. In the words, "Venerable Sir, this intermediate talk of ours was unfinished when the Blessed One arrived," this is also the meaning: "Venerable Sir, our talk concerning the virtues of the Blessed One's omniscience was unfinished; it was not 'lowly talk' (tiracchānakathā) such as talk about kings. While it was unfinished, the Blessed One arrived. Please now complete it and preach it to us."

With words of such extent, the Venerable Ānanda spoke the prologue (nidāna), adorned with time, place, speaker, subject matter, and assembly, so that this Sutta—which is endowed with meaning and phrasing and demonstrates the power of the Buddha's virtues—might be easily understood. This prologue is like a jewelled staircase designed for easy descent into a lotus pond that is bright with paduma, kuvalaya, and other lotuses, and has pure, sweet-tasting water. It is like a landing place filled with white sand resembling a floor of pearls. It is like a staircase shining with the radiance of gems interwoven with golden creepers on ivory planks, for easy ascent to a noble palace that rises high as if wishing to touch the path of the stars, surrounded by well-proportioned walls and curious railings. It is like a great gateway with firm and wide doorposts, illuminated by the brilliance of gold, silver, rubies, pearls, and coral, for easy entry into a great house adorned with the splendor of wealth and power, where the residents move about with sweet voices of talk and laughter mixed with the tinkling of golden bracelets and anklets. The explanation of the meaning of that prologue is finished.

Now, the opportunity has arrived to explain the Sutta delivered by the Blessed One in the manner beginning with: "Monks, if others should speak dispraise of me..." I shall speak the commentary on that Sutta. Since it becomes clear only when the occasion for the delivery of the Sutta (nikkhepa) is investigated, I shall first investigate the occasion for the delivery of the Sutta. There are four occasions for the delivery of a Sutta: by one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya), by the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya), by way of a question (pucchāvasika), and on account of an incident (aṭṭhuppattika).
51:
Among those four occasions for the delivery of a Sutta, there are Suttas which the Blessed One preached solely by his own inclination without being requested by others, such as: the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, the Vattha Sutta, the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta, the Mahāsaḷāyatanavibhaṅga Sutta, the Ariyavaṃsa Sutta, the series of Suttas on the Right Efforts (Sammappadhāna), and the series of Suttas on the Bases of Power (Iddhipāda), the Faculties (Indriya), the Powers (Bala), the Factors of Enlightenment (Bojjhaṅga), and the Path Factors (Maggaṅga). The delivery of these Suttas is called "delivery by one's own inclination" (attajjhāsaya-nikkhepa).

Furthermore, there are Suttas preached according to the inclination of others, after considering their inclination, preference, thought, aspiration, and capacity for enlightenment, such as: "The qualities of Rāhula that lead to liberation are mature; what if I were to further discipline Rāhula for the destruction of the taints (āsavas)?" Examples include the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, the Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, and the Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta. The delivery of these Suttas is called "delivery by the inclination of others" (parajjhāsaya-nikkhepa).

Furthermore, the four assemblies, the four classes, Nāgas, Supaṇṇas, Gandhabbas, Asuras, Yakkhas, the Four Great Kings, devas such as those of Tāvatiṃsa, and Mahābrahmā, etc., approach the Blessed One and ask questions in this manner: "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'Factors of Enlightenment, Factors of Enlightenment'"; "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'Hindrances, Hindrances'"; "Venerable Sir, what are these five aggregates of clinging?"; "What is a person's best wealth here in this world?" When thus asked, the Blessed One preached the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta, etc., and other Suttas such as the Devatā Saṃyutta, Māra Saṃyutta, Brahma Saṃyutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahāvedalla Sutta, Sāmaññaphala Sutta, Āḷavaka Sutta, Sūciloma Sutta, and Kharaloma Sutta. The delivery of these Suttas is called "delivery by way of a question" (pucchāvasika-nikkhepa).

Furthermore, there are Suttas preached on account of an incident that has arisen, such as: the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, the Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, the Candūpama Sutta, the Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta, the Dārukkhandhūpama Sutta, the Aggikkhandhūpama Sutta, the Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta, and the Pāricchattakūpama Sutta. The delivery of these Suttas is called "delivery on account of an incident" (aṭṭhuppattika-nikkhepa).

Among these four types of delivery, this Brahmajāla Sutta is a "delivery on account of an incident" (aṭṭhuppattika-nikkhepa). For the Blessed One delivered this Sutta because an incident had arisen. Because of what incident? Because of praise and dispraise (vaṇṇāvaṇṇa). The teacher spoke dispraise of the Triple Gem, while the student spoke praise. Based on this incident of praise and dispraise, the Blessed One, who is skillful in teaching, began the discourse with: "Monks, if others should speak dispraise of me..." In that discourse—
52:
## 
'Mama' is a word in the genitive case, meaning 'mine.' The word 'vā' expresses the sense of an alternative. 'Pare' refers to beings who are opposed to the Dispensation. 'Tatra' means among those beings who speak dispraise.

Although these monks truly have no resentment (āghāta) through the words beginning with 'no resentment,' the Buddha establishes a guideline of the Dhamma (dhammanetti) to prevent the arising of unwholesome states in clansmen of the future in such situations. In that context, it is called 'resentment' (āghāta) because it strikes the mind; it is a name for anger (dosa). Because of that anger, rapture and happiness do not arise, and there is no liking or joy; thus it is called 'displeasure' (appaccaya), which is a name for mental distress (domanassa). Because it cannot fulfill one's own benefit or the benefit of others, it is called 'dissatisfaction' (anabhiraddhi), which is also a name for anger. Thus, here, two terms describe the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) and one term describes the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha). By the power of these aggregates, the arising of the remaining associated states is also rejected.

Having thus prevented mental malice by the first method, the Buddha spoke the words, 'If, therein, you were to be angry or displeased, that would be an obstacle for you,' showing the danger therein by the second method. In that passage, 'If, therein, you were to be...' means if you were to be [so] toward those who speak dispraise or toward that dispraise. 'Angry' (kupitā) means through anger (kopa); 'displeased' (anattamanā) means through mental distress (domanassa). 'That would be an obstacle for you' means that because of that anger and that displeasure, there would be an obstacle to the higher attainments such as the first jhāna.

Having shown the danger by the second method, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'Would you [know] of others...' to show the inability even to merely note the meaning of the words by the third method. In that passage, 'of others' means of anyone at all. Indeed, an angry person cannot understand the meaning of the well-spoken or ill-spoken words of the Buddhas, Paccekabuddhas, noble disciples, parents, or enemies. As it is said:

'An angry person does not know the benefit;
An angry person does not see the Dhamma.
A blinding darkness then exists
When anger overcomes a man.
Anger gives birth to harm;
Anger is the disturber of the mind.
This danger born from within,
People do not realize.'
53:
## 
Having thus prohibited mental malice in the face of dispraise in every way, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with 'Therein, what is false should be [explained] by you as false,' to show the manner in which one should practice. In that passage, 'Therein, by you' means regarding that dispraise, by you. 'What is false should be explained as false' means that what is untrue should be removed only as being untrue. How should it be removed? In the manner beginning with 'For this reason, this is false.' The connection of meaning here is: upon hearing words such as 'Your Teacher is not all-knowing (Omniscient), the Dhamma is badly proclaimed, the Saṅgha has practiced wrongly,' one should not remain silent. Instead, one should speak thus: 'This word spoken by you is false for this reason; it is false for this reason; it is untrue for this reason; this fault does not exist in us; it is not found in us. Our Teacher is indeed Omniscient; the Dhamma is well-proclaimed; the Saṅgha has practiced well; and there are such reasons for this being so.' Here, it should be understood that the second term is a synonym for the first, and the fourth for the third. Such an explanation should be made only in the case of dispraise, not in every instance. If one remains silent and accepts when it is said, 'You are immoral, your teacher is immoral, this and that was done by you, was done by your teacher,' there may be cause for suspicion. Therefore, without being angry in mind, that dispraise should be cleared up. However, when a person abuses using the ten bases of abuse (akkosavatthu) such as 'You are a camel, you are an ox,' one should only practice patient endurance (adhivāsanakhanti) by ignoring them.

Having thus shown the characteristic of the 'Such' one (tādī) in the stage of dispraise, the Buddha now spoke the words beginning with 'Monks, if others should speak in praise of me,' to show it in the stage of praise. Therein, 'others' means any devas or humans who have confidence. 'Ānanda' (joy) is that by which they rejoice; it is a name for rapture (pīti). 'Somanassa' (gladness) is the state of a good mind; it is a name for mental happiness (cetasika-sukha). 'Uppilāvitatta' is the elation of the mind. Whose elation? Of the mind. This is a name for the rapture that brings about restlessness (uddhacca) and causes the mind to be elated. Here too, two terms describe the aggregate of mental formations and one term describes the aggregate of feeling.

Having thus prevented elation by the first method, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'If, therein, you were to be [joyful],' to show the danger therein by the second method. Here too, 'that would be an obstacle for you' means that because of that elation, there would be an obstacle for you [to the jhānas, etc.].
54:
It should be understood that the meaning is: it would be an obstacle to the higher attainments such as the first jhāna. Why is this said? Has the Blessed One not praised the joy and happiness (pīti-somanassa) regarding the Triple Gem in hundreds of suttas such as:

“The joy that arises in the body of one who praises, saying ‘Buddha’,
That joy is indeed more excellent than the whole of Jambudīpa.
The joy that arises in the body of one who praises, saying ‘Dhamma’,
That joy is indeed more excellent than the whole of Jambudīpa.
The joy that arises in the body of one who praises, saying ‘Saṅgha’,
That joy is indeed more excellent than the whole of Jambudīpa.”

And: “Monks, those who have confidence in the Buddha have confidence in the foremost.”

It is true that it was praised, but that joy is based on renunciation (nekkhamma-nissita). Here, however, it refers to the joy and happiness based on the household life (gehassita), similar to that which arose in Venerable Channa in the manner of “Our Buddha, our Dhamma,” and so on. This kind of joy acts as an obstacle to the attainment of jhāna and other higher states. For this very reason, Venerable Channa was unable to achieve any distinction as long as the Buddha had not yet attained Parinibbāna. Only when he was threatened by the Brahma-punishment (Brahmadanda) prescribed at the time of the Parinibbāna did he abandon that joy and happiness and achieve distinction. Therefore, it should be understood that this was said with reference only to the joy that causes an obstacle. Indeed, this is joy associated with greed (lobha). And greed is just like anger (kodha). As it was said:

“The greedy person does not know the benefit, the greedy person does not see the Dhamma.
When greed overcomes a person, there is then blind darkness.
Greed gives rise to harm, greed is the disturber of the mind.
People do not realize this danger that has arisen from within.” (Itivuttaka 88)

Although the third section (vāra) is not explicitly mentioned here, it should be understood as included by way of meaning. For just as one who is angry does not know the benefit, so too one who is greedy does not know the benefit.

In the section showing the manner of practice to be followed, the interpretation is as follows: Upon hearing such things as “Your teacher is the Omniscient One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One; the Dhamma is well-expounded; the Saṅgha is practicing rightly,” one should not remain silent. Instead, one should acknowledge it thus: “For this reason, this statement of yours is a fact; for this reason, this statement of yours is true.” That Blessed One is called ‘Araham’ for this reason; He is called ‘Sammāsambuddha’ for this reason. The Dhamma is called ‘Svākkhāta’ for this reason; it is called ‘Sandiṭṭhika’ for this reason. The Saṅgha is called ‘Suppaṭipanna’ for this reason; it is called ‘Ujuppaṭipanna’ for this reason.
55:
“What you have said is a fact; for this reason it is a fact, for this reason it is true. For that Blessed One is ‘Araham’ for such a reason, ‘Sammāsambuddha’ for such a reason. The Dhamma is ‘Svākkhāta’ for such a reason, ‘Sandiṭṭhika’ for such a reason. The Saṅgha is ‘Suppaṭipanna’ for such a reason, ‘Ujuppaṭipanna’ for such a reason.”

Even when asked, “Are you virtuous (sīlavā)?” if one is indeed virtuous, one must acknowledge it, saying, “I am virtuous.” Even when asked, “Have you attained the first jhāna... are you an Arahat?” one should acknowledge it only to fellow monks (sabhāga-bhikkhu) of similar standing. By acknowledging in this way, evil desire (pāpicchatā) is avoided, and the fruitfulness of the Dispensation (Sāsana) is made manifest. The rest should be understood in the same manner as previously stated.

## Commentary on the Minor Section on Virtue (Cūḷasīla-vaṇṇanā)

What is the connection (anusandhi) of the words: “Monks, this is a trifling matter”? This sutta is connected with two terms: praise (vaṇṇa) and blame (avaṇṇa). Therein, blame stops like a fire reaching the water’s edge at the very words: “This is not a fact, this is not true.” Praise, however, follows along as: “This is a fact.” That praise is of two kinds: the praise spoken by the youth Brahmadatta, and the praise initiated by the community of monks in the manner of “Friends, it is wonderful,” and so on. Among these, the connection will be shown later in the section explaining emptiness (suññatā) regarding the praise spoken by the community of monks. But here, to show the connection of the praise spoken by Brahmadatta, the teaching was begun with: “Monks, this is a trifling matter.”

In that teaching, ‘appamattakaṃ’ is a name for something small. ‘Oramattakaṃ’ is a synonym for that same term. ‘Mattā’ is said to be the measure (pamāṇa). Because it has a small measure, it is called ‘appamattakaṃ’. Because it has a low measure, it is called ‘oramattakaṃ’. Virtue itself is called ‘sīlamattakaṃ’. This is what is meant: “Monks, this is a trifling matter, a lowly matter, a mere matter of virtue,” which a worldling (puthujjana), even when making an effort to say, “I shall speak the praise of the Tathāgata,” would speak (only of the quality of virtue). Here, there might be an objection: Is this virtue not the supreme ornament of a practitioner (yogi)? As the ancients said:

“Virtue is the ornament of a yogi, virtue is the decoration of a yogi;
The yogi adorned with virtues has reached the supreme state of decoration.”
Is it not so stated?
56:
Has not the Blessed One also spoken of virtue as being truly great in many hundreds of suttas? As the Blessed One said: "Monks, if a monk should desire: 'May I be dear and agreeable to my companions in the holy life, respected and esteemed by them,' he should be one who fulfills the virtues" (MN 1.65). And:

"As a bird protects its egg, as a yak its tail,
As one protects a beloved son, or a single eye,
Even so, constantly guarding your virtue,
Be ever respectful and lovers of good conduct."

And:
"The scent of flowers does not go against the wind,
Nor does the scent of sandalwood, tagara, or jasmine.
But the scent of the virtuous goes against the wind;
The good person pervades all directions.

Sandalwood, tagara, water-lily, or jasmine—
Among these kinds of fragrance, the scent of virtue is supreme.
Faint is this fragrance of tagara and sandalwood,
But the scent of the virtuous is supreme, wafting even among the gods.

Māra cannot find the path of those who are perfected in virtue,
Who dwell in heedfulness, and are liberated through right knowledge."
(Dhp 54-57).

And: "Standing on virtue, the wise man, developing the mind and wisdom, the ardent and sagacious monk—he can untangle this tangle" (SN 1.23).

And: "Just as, monks, whatever seeds and plants reach growth, increase, and expansion, all of them do so by depending on the earth and standing on the earth; even so, monks, a monk, depending on virtue and standing on virtue, by developing the seven factors of enlightenment and cultivating the seven factors of enlightenment, reaches growth, increase, and expansion in the Dhamma" (SN 5.150).

In this way, many other suttas should also be understood. Thus, in many hundreds of suttas, virtue is spoken of as being truly great. That virtue... (Why is it said in this place to be trifling?)
57:
Why is it said in this place that [virtue] is 'trifling' (appamattaka)? It is said in comparison to the higher qualities. For virtue does not reach the level of concentration, and concentration does not reach the level of wisdom. Therefore, in comparison to the higher qualities, the lower quality is called trifling in measure. How does virtue not reach the level of concentration? In the seventh year after his Enlightenment, at the gate of the city of Sāvatthī, at the foot of the Kaṇḍamba mango tree, the Blessed One sat on a jeweled throne measuring one league within a jeweled pavilion measuring twelve leagues. While a divine white parasol measuring three leagues was being held over him, in the midst of an assembly measuring twelve leagues, he displayed the Twin Miracle (Yamaka Pāṭihāriya) to crush the pride of the sectarians and manifest his own power, in this manner: 'From the upper part of the body, a mass of fire proceeds; from the lower part of the body, a stream of water proceeds... [pe]... from each pore of the skin, a mass of fire proceeds; from each pore of the skin, a stream of water proceeds; and the six colors [appear].' From his golden-colored body, golden-colored rays issued forth and went as far as the highest heaven (bhavagga). It was like the time of decorating the entire ten-thousandfold world system. The successive rays proceeded simultaneously, as if they were pairs with the preceding ones.

There is no such thing as two thoughts occurring at the same moment. However, because of the swiftness of the Blessed Ones' life-continuum (bhavaṅga) and because of their mastery (vasībhāva) practiced in five ways, those rays appear to proceed at the same moment. But the reflection (āvajjana), preliminary work (parikamma), and resolution (adhiṭṭhāna) for each of those rays are indeed separate.

For the sake of the blue rays, the Blessed One enters the blue kasiṇa (nīla-kasiṇa). For the sake of the yellow rays, the yellow kasiṇa (pīta-kasiṇa). For the sake of the red and white rays, the red and white kasiṇas (lohita and odāta-kasiṇa). For the sake of the mass of fire, the fire kasiṇa (tejo-kasiṇa). For the sake of the stream of water, the water kasiṇa (āpo-kasiṇa). While the Teacher walks, the created (nimmita) Buddha stands, sits, or lies down—all this should be detailed. In this matter, there is not even a single function of virtue; it is entirely the function of concentration. Thus, virtue does not reach the level of concentration.

The Blessed One, having fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, at the age of twenty-nine, departed from the palace which was the abode of the glory of a Universal Monarch, and having gone forth as a monk on the banks of the Anomā River, practiced asceticism (dukkara-cariyā) for six years. On the full moon day of Visākha, having partaken of the honey-milk rice infused with divine essence offered by Sujātā in the village of Uruvelā, he entered the Bodhimanda (the area around the Bodhi tree) in the evening along the south-north path. Having circumambulated the king of Bodhi trees three times in a clockwise direction to show respect, he stood at the northeast corner, spread the grass mat, and [assumed] the triple-jointed cross-legged posture...
58:
Having entered the vicinity of the King of Bodhi trees (Assattha), he circumambulated it three times clockwise. Standing at the northeast corner, he spread the grass mat and sat in the triple-jointed cross-legged posture. Making the loving-kindness meditation endowed with four factors his precursor, he made a resolution of energy and reached the noble throne, fourteen cubits wide. With his back against the fifty-cubit Bodhi trunk, which was like a silver trunk placed on a golden pedestal, he was sheltered by the Bodhi branches as if by a jeweled parasol. While the coral-like Bodhi sprouts fell upon his golden-colored robes, he defeated Mara’s army as the sun was setting. In the first watch of the night, he recollected his past lives; in the middle watch, he purified the divine eye; and at dawn, he applied his knowledge to Dependent Origination, which is the practice of all Buddhas. Having attained the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing and using that very jhāna as a basis, he developed insight. By means of the fourth path attained through the sequence of paths, he exhausted all defilements and penetrated all the qualities of a Buddha. This is his function of wisdom. Thus, concentration cannot reach (equal) wisdom.
