In this regard, the analogy for concentration not reaching wisdom is as follows: water in the hollow of the hands cannot reach the water in a drinking cup; water in a drinking cup cannot reach the water in a water pot; water in a water pot cannot reach the water in a thirty-two-measure vessel; water in a thirty-two-measure vessel cannot reach the water in a large jar; water in a large jar cannot reach the water in a great storage jar; water in a great storage jar cannot reach the water in a small pond; water in a small pond cannot reach the water in a ravine; water in a ravine cannot reach the water in a small river; water in a small river cannot reach the water in the five great rivers; water in the five great rivers cannot reach the water in the great ocean of the universe; and water in the great ocean of the universe cannot reach the water in the great ocean at the foot of Mount Sineru. Compared to the water in a drinking cup, the water in the hollow of the hands is very little. ...pe... Compared to the water in the great ocean at the foot of Mount Sineru, the water in the great ocean of the universe is very little. Thus, based on the increasing volume of water in the higher levels, the volume of water in the lower levels is very little.

In the same way, based on the higher qualities, the lower virtue (sīla) should be understood as insignificant and inferior. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, this much virtue is insignificant, inferior, and merely virtue."

In the phrase "which worldling":
"Two kinds of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun: one is the blind worldling, and the other is the noble worldling."
59:
Among those worldlings, one who lacks learning, repeated inquiry, hearing, memorizing, and reflecting upon the aggregates, elements, sense bases, and so forth, is called a blind worldling (andhaputhujjana). One who possesses these qualities is called a noble worldling (kalyāṇaputhujjana). Furthermore, this worldling is of two kinds—

"He is called a worldling (puthujjana) because he generates many defilements, because he is included among the many folk, and because he is distinct from the Noble Ones."

Indeed, he is a worldling because of reasons such as generating many various defilements. As it is said—

"They are worldlings because they generate many defilements; they are worldlings because they have many unabandoned identity views; they are worldlings because they look up to the faces of many teachers; they are worldlings because they have not yet emerged from many destinations (gati); they are worldlings because they perform many various volitional formations; they are worldlings because they are swept away by many various floods, because they are tormented by many various torments, and because they are burned all around by many various fevers of defilement. They are worldlings because they are attached to, greedy for, tied to, infatuated with, overwhelmed by, clung to, entangled in, and obstructed by the five cords of sensual pleasure. They are worldlings because they are closed off, hindered, enveloped, obstructed, covered, and overturned by the five hindrances." He is also a worldling because he is included among the many folk who have exceeded the path of counting, who have turned their backs on the Dhamma of the Noble Ones, and who practice inferior dhammas. He is also a worldling because he is distinct and separate from the Noble Ones who are endowed with qualities such as virtue and learning.

## Tathāgatassa
The Blessed One is called the Tathāgata for eight reasons: He is the Tathāgata because he has come in that way (tathā āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has gone in that way (tathā gato); he is the Tathāgata because he has come to the real characteristic (tathalakkhaṇaṃ āgato); he is the Tathāgata because he has awakened to the real dhammas as they truly are (tathadhamme yāthāvato abhisambuddho); he is the Tathāgata because he is a seer of the real (tathadassitāya); he is the Tathāgata because he is a speaker of the real (tathavāditāya); he is the Tathāgata because he is a doer of the real (tathākāritāya); and he is the Tathāgata in the sense of overcoming (abhibhavanaṭṭhena).

How is the Blessed One the Tathāgata because he has come in that way? Just as the previous Perfectly Enlightened Buddhas, who exerted themselves for the welfare of the entire world, came. Just as the Blessed One Vipassī came, just as the Blessed One Sikhī, just as the Blessed One Vessabhū, just as the Blessed One Kakusandha, just as the Blessed One Koṇāgamana, and just as the Blessed One Kassapa came. What is meant? By whatever aspiration (abhinīhāra)...
60:
These Blessed Ones have come; because of that coming, our Blessed One has also come. Or else, just as the Blessed One Vipassī... (and so forth)... just as the Blessed One Kassapa, having fulfilled the Perfection of Giving (dāna-pāramī), having fulfilled the Perfections of Virtue, Renunciation, Wisdom, Energy, Patience, Truthfulness, Determination, Loving-kindness, and Equanimity—having fulfilled these ten perfections, ten higher perfections, and ten ultimate perfections, thus the thirty perfections—having renounced the five great renunciations, namely the renunciation of limbs, eyes, wealth, kingdom, and children and wife; having fulfilled the previous applications (pubbayoga), previous conduct (pubbacariya), the teaching of the Dhamma (dhammakhāna), conduct for the benefit of relatives (ñātattha-cariya), and so forth; and having reached the pinnacle of conduct for the sake of enlightenment (buddhi-cariya), he has come. In the same way, our Blessed One has also come.

Or else, just as the Blessed One Vipassī... (and so forth)... just as the Blessed One Kassapa, having developed and increased the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), the four right efforts (sammappadhāna), the four bases of power (iddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya), the five powers (bala), the seven factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga), and the Noble Eightfold Path, he has come. In the same way, our Blessed One has also come. Because he has come in the same way (as the previous Buddhas), he is called the 'Tathāgata'.

"Just as in this world, the Sages such as Vipassī and others,
Have come here to the state of Omniscience,
So too has this Sakyamuni come,
Therefore, the One with Five Eyes is called 'Tathāgata'."

Thus, because he has come in the same way, he is called the 'Tathāgata'.

In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has gone in the same way? Just as the Blessed One Vipassī, when just born, went... (and so forth)... the Blessed One Kassapa went.

And how did that Blessed One go? Indeed, as soon as he was born, standing on the earth with level feet and facing the north, he went with a stride of seven steps. As it is said: "Ananda, as soon as the Bodhisatta is born, he stands with level feet and, facing the north, goes with a stride of seven steps; while a white parasol is held over him, he surveys all directions and utters the fearless words: 'I am the foremost in the world, I am the eldest in the world, I am the best in the world. This is my last birth; now there is no more renewed existence'" (Dīgha Nikāya, 2, 31).
61:
And that going of the Blessed One was true (tatha) and unerring (avitatha), being the precursor (pubbanimitta) for the attainment of many special qualities. For when the Bodhisatta, just born, stood on the earth with level feet, this was the precursor for his attainment of the four bases of power (iddhipāda).

His facing the north was the precursor for his being supreme in the entire world (or his transcendence of the world).

His taking seven steps was the precursor for his attainment of the seven jewels of the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅga).

As for the waving of the yak-tail fly-whisks mentioned in the passage, "Fly-whisks with golden handles were waved," this was the precursor for his subduing of all heretics.

The holding of the white parasol was the precursor for his attainment of the noble and stainless white parasol of liberation, which is the fruit of Arahatship.

His surveying of all directions while standing at the end of the seventh step was the precursor for his attainment of the unobstructed knowledge of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa).

His uttering of the fearless words was the precursor for his setting in motion the noble Wheel of Dhamma (dhammacakka), which cannot be turned back by others.

In that manner, this Blessed One also went. And that going was true and unerring, being the precursor for the attainment of those very special qualities.

Therefore, the ancient teachers (porāṇā) said:

"Just as a bull, born but a moment ago,
Touches the earth with level feet,
So did Gotama stride seven steps,
And the gods followed, holding the white parasol.
Having gone those seven steps, Gotama
Surveyed all directions equally around,
And uttered words endowed with eight qualities,
Like a lion standing on a mountain peak."

Thus, because he has gone in the same way, he is called the 'Tathāgata'.

Alternatively, just as the Blessed Ones from Vipassī to Kassapa went, this Blessed One also went in the same way, having abandoned sensual desire (kāmacchanda) through renunciation (nekkhamma), ill-will (byāpāda) through non-ill-will (abyāpāda), sloth and torpor (thina-middha) through the perception of light (āloka-saññā), restlessness and remorse (uddhacca-kukkucca) through non-distraction (avikkhepa), and doubt (vicikicchā) through the definition of phenomena (dhamma-vavatthāna), and having pierced through ignorance (avijjā) with knowledge (ñāṇa)...
62: Having dispelled dissatisfaction in the meditative attainments through the tender rapture of joy, having opened the door-leaves of the hindrances through the first jhāna, having stilled initial and sustained application through the second jhāna, having transcended rapture through the third jhāna, having abandoned pleasure and pain through the fourth jhāna, having transcended the perception of form, the perception of sensory impact, and the perception of diversity through the attainment of the base of infinite space, having transcended the perception of the base of infinite space through the attainment of the base of infinite consciousness, having transcended the perception of the base of infinite consciousness through the attainment of the base of nothingness, and having transcended the perception of the base of nothingness through the attainment of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, he has gone. Having abandoned the perception of permanence through the contemplation of impermanence, the perception of pleasure through the contemplation of suffering, the perception of self through the contemplation of non-self, delight (nandi) through the contemplation of revulsion, lust through the contemplation of dispassion, origin through the contemplation of cessation, grasping (ādāna) through the contemplation of relinquishment, the perception of compactness (ghanasaññā) through the contemplation of destruction, accumulation (āyūhana) through the contemplation of fall, the perception of stability (dhuvasaññā) through the contemplation of change, the sign through the contemplation of the signless, desire (paṇidhi) through the contemplation of the desireless, adherence (abhinivesa) through the contemplation of emptiness, the adherence to taking as essence through the insight into phenomena of higher wisdom, the adherence through delusion through the knowledge and vision of things as they really are, the adherence to attachment through the contemplation of danger, non-reflection through the contemplation of reflection, and the adherence to bonds through the contemplation of turning away; having destroyed the defilements associated with wrong view through the path of stream-entry, having abandoned the gross defilements through the path of once-returning, having completely uprooted the subtle defilements through the path of non-returning, and having completely cut off all defilements through the path of arahantship, he has gone. In this way also, because he has gone in accordance with the truth, he is called 'Tathāgata'. In what way is he called 'Tathāgata' because he has arrived at the true characteristics? The characteristic of hardness of the earth element is true and unerring. The characteristic of flowing of the water element, the characteristic of heat of the fire element, the characteristic of supporting of the air element, the characteristic of non-contact of the space element, and the characteristic of cognizing of the consciousness element are true. The characteristic of being deformed of form, the characteristic of feeling of feeling, the characteristic of perceiving of perception, the characteristic of volitional activity of mental formations, and the characteristic of cognizing of consciousness are true.
63: Initial application has the characteristic of directing onto the object. Sustained application has the characteristic of repeatedly pressing onto the object. Rapture has the characteristic of pervading. Happiness has the characteristic of being pleasant. One-pointedness of mind has the characteristic of non-distraction. Contact has the characteristic of touching. The faith faculty has the characteristic of resolution. The energy faculty has the characteristic of exertion. The mindfulness faculty has the characteristic of establishing upon the object. The concentration faculty has the characteristic of non-distraction. The wisdom faculty has the characteristic of knowing in various ways. The power of faith has the characteristic of being unshakable by lack of faith. The power of energy has the characteristic of being unshakable by laziness; the power of mindfulness by forgetfulness; the power of concentration by distraction; and the power of wisdom by ignorance. The mindfulness enlightenment factor has the characteristic of establishing upon the object. The investigation-of-phenomena enlightenment factor has the characteristic of investigating in various ways. The energy enlightenment factor has the characteristic of exertion. The rapture enlightenment factor has the characteristic of pervading. The tranquility enlightenment factor has the characteristic of calming. The concentration enlightenment factor has the characteristic of non-distraction. The equanimity enlightenment factor has the characteristic of reflecting appropriately. Right view has the characteristic of seeing. Right intention has the characteristic of directing onto the object. Right speech has the characteristic of embracing. Right action has the characteristic of well-originating. Right livelihood has the characteristic of purity. Right effort has the characteristic of exertion. Right mindfulness has the characteristic of establishing upon the object. Right concentration has the characteristic of non-distraction. Ignorance has the characteristic of not knowing. Volitional formations have the characteristic of urging. Consciousness has the characteristic of cognizing. Mentality has the characteristic of inclining towards the object. Form has the characteristic of being deformed. The six sense bases have the characteristic of being bases (causing the arising of mind and mental factors). Contact has the characteristic of touching. Feeling has the characteristic of feeling. Craving has the characteristic of being a cause (the cause that gives rise to the suffering of the round of rebirths). Clinging has the characteristic of firmly grasping the object. Existence has the characteristic of striving (striving for the next life). Birth has the characteristic of arising. Aging has the characteristic of maturing. Death has the characteristic of passing away. Elements have the characteristic of emptiness (being void of a living soul). Sense bases have the characteristic of being bases (causing the arising of mind and mental factors). Foundations of mindfulness have the characteristic of establishing upon the object. Right strivings have the characteristic of exertion. Bases of power have the characteristic of fulfillment. Faculties have the characteristic of predominance (as a master). Powers have the characteristic of being unshakable. Enlightenment factors have the characteristic of leading out from the round of rebirths. The path has the characteristic of being a cause (the cause that leads to Nibbāna).
64:
The true characteristic of the Truths; the non-distraction characteristic of tranquillity; the contemplation characteristic of insight; the single-function characteristic of tranquillity and insight; the non-overtaking characteristic of tranquillity and insight coupled together.

The restraint characteristic of purification of virtue; the non-distraction characteristic of purification of mind; the seeing characteristic of purification of view.

The characteristic of total eradication of the knowledge occurring in the destruction [of defilements]; the characteristic of stilling of the knowledge occurring in the non-arising [of defilements].

The characteristic of being the root of desire; the characteristic of originating of attention; the characteristic of meeting of contact; the characteristic of converging of feeling; the characteristic of being the leader of concentration; the characteristic of being the sovereign of mindfulness; the characteristic of being the supreme of wisdom; the characteristic of being the essence of liberation... the characteristic of being the culmination of Nibbāna which is plunged into the Deathless—these are the true nature, the unerring nature. Because he has arrived at such true characteristics through the sequence of knowledge, has reached them without fail, and has attained them in due order, he is called 'Tathāgata'. Because he has thus come to the true characteristics, he is called 'Tathāgata'.

How is he a 'Tathāgata' because of having awakened to true phenomena as they really are? True phenomena are the four Noble Truths. As it is said: 'Monks, these four are true, unerring, and not otherwise. Which four? Monks, "This is suffering"—this is true, this is unerring, this is not otherwise,' and so on in detail. The Blessed One has awakened to these; therefore, because of having awakened to true phenomena, he is called 'Tathāgata'. Here, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'awakened' (abhisambuddha).

Furthermore, the nature of old age and death arising and originating due to the cause of birth is true, unerring, and not otherwise... the nature of volitional formations arising and originating due to the cause of ignorance is true, unerring, and not otherwise... similarly, the causal nature of ignorance for volitional formations, the causal nature of volitional formations for consciousness... the causal nature of birth for old age and death is true, unerring, and not otherwise. The Blessed One has awakened to all that; therefore, because of having awakened to true phenomena, he is called 'Tathāgata'. Thus, he is a 'Tathāgata' because of having awakened to true phenomena as they really are.

How is he a 'Tathāgata' because of seeing truly? In the world with its devas... among the generation of devas and humans, in the immeasurable world-systems...
65:
...there is the visible object that comes into the range of the eye-door of immeasurable beings; he knows and sees that in every aspect. To the Blessed One who thus knows and sees, that visible object—whether by way of desirable or undesirable, or by way of the terms 'seen, heard, sensed, or cognized'—when analyzed by many names such as 'What is the matter that is the base of visible form? It is the matter derived from the four great essentials, having color and brightness, visible and impacting, blue, yellow...' and so on, through thirteen sections and fifty-two methods, it is just as it is, and there is no falsity. This same method applies to sounds and so on that come into the range of the ear-door and so forth. And this was said by the Blessed One: 'Monks, in the world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, in this generation with its recluses and brahmins, its princes and people, whatever is seen, heard, sensed, cognized, reached, sought after, and examined by the mind—that I know. That I have fully realized; that is known to the Tathāgata, but the Tathāgata does not take his stand upon it.' Thus, he is a Tathāgata because of seeing truly. In this sense of 'seeing truly', the derivation of the word 'Tathāgata' should be understood.

How is he a Tathāgata because of speaking truly? From the night the Blessed One sat on the unconquered seat at the foot of the Bodhi tree, crushed the heads of the three Māras, and awakened to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment, until the night he attained parinibbāna by the Nibbāna-element without residue between the twin Sāla trees—during the interval of forty-five years, whatever the Blessed One spoke in the periods of the first enlightenment, the middle enlightenment, and the last enlightenment—the Sutta, Geyya... Vedalla, and so on—all that is faultless in meaning and phrasing, without deficiency or excess, complete in every aspect, and crushes the intoxication of lust, the intoxication of hatred, and the intoxication of delusion. There is not even a hair's breadth of deviation in that teaching; all of it is as if marked with a single seal, as if measured with a single measure, or weighed with a single balance—it is just so, unerring, and not otherwise. Therefore, he said: 'Cunda, from the night the Tathāgata awakens to the unsurpassed perfect enlightenment until the night he attains parinibbāna by the Nibbāna-element without residue, whatever he speaks, utters, or points out in that interval, all that is just so and not otherwise. Therefore, he is called "Tathāgata".' Here, the word 'gata' has the meaning of 'speaking' (gada). Thus, he is a Tathāgata because of speaking truly.
66:
Alternatively, *āgadana* or *āgada* means utterance (*vacana*). In the sense that the Blessed One possesses a true and unerring utterance (*āgada*), the letter 'd' is changed to 't', and thus the formation of the term '*Tathāgata*' should be understood.

How is he the *Tathāgata* because of acting according to what he says? For the Blessed One's body conforms to his speech, and his speech also conforms to his body. Therefore, as he speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. In this way, as the speech of the Blessed One is, so his body proceeds (*gata* - *pavatta*). As his body is, so his speech proceeds; thus he is the *Tathāgata*. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Monks, as the Tathāgata speaks, so he acts; as he acts, so he speaks. Thus, because he acts as he speaks and speaks as he acts, he is called the 'Tathāgata'" (AN 4.23). Thus, he is the *Tathāgata* because of acting accordingly.

How is he the *Tathāgata* in the sense of overcoming? From the highest realm of existence (*bhavagga*) above to the *Avīci* hell below, and across the immeasurable world systems in between, he overcomes all beings through virtue (*sīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), wisdom (*paññā*), liberation (*vimutti*), and the knowledge and vision of liberation (*vimutti-ñāṇadassana*). For that Blessed One, there is no comparison or measure. He is without equal, immeasurable, supreme, the King of kings, the God of gods, the Sakka surpassing Sakkas, and the Brahmā surpassing Brahmās. For this very reason, he said: "Monks, in the world with its devas... among the generation of devas and humans, the Tathāgata is the overcomer, the unvanquished, the one who sees everything, the wielder of power. Therefore, he is called the 'Tathāgata'."

In that term, the word formation should be understood as follows: He is called *agada* because he is like a divine medicine (*agada*) that cuts off disease. What is this? It is the grace of the teaching (*desanā-vilāsa*) and the accumulation of merit (*puññussaya*). Just as a powerful physician overcomes snakes with divine medicine, the Blessed One overcomes all those with opposing views and the world with its devas through that grace of teaching and accumulation of merit. Thus, in overcoming the entire world, he possesses the grace of teaching and accumulation of merit which are like a true and unerring divine medicine; therefore, by changing the letter 'd' to 't', he should be known as the *Tathāgata*. Thus, he is the *Tathāgata* in the sense of overcoming.

Furthermore, he is the *Tathāgata* because he is '*tathāya gata*' or '*tathāṃ gata*'. Here, '*gata*' means understood (*avagata*), transcended (*atīta*), attained (*patta*), and practiced (*paṭipanna*). The detailed meaning of the terms '*tathāya gata*' and '*tathāṃ gata*' should be understood as follows: He is the *Tathāgata* because he has understood the world, which is the entire Truth of Suffering, through the correct full understanding of investigation (*tīraṇa-pariññā*). He is the *Tathāgata* because he has transcended the origin of the world, which is the Truth of Origin, through the correct full understanding of abandoning (*pahāna-pariññā*). He is the *Tathāgata* because he has attained the cessation of the world, which is the Truth of Cessation (Nibbāna), through correct realization (*sacchikiriyā*). He is the *Tathāgata* because he has practiced the path, which is the Truth of the Path, leading to the cessation of the world. For this very reason, the Blessed One said: "Monks, the world has been fully understood by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world."
67:
In those passages, he is called the *Tathāgata* because he has understood the world, which is the entire Truth of Suffering, through the correct *tīraṇa-pariññā* (full understanding of investigation). He is called the *Tathāgata* because he has transcended the origin of the world, which is the Truth of Origin, through the correct *pahāna-pariññā* (full understanding of abandoning). He is called the *Tathāgata* because he has attained the cessation of the world, which is the Truth of Cessation, through correct realization. He is called the *Tathāgata* because he has practiced the path, which is the Truth of the Path, leading to the cessation of the world. Therefore, the Blessed One said this:

"Monks, the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is detached from the world. Monks, the origin of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the origin of the world has been abandoned by the Tathāgata. Monks, the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the cessation of the world has been realized by the Tathāgata. Monks, the path leading to the cessation of the world has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata; the path leading to the cessation of the world has been developed by the Tathāgata. Monks, in the world with its devas... all that object has been fully awakened to by the Tathāgata. Therefore, he is called the 'Tathāgata'" (AN 4.23).

The meaning of this statement should also be understood in the manner already described. This explanation is merely a brief indication of the nature of the Tathāgata. In truth, only the Tathāgata himself could fully describe the nature of the Tathāgata in all its aspects.

Regarding the phrase "Monks, what is that?", when a worldling (*puthujjana*) speaks of the virtues of the Tathāgata, he might speak of them in terms of minor, low, or mere virtue (*sīla*). He asks, "What is that?" In connection with this question, there are five kinds of questions (*pucchā*): *adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā*, *diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā*, *vimaticchedanā-pucchā*, *anumatipucchā*, and *kathetukamyatā-pucchā*.

Among these five, what is *adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā*? When a characteristic to be noted is naturally not yet known by wisdom, not yet seen, not yet weighed, not yet investigated, not yet manifest, and not yet clarified, a question asked for the purpose of knowing, seeing, weighing, investigating, and clarifying that nature by wisdom is called *adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā*.

What is *diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā*? When a characteristic to be noted is naturally already known by wisdom, seen, weighed, investigated, and clarified, a question asked for the purpose of comparing and cross-checking that nature with other wise people is called *diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā*.
68:
What is the question for cutting off doubt (vimaticchedanā pucchā)? Naturally, there is a tendency to fall into doubt, to fall into uncertainty, to be of two minds, thinking: 'Is it thus? Is it not thus? How can it be? In what way can it be?' He asks a question for the purpose of cutting off that doubt. This is called the question for cutting off doubt.

What is the question for seeking agreement (anumati pucchā)? The Blessed One asks a question to seek the agreement of the monks: 'What do you think, monks, is form permanent or impermanent?' 'Impermanent, Bhante.' 'That which is impermanent, is it suffering or happiness?' 'Suffering, Bhante.' All such scriptural passages should be cited; this is called the question for seeking agreement.

What is the question from a desire to teach (kathetukamyatā pucchā)? The Blessed One asks a question because of a desire to teach the monks: 'Monks, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?' ... 'Monks, there are these eight path factors. Which eight?' This is called the question from a desire to teach.

Thus, among these five types of questions, there is no 'question for illuminating the unseen' (adiṭṭhajotanā pucchā) for the Tathāgata, because there is no phenomenon unseen by him. There is also no 'question for comparing the seen' (diṭṭhasandandanā pucchā), because the thought 'I will teach this after comparing it with other wise recluses and brahmins' never arises in him. Furthermore, since the Buddhas have no wavering or hesitation (āsappanā, parisappanā) regarding even a single phenomenon, and all doubts were severed at the foot of the Bodhi tree, there is no 'question for cutting off doubt' either. Only the remaining two types of questions exist in the Buddhas; among them, this [current] question is called the 'question from a desire to teach.'

Now, to explain the meaning asked by that question from a desire to teach, he said the words beginning with 'having abandoned the taking of life' (pāṇātipātaṃ pahāya).

In that passage, the rapid falling (killing) of a living being's life is 'taking life' (pāṇātipāta). It means the slaughter of a being, the destruction of a being. Here, 'living being' (pāṇa) is a conventional term (vohāra) for a being, but in the ultimate sense (paramattha), it is the life faculty (jīvitindriya). The volition to kill, which arises in one of the two doors—body or speech—and which triggers the effort to cut off the life faculty of a being while perceiving it as a living being, is called 'taking life.' That taking of life is of small blame in the case of beings without virtue, such as animals, when the being is small; it is of great blame when the body is large. Why? Because of the greatness of the effort (payoga). Even when the effort is equal, it is because of the greatness of the object (vatthu). Among beings with virtue, such as humans, it is of small blame when the being has little virtue, and of great blame when the being has great virtue. When the body and virtue are equal, [it depends on] the defilements...
69:
It should be understood that if the effort is weak, the blame is small; if the effort is intense, the blame is great. There are five factors for that act of taking life: a living being, the perception of a living being, the thought of killing, the effort to kill, and death resulting from that effort. There are six types of effort (payoga): doing it with one's own hand (sāhatthika), by command (āṇattika), by missiles or throwing (nissaggiya), by permanent means such as digging pits (thāvara), by magical spells (vijjāmaya), and by psychic power (iddhimaya). If this meaning were expanded, it would be too extensive; therefore, we shall not expand upon it. Those who desire more detail should look into and take it from the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary.

'Having abandoned' (pahāya) means having given up this bad conduct known as the volition to take life. 'Abstaining' (paṭivirato) means being one who has desisted and abstained from that bad conduct from the time it was abandoned. In the Blessed One, even the unwholesome states known through eye-consciousness and ear-consciousness—such as 'I will transgress'—do not exist; how then could there be coarse unwholesome bodily actions? In this same way, the meaning of other terms should also be understood.

The Blessed One is called a 'recluse' (samaṇa) because he has calmed evil. He is called 'Gotama' by way of his lineage. It is not only the Blessed One who abstains from taking life; the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha) also abstains. However, because the teaching has come down in this way from the beginning, it is appropriate to show the meaning also by way of the community of monks.

'He has laid down the stick, laid down the sword' (nihitadaṇḍo nihitasattho) means he is one who has put down the stick and put down the sword because he does not go about taking up a stick or a sword to harm others. Here, except for the stick, all other instruments for harming beings should be understood as 'sword' (sattha). Although monks go about carrying a walking staff, a tooth-stick, a small knife, or a nail-cutter, these are not for the purpose of harming others; therefore, they are still reckoned as 'having laid down the stick, having laid down the sword.'

'Conscientious' (lajjī) means endowed with shame (lajjā), which has the characteristic of loathing evil. 'Compassionate' (dayāpanno) means one who has reached a state of loving-kindness that protects beings. 'Sympathetic to the welfare of all living beings' (sabbapāṇabhūtahitānukampī) means one who sympathizes with the welfare of all living beings. It means that because of that compassion, he has a mind desiring the welfare of all living beings. He dwells, proceeds, and maintains himself through the postures. 'Monks, even in this way' (even by this virtue of abstaining from taking life) is the meaning.
70:
He protects. 'Monks, even thus' means 'Monks, in this way'. The word 'vā' (or) expresses the sense of distinction (vikkapa) in relation to 'abstaining from taking what is not given' and so forth, which will be mentioned above. Thus, in all aspects of virtue (sīla), the nature of distinction should be understood in relation to the preceding or succeeding virtue.

The summary here is: Monks, when an ordinary person (puthujjana) wishes to speak in praise of the Tathāgata, he might say: 'The Ascetic Gotama does not kill living beings, nor does he cause them to be killed, nor does he approve of such killing; he abstains from such immorality. Oh, how great and wonderful are the virtues of the Buddha!' Thus, even if he wishes to speak praise with great effort, he will only speak of minor, inferior matters, merely of conduct and virtue (ācāra-sīla). He will not be able to speak praise based on the extraordinary and unique virtues mentioned above. Not only an ordinary person, but even Stream-enterers, Once-returners, Non-returners, Arahants, and even Paccekabuddhas are unable to do so. Only the Tathāgata himself is able. I shall speak of those virtues to you further on—this is the meaningful explanation here. From here on, we shall only explain the new terms not previously mentioned.

In the phrase 'abstaining from taking what is not given' (adinnādāna), 'adinnādāna' means taking what is not given, carrying away another's property, theft, or robbery. Therein, 'what is not given' refers to property possessed by another, where the owner can act according to his will and where (the taker) deserves neither punishment nor blame. In such property possessed by another, the intention to steal (theyya-cetanā) which initiates the effort to take it, while being aware that it is possessed by another, is called 'adinnādāna'. This 'adinnādāna' is of minor blame in the case of inferior (low-value) property belonging to another, and of great blame in the case of excellent (high-value) property. Why? Because of the excellence of the object. When the objects are equal, it is of great blame to take the property of a person of superior virtue. Compared to such a person of great virtue, it is of minor blame in the case of property belonging to a person of lesser virtue.

There are five factors for it: property possessed by another, the perception that it is possessed by another, the thought of theft, the effort, and the carrying away by that effort. There are six methods (payoga), starting with 'taking with one's own hand' (sāhattika). These occur according to the types of theft such as: theft by stealth (theyyāvahāra), theft by force (pasahyāvahāra), theft by concealment (paṭicchannāvahāra), theft by stratagem (parikappāvahāra), and theft by switching lots (kusāvahāra). This is the summary here. The detailed explanation is given in the Samantapāsādikā.
71:
Because he takes only what is given, he is called 'dinnādāyī'. Because even in his mind he expects only what is given, he is called 'dinnapāṭikaṅkhī'. One who steals is called 'thena' (a thief). Because he is not a thief, he is 'athena'. Because of being a non-thief, he dwells with a pure self (attabhāva). It means he dwells having made himself a non-thief and a pure person. The remaining sequence of words should be applied in the same manner as explained in the first training rule. As in this training rule, so it is in all training rules.

'Abrahmacariya' means non-noble conduct. Because he practices noble conduct, he is called 'brahmacārī'. 'Ārācārī' means practicing far away from the non-noble conduct of unchastity. 'Methuna' refers to the ignoble practices called 'sexual union' because they are to be indulged in by those who are called 'mithuna' (a couple) due to being similar through the power of the outburst of lust. 'Gāmadhamma' means the practice of those who live in villages (laypeople).

In the phrase 'abstaining from false speech' (musāvāda), 'musā' means a vocal or bodily action that destroys benefit with the intent to deceive. Alternatively, the intention (cetanā) that produces bodily or vocal actions that deceive others with the desire to deceive is called 'musāvāda'.

Another way: 'musā' is an untrue, false matter. 'Vāda' is the making known of that matter as true and real. According to its characteristic, the intention that produces the communication to make another person perceive an untrue matter as true is called 'musāvāda'. That false speech is of minor blame if the benefit it destroys is small, and of great blame if it is large.

Furthermore, for laypeople, false speech such as saying 'I don't have it' because of not wanting to give one's own property is of minor blame. False speech spoken while standing as a witness to destroy someone's benefit is of great blame. For monks, if they receive a little oil or ghee and, wishing to be humorous, say 'Today in the village, oil is flowing like a river,' such exaggerated speech is of minor blame. For those who say they have seen what they have not seen, it is of great blame.

There are four factors for that false speech: an untrue matter, the intent to deceive, the corresponding effort, and the other person's understanding of that meaning. There is only one method (payoga): 'sāhattika' (by oneself). This should be understood as performing the act of deceiving another by means of the body, something connected to the body, or by speech. If, through that action, the other person understands that matter, then at the very moment of the intention that produced the action, one is bound by the kamma of false speech.
72:
Just as one deceives another through the body, through objects connected to the body, or through speech, so too can one deceive another by commanding, "Tell this lie to that person," or by writing it down and placing it before them, or by writing on a wall, etc., saying, "This meaning should be understood in this way." Therefore, in this false speech (musāvāda), the efforts of command (āṇattika), handing over (nissaggiya), and stationary (thāvara) are also applicable. However, since they do not appear directly in the ancient Commentaries (Aṭṭhakathā), they should be accepted only after careful investigation.

One is called a truth-speaker (saccavādī) because one speaks the truth. One is called reliable in truth (saccasandha) because one connects the former truth with the latter truth. It means one does not speak falsely in between. If a person speaks falsely at one time and speaks the truth at another, their truth is interrupted by falsehood and thus the truths are not connected. Therefore, such a person is not called saccasandha. The Buddha, however, is not like that; even for the sake of life, He does not speak falsely and only connects truth with truth, thus He is called saccasandha.

Theta means having firm speech. Some individuals do not have firm speech, like the color of turmeric, like a stake driven into a heap of chaff, or like a pumpkin placed on a horse's back. Some individuals, however, have firm speech like an inscription on stone or like a doorpost (indakhīla). Even if their head is cut off with a sword, they do not speak two different words; such a person is called theta.

Paccayika means a person who is worthy of trust. Some people are not trustworthy. If asked, "Who said this?" and the answer is "So-and-so said it," people might say, "Do not believe his words." Some people, however, are trustworthy. If asked, "Who said this?" and the answer is "So-and-so said it," people might say, "If he said it, this word alone is the standard; there is no need to investigate further, it must be exactly so." Such a person is called paccayika. Not deceiving the world means not failing the people by speaking such truth.

In the phrases beginning with "pisuṇā vācā pahāya" (abandoning slanderous speech), the speech by which one makes oneself dear to the listener's heart while making another person distant (empty of love) is called slanderous speech (pisuṇā vācā).

The speech by which one makes oneself and others harsh, which is itself harsh, neither pleasant to the ear nor entering the heart, is called harsh speech (pharusā vācā).
73:
The speech by which one speaks useless and essence-less words in various ways is called frivolous talk (samphappalāpa). The intention (cetanā) that is the root of that slanderous speech, harsh speech, and frivolous talk also receives the names "slanderous speech" and so on. In this context, it is that intention which is intended.

Among those, the intention of one with a defiled mind that originates bodily or vocal effort for the purpose of dividing others or out of a desire to be loved is called slanderous speech (pisuṇā vācā). If that slanderous speech causes the division of one with few virtues, the fault is small; if it divides one with great virtues, the fault is great.

The four factors of that slanderous speech are: another person to be divided; the aim of dividing them, thinking "Thus these people will be divided and separated," or the desire to be loved, thinking "Thus I will be loved and trusted"; the corresponding effort; and the other person's understanding of that meaning. "For the purpose of dividing these" means for the purpose of dividing those from whom one heard the talk.

A reconciler of the divided (binnānaṃ vā sandhātā) is one who approaches friends or fellow students (upajjhāya) who are divided for some reason and reconciles them by saying, "It is not proper for you, who are born of such families and possess such great learning, to be divided in this way." Such a person is a follower and a giver of concord. When seeing two people in harmony, one strengthens it by saying, "It is appropriate for those born of such families and endowed with such virtues to be in harmony in this way."

One is called samaggārāma because those in harmony are one's delight. It means one does not even wish to live in a place where there is no harmony. There is also the Pali term "samaggaraama," which has the same meaning. One is called samaggarata because one delights in those who are in harmony and does not wish to leave them to go elsewhere. One is called samagganandī because one rejoices when seeing or hearing of those in harmony. One speaks only speech that creates harmony among beings; one speaks only speech that illustrates the virtue of concord and not otherwise.

The absolutely harsh intention that originates bodily or vocal effort which cuts to the heart of another is called harsh speech (pharusā vācā). To clarify the nature of this intention, there is this story: A boy went to the forest, disregarding his mother's words. The mother, unable to make the boy turn back, cursed him, saying, "May a fierce buffalo cow chase you!"

Then, in the forest, a buffalo cow appeared just as the mother had cursed. At that time, the boy made an act of truth, saying, "May the words spoken by my mother's mouth not come to pass; may only the thought intended by her heart come to pass." The buffalo cow then stopped right there as if tied with a rope.

In this way, even though it was an effort that could cut the heart, because the mind was soft, it is not called harsh speech (pharusā vācā). Parents sometimes speak to their children in this manner.
74:
The mother buffalo stood up. The young calf made an act of truth (saccakiriya), saying: "May the words my mother spoke with her mouth not come to pass, but may the thought she conceived in her mind be fulfilled." The mother buffalo stood still as if bound right there. Thus, even if there is an action that seems heart-rending, if the mind is gentle, it is not considered harsh speech (pharusā vācā). Indeed, parents sometimes say to their children, "May thieves cut you into pieces," yet they do not wish for even a lotus petal to fall upon them. Teachers and preceptors (ācariya-upajjhāya) also sometimes say to their dependents, "Why are these shameless and fearless ones wandering about? Drive them out!" yet they only desire for those disciples to achieve success in learning (āgama) and realization (adhigama). Just as harsh speech is not such when the mind is gentle, speech is not necessarily un-harsh simply because the words are gentle. For one who desires to kill, saying "Let this person sleep comfortably" is still harsh speech because of the harshness of the mind. That harsh speech is of little blame if the person targeted has few virtues, and of great blame if they have great virtues. Its three factors are: another person to be reviled, a mind full of anger, and the act of reviling.

'Nelā' means faultless; 'ela' refers to a fault, and because this speech has no fault, it is called 'nelā,' meaning faultless speech. It is like the 'nelā' mentioned in the verse "nelango setapacchādo." 'Kaṇṇasukhā' means pleasant to the ears due to the sweetness of the syllables; it does not cause pain to the ear like the piercing of a needle. 'Pemanīyā' means endearing, as it does not provoke anger throughout the body but generates love due to the sweetness of its meaning. 'Hadayaṅgamā' means heart-reaching; it enters the mind comfortably without being obstructed (by anger). 'Porī' means polite or urbane, either because it is full of virtues, or because it is delicate like a woman raised in a city, or because it is the speech of city-dwellers. City-dwellers have appropriate speech. They call those who are like a father 'father,' those like a brother 'brother,' and those like a mother 'mother.' Such speech is 'bahujanakantā' because it is loved by many people. Because it is lovable and increases the joy of many people's minds, it is 'bahujanamānapā.'

'Samphappalāpa' (idle chatter) is the unwholesome intention that communicates what is useless and originates from bodily or vocal effort. This idle chatter is of little blame if practiced little, and of great blame if practiced much. Its two factors are: the preoccupation with useless talk such as the Bharata war or the abduction of Sītā, and the actual speaking of such talk.
75:
One is called 'kālavādī' because they speak at the appropriate time; it means speaking after noting the time suitable for speaking. One is called 'bhūtavādī' because they speak only of what is manifest, real, and true. One is called 'atthavādī' because they speak only based on the welfare of the present life and the future life. One is called 'dhammavādī' because they speak based on the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). One is called 'vinayavādī' because they speak based on the Vinaya of restraint (saṃvara) and the Vinaya of abandonment (pahāna).

A place for storing is called 'nidhāna'; speech that has such a place is 'nidhānavatī.' It means speaking words that are worthy of being stored in the heart. Regarding 'kālena' (at the right time), even when speaking such words, one does not speak at an inappropriate time thinking 'I will speak words worth treasuring,' but speaks only after considering the proper time. 'Sāpadesaṃ' means speech with illustrations or with reasons. 'Pariyantavatī' means speaking in a way that shows the limits or boundaries so that the end of the speech is clear. 'Atthasaṃhitaṃ' means speaking words full of meaning such that they cannot be exhausted even when analyzed through various methods. Or, it is called 'atthasaṃhitaṃ' because it is accompanied by the meaning that the 'atthavādī' person speaks. It means not setting aside one thing and speaking another. 'Bījagāma-bhūtagāma-samārambhā' refers to abstaining from damaging by cutting, breaking, cooking, etc., the five kinds of seeds (bījagāma)—root-seeds, trunk-seeds, joint-seeds, bud-seeds, and seed-seeds—and the group of plants (bhūtagāma) such as green grass and trees. 'Ekabhattiko' means there are two types of meals: the morning meal and the evening meal. Among them, the morning meal is defined by the period within noon; the other (evening meal) is defined from noon until dawn. Therefore, even if one eats ten times within the period before noon, they are still considered 'ekabhattika' (one who eats one meal). It is in reference to that single mealtime that 'ekabhattiko' is said. Eating at night is called 'ratti'; because of abstaining from that night meal, one is called 'rattūparato.' Eating from past noon until sunset is called 'vikālabhojana' (untimely eating). Because of abstaining from such afternoon and night meals, one is 'virato vikālabhojanā.' From when does one abstain? One has abstained since the day of ordaining on the banks of the Anomā River. 'Visūkadassana' refers to watching shows that are contrary to the Buddha's Dispensation (Sāsana) and act as obstacles, like a stake. It includes dancing, singing, and music performed by oneself or by others...
76:
At the very least, watching or listening to dancing and so forth, which occur through the dancing of peacocks and such, and which are like a thorn [contrary] to the Buddha's teaching, is called 'nicca-gīta-vādita-visūka-dassana'. Indeed, it is not proper for monks or nuns to perform dancing and so forth themselves, to cause others to perform them, or to watch them being performed.

Among flowers and so forth, 'mālā' refers to all kinds of flowers. 'Gandha' refers to any kind of scent. 'Vilepana' refers to cosmetics, perfumes, or ointments used to make the complexion attractive. Therein, one who wears flowers is said to 'dhāreti' (wear); one who fills in low spots [on the body] is said to 'maṇḍeti' (adorn); and one who delights in the power of the scent and the attractiveness of the complexion is said to 'vibhūseti' (beautify). 'Ṭhāna' means cause. Therefore, it means abstaining from that unvirtuous intention with which the multitude of people perform such acts as wearing flowers and so forth.

'Uccāsayana' refers to a place [for sitting or sleeping] that exceeds the [prescribed] measurement (higher than eight finger-breadths). 'Mahāsayana' refers to improper rugs or coverings. It means abstaining from those.

'Jātarūpa' refers to gold. 'Rajata' refers to silver, which is used as currency such as kahāpaṇa, copper coins, lac coins, or wooden coins. It means abstaining from accepting both of these; he neither takes it himself, nor causes others to take it, nor delights in it when it is placed near him.

'Āmakadhañña-paṭiggahaṇā' refers to accepting the seven kinds of raw grains: hill rice, paddy, barley, wheat, millet, beans/pulses, and rye/maize. For monks, not only is accepting these grains improper, but even touching them is improper. In 'āmakamaṃsa-paṭiggahaṇā', except for what is specifically permitted, only the acceptance of raw meat and fish is improper for monks; touching them is not improper (it is permitted).

In 'itthikumārika-paṭiggahaṇā': 'itthi' refers to a woman who has had relations with a man; the other is called 'kumārikā' (a maiden). Both accepting and touching them is improper.

In 'dāsidāsa-paṭiggahaṇā': it is improper to accept them specifically as female or male slaves. However, if one says, 'I donate a kappiyakāraka (attendant)' or 'I donate an ārāmika (monastery worker),' then it is proper.

From goats and sheep down to fields and land, what is proper and improper should be investigated according to the Vinaya. Therein, 'khetta' (field) refers to a place where early crops (rice) grow. 'Vatthu' (land) refers to a place where late crops (pulses) grow. Or, a place where both grow is called 'khetta'.
77:
A portion of land not yet prepared for the purpose of farming is called 'vatthu'. Here, by using 'khetta' and 'vatthu' as headings, long reservoirs, embanked tanks, and so forth are also included.

The work of a messenger, which involves taking a letter or a verbal message and going to various places at the behest of laypeople, is called 'dūteyya'. The short journey of a monk sent from house to house is called 'pahiṇagamana'. Engaging in both of these is called 'anuyoga'. Therefore, the meaning of 'dūteyya-pahiṇagamanānuyoga' should be understood in this way.

'Kayavikkaya' means buying and selling. In terms such as 'tulākūṭa', 'kūṭa' means deception (fraud). Therein, 'tulākūṭa', which is deception by scales, is of four types: 'rūpakūṭa', 'aṅgakūṭa', 'gahaṇakūṭa', and 'paṭicchannakūṭa'. Among these four, 'rūpakūṭa' means making two scales of similar appearance and, when taking for oneself, taking with the large scale, and when giving, giving with the small scale. 'Aṅgakūṭa' means pressing the scale with the hand at the back when taking, and at the front when giving. 'Gahaṇakūṭa' means holding the scale-string at the base when taking, and at the tip when giving. 'Paṭicchannakūṭa' means making the scale hollow and putting iron powder inside; when taking, one keeps that iron powder at the back, and when giving, one keeps it at the front.

A gold bowl is called 'kaṃsa'; deception with such a gold bowl is 'kaṃsakūṭa'. How is the deception carried out? One makes one genuine gold bowl and two or three other bronze bowls to look like the color of gold. Then, going to the countryside and entering a wealthy family, one says, 'Please buy these gold vessels.' When the price is asked, one expresses a desire to give them at a very cheap price. Then, when they ask, 'How can the golden nature of these be known?', one says, 'Buy them after testing,' and rubs the genuine gold bowl on a touchstone, then gives all the bowls and leaves.

'Mānakūṭa', which is deception by measures, is of three types: 'hadayabheda', 'sikhābheda', and 'rajjubheda'. Therein, 'hadayabheda' is found when measuring ghee, oil, and so forth. When taking those items, using a measure with a hole at the bottom, one says, 'Pour slowly,' and allows much to leak into one's own vessel while taking. When giving, one closes the hole, fills it quickly, and gives. 'Sikhābheda' is found when measuring sesame, rice, and so forth. When taking those items, one slowly lets the heap (peak) rise and takes. When giving, one fills it quickly and cuts off the heap while giving.
78:
Fraud by rope (rajju-bheda) is often found when measuring fields and lands. Indeed, land-surveyors who do not receive bribes measure even a small field to make it appear large.

Among the terms beginning with 'ukkoṭana', 'ukkoṭana' (bribery) refers to taking a bribe to make someone who is not the owner become the owner. 'Vañcana' (deception) refers to deceiving others by various fraudulent means. Regarding this deception, there is this story: A certain hunter came carrying a large deer and a young deer. Then, a rogue asked, "Friend, how much is the large deer worth, and how much is the young deer worth?" When the hunter replied, "The large deer is worth two kahāpaṇas, and the young deer is worth one," the rogue gave one kahāpaṇa, took the young deer, went a little way, and then turned back, saying, "Friend, the young deer is of no use to me; give me the large deer instead." The hunter said, "In that case, give me two kahāpaṇas." The rogue asked, "Friend, did I not give you one kahāpaṇa first?" The hunter replied, "Yes, you did." The rogue then said, "Take this young deer; thus, the one kahāpaṇa given previously and this young deer worth one kahāpaṇa, these two together will make two kahāpaṇas." Thinking that he was speaking reasonably, the hunter took back the young deer and gave him the large deer. 'Nikati' (fraud) refers to deceiving with counterfeits by means of spells or magic, such as making what is not a neck-ornament appear as a neck-ornament, what is not a gem appear as a gem, or what is not gold appear as gold. 'Sāci-yoga' refers to crooked deception; this is simply another name for the aforementioned 'ukkoṭana' and others. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood as 'ukkoṭana-sāci-yoga' (crookedness in bribery), 'vañcana-sāci-yoga' (crookedness in deception), and 'nikati-sāci-yoga' (crookedness in fraud). Some teachers say that 'sāci-yoga' refers to showing one object and then substituting it with another. However, that substitution is already included within 'vañcana'.

Among the terms beginning with 'chedana', 'chedana' refers to the cutting off of hands and so on. 'Vadha' refers to oppression and torture. 'Bandha' refers to binding with ropes and so on. 'Viparamosa' (highway robbery) is of two kinds: 'hima-viparamosa', plundering while concealed by mist or snow, and 'gumba-viparamosa', plundering while concealed by bushes. Plundering travelers while concealed by mist when the mist falls is called 'hima-viparamosa'. Plundering while concealed by bushes and such is called 'gumba-viparamosa'. 'Ālopa' (pillage) refers to the plundering and destruction of villages, market towns, and so on. 'Sahasākāra' refers to acts of violence (dacoity). It is the act of entering a house, placing a weapon on the chests of people, and taking the desired goods. In this way, the Ascetic Gotama abstains from cutting, torturing, binding, highway robbery, plundering villages and towns, and dacoity. Thus, monks, when a worldling speaks in praise of the Tathāgata, he might speak in this manner.

## Here ends the Small Section on Virtue (Cūḷa-sīla).
79:
## Commentary on the Middle Section on Virtue (Majjhima-sīla-vaṇṇanā)

Now, having shown the Small Section on Virtue, and wishing to elaborate on the Middle Section on Virtue, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Yathā vā paneke bhonto." In that passage, the explanation of the obscure terms is as follows: 'Saddhā-deyyāni' refers to items donated out of faith in kamma, the results of kamma, this world, and the next world. It means they are not donated because of reasons such as "This person is my relative," or "He is my friend," or "This person will repay my favor," or "This person has favored me in the past." This is because items donated with such intentions are not called 'saddhā-deyya' (offerings given in faith). The word 'bhojanāni' (foods) is merely the primary head of the teaching. In truth, by way of meaning, it refers to the use of all things: consuming foods given in faith, wearing robes, using dwellings and bedding, and using medicinal requisites for the sick.

'Seyyathidaṃ' is an indeclinable particle. Its meaning is: "Which are those seed-groups and plant-groups that they remain intent on destroying?" Then, wishing to show those seed-groups and plant-groups, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with 'mūla-bījaṃ'. In that passage, 'mūla-bīja' (root-seeds) refers to turmeric, ginger, orris root, sweet flag, aconite, black hellebore, khus-khus grass, nut-grass, and so on. 'Khandha-bīja' (trunk-seeds) refers to the Bodhi tree, the Banyan tree, the waved-leaf fig, the cluster fig, the wood-apple, the sour fig, and so on. 'Phaḷu-bīja' (joint-seeds) refers to sugar cane, reed, bamboo, and so on. 'Agga-bīja' (bud-seeds) refers to basil, holy basil, pavonia, and so on. 'Bīja-bīja' (seed-seeds) refers to grains, beans, and so on. Indeed, all these groups of species are called 'bījagāma' (seed-group) only when they are detached from the tree but are still capable of sprouting. However, a plant that is not yet detached from the tree and is not yet dry is called 'bhūtagāma' (plant-group). Among these, it should be understood that destroying 'bhūtagāma' is a ground for a Pācittiya offense, while destroying 'bījagāma' is a ground for a Dukkaṭa offense.

'Sannidhikāra-paribhogaṃ' refers to the consumption of food and other items that have been stored up. Regarding the consumption of stored items, there are two perspectives: according to the Vinaya (Discipline) and according to Sallekha (Effacement). To speak first according to the Vinaya: any food received today becomes 'sannidhikāraka' (stored food) on the next day; if one consumes that food, it is a Pācittiya offense. However, it is allowable to give food one has received to novices, and then eat the food that those novices have kept on the second day. Nevertheless, doing so is not the practice of Sallekha, which involves the effacement of defilements.

This same principle applies to the storing of drinks (pāna). In 'pāna-sannidhi', 'pāna' (drinks) refers to the eight kinds of drinks, such as mango juice, and the 'anuloma' (allowable) drinks that are similar to those eight. The decision regarding these drinks has been stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.
80:
Regarding the hoarding of robes (vatthasannidhi), keeping a robe that has not been formally determined (anadhiṭṭhita) or assigned (avikapita) constitutes hoarding (sannidhi) and also violates the practice of effacement (sallekha). This is an indirect explanation (pariyāyakathā). In the direct sense (nippariyāyato), one should be content with only the triple robe; if a fourth robe is obtained, it must be given to another. If one is unable to give it to a specific person because that person is away for teaching or inquiry, it must be given as soon as they return; it is not proper to withhold it. However, if robes are insufficient and there is hope of obtaining more, it is permissible to keep them within the allowed period. If needles, thread, and robe-makers are not yet available, it is permissible to keep them beyond that period by performing a Vinaya procedure. It is not proper to keep a robe with the thought, "When this robe wears out, where will I find another like it?" Such keeping constitutes hoarding and violates the practice of effacement.

Regarding the hoarding of vehicles (yānasannidhi), vehicles include covered carts, chariots, wagons, palanquins, litters, and sedan chairs; these are vehicles unsuitable for renunciants. Sandals, however, are the only vehicle for renunciants. For a single monk, a maximum of two pairs of sandals is permissible: one for use in the forest and one for use after washing the feet. If a third pair is obtained, it must be given to another. It is not proper to keep them with the thought, "When these sandals wear out, where will I find others?" Such keeping constitutes hoarding and violates the practice of effacement.

Regarding the hoarding of beds (sayanasannidhi), a bed refers to a couch (mañca). For a single monk, a maximum of two couches is permissible: one for the room and one for the day-resting place. If more than that are obtained, they must be given to another monk or to the Saṅgha; it is not proper to withhold them. Such keeping constitutes hoarding and violates the practice of effacement.

Regarding the hoarding of perfumes (gandhasannidhi), perfumes are permissible for a monk if he has an illness such as itch, scabies, or skin diseases. Having procured those perfumes, once the illness is cured, they must be given to others who are ill, or used for making five-finger marks at the door or for fumigating the monastery buildings. It is not proper to keep them with the thought, "They will be useful if the illness occurs again." Such keeping constitutes hoarding and violates the practice of effacement.

Material provisions (āmisa) refers to things remaining other than those mentioned above. For example, in this Dispensation, a certain monk, thinking, "It will be of use at such a time," procures and stores sesame, rice, mung beans, kidney beans, coconuts, salt, fish, meat, dried meat, jars of ghee, jars of oil, jars of molasses, and so on. During the rainy season, that monk has the novices cook gruel early in the morning, and after consuming it, says, "Novice, it is very difficult to enter the village because of the water and mud; go to such-and-after family's house and say that I am staying only at the monastery..."
81:
"...Go to that house and inform them that I am staying at the monastery. Bring back curd and other items from such-and-such a family." When asked by other monks, "Venerable sir, will you enter the village?" he says, "Friends, it is very difficult to enter the village now." Those monks say, "Very well, venerable sir, please stay; we will search for almsfood and bring it back," and then they leave. Then the novice also brings curd and other items, prepares rice and curry, and offers them. While eating that food, his lay supporters send almsfood, and from that too, he picks and eats the choice portions. Later, when the monks return from their almsround, he again eats the choice portions from their food until his neck is stretched (eating to the full). In this way, he passes the four months of the rainy season. Such a monk is said to "live the life of a shaven-headed householder, not the life of a recluse." This kind of hoarding is called the hoarding of material things (*āmisasannidhi*).

In a monk's dwelling, it is permissible to store one *nāḷi* (measure) of rice, a lump of molasses, and about a quarter-measure of ghee for the sake of robbers and bandits who might arrive at an improper time. For if they do not receive even this much material hospitality, they might even take one's life. Therefore, if such items are not available, it is permissible even to request and store them. In times of ill health, one may personally consume what is allowable among those items. There is no such thing as [wrongful] hoarding (*sannidhi*) even if much is stored in a *kappiyakuṭi* (allowable storehouse). However, for the Tathāgata, there was no such thing as storing even a *nāḷi* of rice or a piece of rag about four cubits long with the thought, "This will be for me today or tomorrow."

Regarding unseemly spectacles (*visūkadassana*), it is not proper to stretch one's neck to watch any kind of dancing, even while traveling on a road. The detailed decision on this should be understood according to the method stated in the *Samantapāsādikā* (the Vinaya Commentary). This applies to all Sutta passages connected with the training rules. Hereafter, I shall not say even this much of an introductory word, but will only explain the application of the meaning in various places.

'Pekkhaṃ' refers to the dance performances of actors. 'Akkhānaṃ' refers to the recitation of stories such as the Bhārata war; it is not proper even to go to the place where such stories are told. 'Pāṇissaraṃ' refers to the sound of bronze gongs; some also say it means the clapping of hands. 'Vetāḷaṃ' refers to the sound of solid instruments (*ghana-turiya*); some say it is the raising of a corpse by means of a mantra. 'Kumbhathūṇaṃ' refers to the sound of a drum shaped like a four-sided *ambaṇa* measure; some say it is the sound of a pot-drum (*kumbha-saddu*).
82:
Sobhanaka refers to the offerings made by actors to deities, or otherwise, it means artistic paintings or sculptures made beautiful and vivid through ingenious intellect. Caṇḍāla refers to sports with iron balls, or as some say, the game of hitting one another with wet hemp as practiced by the Caṇḍāla people. Vaṃsa refers to games involving climbing a raised bamboo pole.

Dhovana refers to the bone-washing ceremony. It is said that in certain regions, when relatives pass away, they do not cremate them but bury them in the ground. Later, when they know the bodies have decomposed, they exhume them, wash the bones, anoint them with perfumes, and store them. During festivals, they place the bones in one spot and liquor and such in another, and then drink liquor while weeping and lamenting. Regarding this, it was said in the Aṅguttara Nikāya: "Bhikkhus, in the southern regions, there is a ceremony called bone-washing. There, there is food, drink, snacks, meals, lickables, and beverages, as well as dancing, singing, and music. Bhikkhus, that bone-washing ceremony exists; I do not say it does not." Some teachers, however, say that dhovana refers to making bones appear through sleight of hand.

In elephant battles and so on, it is not proper for a monk to fight with elephants etc., nor to instigate them to fight, nor to watch them fighting. Nibbudda refers to boxing or wrestling. Uyyodhika refers to a place where combat (a battlefield) can be seen. Balagga refers to a place where troops are counted. Senābyūha refers to the arraying of an army, such as in a wagon array. Anīkadassana refers to viewing the forces, such as the elephant force described in the manner: "Three elephants constitute the smallest elephant force."

Because negligence (pamāda) resides in these games, they are called occasions for negligence (pamādaṭṭhāna). Since it is both gambling and a cause for negligence, it is called jūtapamādaṭṭhāna. Aṭṭhapada is so called because there are eight squares in each row of the board; the same principle applies to Dasapada (ten squares). Ākāsa refers to playing as if on an Aṭṭhapada or Dasapada board but in the air (mentally) without a physical board. Parihārapatha refers to a game of following various paths marked on the ground while avoiding overlapping. Santika refers to a game of flicking or picking. Pieces or pebbles placed together are removed or moved with only the fingernail without disturbing the others; if any piece moves, it is a loss. This is the name for such a game. Khalika refers to playing with dice on a gambling board. Ghaṭikā refers to the game of hitting a short stick with a long stick (tip-cat). Salākahattha refers to dipping a bundle of coconut fibers into lac, madder dye, or flour-water and striking it against the ground or a wall to create figures such as elephants or horses.
83:
Asking "What do you want it to be?" and then hitting the ground or wall with that brush of coconut or palm fiber to show figures of elephants, horses, etc., is called "kiṃ hotu." Akkha refers to playing with nuts or marbles. They play by blowing a small flute made of leaves called "paṅgacīra." Vaṅkaka is a toy plow used by village children. Mokkhacikā refers to acrobatic somersaults, either by holding a bar in the air or by placing the head on the ground and turning upside down. Ciṅgulika refers to a windmill made of palm leaves and such that spins when hit by the wind. Pattāḷhaka refers to a leaf-cup used to measure sand and such while playing. Rathaka is a toy chariot. Dhanuka is a toy bow. Akkharikā refers to a game of identifying letters written with the hand in the air or on someone's back. Manesikā refers to a game of identifying what is thought of in the mind. Yathāvajja refers to a game of mimicking the defects of the blind, the crippled, the hunchbacked, etc.

Āsandī refers to a couch or seat that exceeds the prescribed measurements. The use of the accusative case in all these terms is in relation to the phrase "anuyuttā viharanti" (they live devoted to...). Pallaṅka refers to a small couch with legs carved in the shapes of wild animals such as lions, leopards, or tigers. Gonaka refers to a large black woolen rug with hair longer than four finger-breadths. Cittaka refers to a woolen coverlet woven in variegated patterns. Paṭika refers to a white woolen coverlet. Paṭalikā refers to a woolen coverlet with dense floral patterns, also called a coverlet with patterns like gooseberry leaves. Tūlikā refers to a mattress stuffed with one of the three types of cotton or floss. Vikatikā refers to a woolen coverlet variegated with figures of lions, tigers, etc. Uddalomī refers to a woolen coverlet with fringe on both sides; some say it is a coverlet with flowers appearing on one side. Ekantalomī refers to a woolen coverlet with fringe on one side; some say it is a coverlet with flowers appearing on both sides. Kaṭṭissa refers to an upper coverlet woven with coarse silk and embroidered with gems, gold, or silver thread. Koseyya refers to a silk coverlet embroidered with gems, gold, or silver thread. While the Vinaya states that a plain silk coverlet is allowable, the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary says that, except for the cotton-stuffed mattress, all coverlets like the gonaka that are embroidered with gems are not allowable.

Kuttaka refers to a woolen rug large enough for sixteen dancing women to stand and dance upon. Hatthatthara and Assatthara refer to rugs spread on the backs of elephants and horses. The same applies to rugs for chariots. Ajinappaveṇī refers to rugs made of panther skins the size of a couch...
84:
It is a multi-layered covering made by sewing. Kadalīmigapavarapaccattharaṇa means a noble upper covering made from the skin of the creature called Kadalī (antelope); it refers to an excellent upper covering. It is said that this covering is made by spreading and sewing the Kadalī skin over a white cloth. Sauttaracchada means a covering together with a red canopy fastened above. Even a white canopy is not allowable if there is an unallowable upper covering beneath it; however, if there is none, it is allowable. Ubhatolohitakūpadhāna refers to having red pillows at both the head and the foot of the couch; this is not allowable. However, if it is a single pillow that is red, lotus-colored, or variegated on both sides, it is allowable if it is of the proper size. A large pillow, however, is forbidden. Two pillows that are not red are indeed allowable. If one obtains more than those two, they should be given to others. If one is unable to give them away, one is allowed to sleep by laying them crosswise on the couch and placing an upper covering over them. In places such as the āsandī (long chair), one should practice in the same manner as mentioned. For it was said: 'Bhikkhus, I allow you to use an āsandī after cutting off its legs, to use a pallanka (couch) after removing the animal carvings, to make a pillow by unraveling a stuffed covering, and to use the remaining materials as floor coverings' (Cullavagga).

Regarding the terms such as uccādana (rubbing): the body odor of children born from the mother's womb disappears only when they reach the age of twelve; to remove the bad body odor of those children, they are rubbed with scented powders and such; such rubbing is not allowable. Furthermore, they place meritorious children on their laps, smear them with oil, and massage their hands, feet, thighs, navel, etc., to make the shape of their limbs beautiful; such massaging is not allowable.

Nhāpana means bathing those same children with scented water and such. Sambāhana means striking the hands and feet with mallets and such, like great wrestlers, to make the arms grow large. Ādāsa means it is not allowable to carry any kind of mirror as a personal possession. Añjana refers only to applying collyrium for the sake of adornment. Māla refers to either strung flowers or unstrung flowers. Vilepana refers to the application of any kind of scented ointment that beautifies the skin. Mukhacuṇṇa and mukhalepana mean: to remove freckles, pimples, etc., from the face, they apply a fine medicinal clay; when the blood circulates due to that application, they apply mustard powder; when the blood defects are eliminated by that mustard powder, they apply sesame powder; when the blood becomes settled by that sesame powder, they apply turmeric powder; when the complexion of the skin improves due to that turmeric powder, they rub the face with face powder; all of that is not allowable.
85:
Regarding hand ornaments and such, people wander about with ornate shells and the like tied to their hands. Neither those shell ornaments nor any other kind of hand ornament is allowable. Others wander about with their hair tied in a topknot. They encircle that topknot with gold pins, strings of pearls, and so on. All such ornamentation is not allowable. Some people wander about carrying a four-cubit staff or other decorated sticks. Likewise, it is not allowable to carry a medicine tube or container that is decorated with figures of women and men, well-encased, and hung on the left side. Some carry a very sharp sword with a scabbard encrusted with crest-gems, or an umbrella sewn with five-colored threads and decorated with makara patterns and such, or sandals decorated with gold, silver, etc., and bordered with peacock feathers and the like. Some, showing the hairline, bind a diadem plate on the forehead like a flash of lightning in a cloud, the plate being about one cubit long and four finger-breadths wide. They wear a crest-gem (cūḷāmaṇi). They carry a fly-whisk made of a yak's tail. All such practices are not allowable.

Because it is contrary to the path to heaven and the path to Nibbāna, and because it does not lead out of saṃsāra, such talk is called tiracchānakathā (lowly talk). Among those lowly talks, talk concerning kings, such as "King Mahāsammata, King Mandhātu, and King Dhammāsoka possessed such great power and majesty," is called rājakathā (talk about kings). This same method applies to talk about thieves and so on. Among those, talk that is based on sensual pleasure, such as "Such and such a king is very handsome and beautiful to look at," is indeed tiracchānakathā. However, talk that proceeds as, "Even a king of such great power and majesty has come to destruction," stands as a subject of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna). Among thieves, talk based on sensual pleasure concerning their deeds, such as "The great thief Mūladeva was so powerful; the great thief Meghamāla was so powerful; oh, how brave they were!" is indeed tiracchānakathā. In the case of war, talk about the Bhārata war and such, spoken for the sake of sensual enjoyment, such as "This person killed that person in this way; he struck him in that way," is tiracchānakathā. However, talk that proceeds as, "Even those people have come to destruction," is indeed a subject of meditation in all instances.

Furthermore, regarding food and such, it is not allowable to speak for the sake of sensual enjoyment, saying, "We have chewed and eaten food so endowed with color, scent, taste, and texture." However, it is allowable to speak for a purposeful reason, saying, "In the past, we offered alms-food, hard food, drinks, clothing, beds, flowers, and scents endowed with such color and so on to virtuous persons, and we performed offerings at the shrine."
