Now, with the turn (vāra) beginning with "Monks, by these things...", He concludes all those speculators about the future (aparantakappika) together and reveals His omniscience (sabbaññutañāṇa). Again, with the turn beginning with "Monks, by these things...", He concludes all those speculators about the past and the future (pubbantāparantakappika) together and reveals that same omniscience. Thus, even when asking, "Monks, what are those things?", He asks only about His omniscience; and when answering, He reveals only His omniscience, having extracted the sixty-two views as if weighing the dispositions (ajjhāsaya) of beings with a scale, or as if extracting sand from the foot of Mount Sineru. Thus, this teaching has come by way of connection (anusandhi).

There are three types of connections in a Sutta: connection by question (pucchānusandhi), connection by disposition (ajjhāsayānusandhi), and connection by sequence (yathānusandhi). Among these, when it was said, another monk said this to the Blessed One: "What..."
113:
"Venerable Sir, what is the near shore? What is the far shore? What is sinking in the middle? What is grounding on a sandbank? What is being caught by humans? What is being caught by non-humans? What is being caught by a whirlpool? What is internal rottenness?" (Saṃ. Ni. 4.241). The connection by question (pucchānusandhi) should be understood by way of the Sutta answered by the Blessed One to those asking in this manner.

Then, a reflection arose in the mind of a certain monk: "So it seems, friends, form is non-self... feeling... perception... formations... consciousness is non-self. What self will the deeds done by the non-self touch?" Then the Blessed One, knowing the reflection in that monk's mind with His own mind, addressed the monks: "Monks, it is possible that some hollow man here, being ignorant and fallen into nescience, with a mind dominated by craving, might think he should overstep the Teacher's instruction thus: 'So it seems, friends, form is non-self... [as above] ...will they touch?' Monks, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?" (Ma. Ni. 3.10). Thus, the connection by disposition (ajjhāsayānusandhi) should be understood by way of the Sutta spoken by the Blessed One after knowing the desires and dispositions of others.

In those Suttas where the teaching proceeds further by way of a doctrine that is either suitable to or opposite to the doctrine with which the teaching began at the start, the connection by sequence (yathānusandhi) should be understood by way of those. For example: in the Ākaṅkheyya Sutta, the teaching begins with virtue (sīla) in the lower part, and the six super-knowledges (abhiññā) come in the upper part. In the Vattha Sutta, the teaching begins with defilements (kilesa) in the lower part, and the divine abodes (brahmavihāra) come in the upper part. In the Kosambaka Sutta, it begins with quarreling in the lower part, and the principles of cordiality (sāraṇīyadhamma) come in the upper part. In the Kakacūpama Sutta, it begins with intolerance in the lower part, and the simile of the saw comes in the upper part. In this Brahmajāla Sutta also, the teaching begins by way of views (diṭṭhi) in the lower part, and the explanation of emptiness (suññatā) comes in the upper part. Therefore, it is said: "Thus, this teaching has come by way of connection by sequence (yathānusandhi)."

## Commentary on the Section on Agitation and Vacillation

105-117. Now, for the purpose of showing the division of boundaries, the teaching beginning with "Therein, monks..." is commenced. That teaching also [shows] that the experience of those venerable recluses and brahmins who do not know and do not see, and who are possessed by craving, is merely the agitation and vacillation of craving by which...
114:
Those recluses and brahmins, being joyful through the enjoyment of views, the pleasure of views, and the experience of views, proclaim the self and the world to be eternal based on four grounds. For those venerable recluses and brahmins who thus proclaim, not knowing and not seeing the nature of things as they really are, their experience (vedanā) is merely the arrival of craving for those who are possessed by craving. That experience is indeed only the agitation and vacillation of one who is anxious through craving and views. This agitation and vacillation through what is called view and what is called craving is like a stake driven into a heap of chaff; it is not stable and steady like the vision of a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). This method applies also to the partial-eternalists and so forth.

## Explanation of the Section on the Condition of Contact

118-130. Again, the Buddha began the teaching with "Therein, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists..." and so forth, in order to show the sequence of conditions. Therein, by the words "that too is conditioned by contact," he shows that the experience agitated by craving and views—whereby they proclaim the self and the world to be eternal based on four grounds while being joyful through the enjoyment of views, the pleasure of views, and the experience of views—is also conditioned by contact. This method is the same in all cases.

131-143. Now, to show the powerful nature of contact as a condition for the experience of views, he said again: "Therein, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists..." and so forth. Therein, "they [cannot experience] apart from contact" means there is no possibility that those recluses and brahmins would experience that feeling without contact. For example, just as a pillar is a powerful condition for supporting a house that is about to fall, and that house cannot stand without the support of the pillar, so too contact is a powerful condition for feeling; he shows that without contact, this experience of views cannot exist. This method is the same in all cases.

## Explanation of the Discourse on the Cycle of Existence as the Basis for Those Following Views

Now, by the method starting with "Therein, bhikkhus, those recluses and brahmins who are eternalists and proclaim the self and the world to be eternal based on four grounds," he summarizes all experiences of views with "those recluses and brahmins who are partial-eternalists," and so forth. Why? For the purpose of including them under contact further on. How? By saying, "All of them experience by repeatedly touching with the six bases of contact." Therein, the six bases of contact are: the eye-contact base, the ear-contact base, the nose-contact base, the tongue-contact base, the body-contact base, and the mind-contact base. In the senses of origin, meeting place, cause, and mere designation...
115:
This word 'āyatana' occurs [in various senses]. Among those senses, in the passage "Kamboja is the āyatana of horses, the Southern Path (Dakkhiṇāpatha) is the āyatana of cattle," it occurs in the sense of origin (sañjāti), meaning the place of birth. In the passage "Birds resort to that āyatana which is delightful to the mind," it occurs in the sense of a meeting place (samosaraṇa). In the passage "When there is a cause (āyatana), there is [the result]," it occurs in the sense of cause (kāraṇa). In the passage "They dwell in leaf-huts in the forest-base (araññāyatana)," it occurs in the sense of mere designation (paṇṇattimatta). This word āyatana is suitable in all three senses—origin and so forth—in this context [of the bases of contact]. For in the eye and so forth, the states beginning with contact as the fifth arise and meet; and those [bases] are the cause of those states; therefore, they are called āyatanas.

In this context, however, by the method "Dependent on the eye and forms, eye-consciousness arises; the meeting of the three is contact," the teaching is presented with contact as the head. Starting with contact, the sequence of conditions is shown, and thus "bases of contact" and so forth are spoken.

"They experience by repeatedly touching" (phussa phussa paṭisaṃvedenti) means they experience after having touched again and again. Here, although it is spoken as if the bases have the function of touching, it should not be understood that they have the function of touching. For the bases do not touch; only contact touches the respective objects. The bases are shown by being included within contact. Therefore, the meaning here should be understood thus: all those recluses and brahmins, through contact produced by the six bases of contact, touch objects such as forms and experience the feeling that is the cause of those views.

In the passages such as "With feeling as condition, craving [arises]," feeling refers to the feeling produced by the six bases of contact. That feeling is a condition for craving—divided into craving for forms and so forth—by way of the proximity (decisive support) condition (upanissaya). Therefore, it is said: "With feeling as condition, craving [arises]." That craving is a condition for the four types of clinging by way of both the proximity condition and the conascence condition (sahajāta). Likewise, clinging is a condition for existence, and existence is a condition for birth by way of the proximity condition.

Here, "birth" (jāti) should be understood as the five aggregates along with their transformations. Birth is a condition for aging and death, as well as for sorrow and so forth, by way of the proximity condition. This is a summary here; the detailed explanation of Dependent Origination is stated in the Visuddhimagga. Here, only what is necessary for this [Brahmajāla Sutta] should be understood. For when the Blessed One speaks the discourse on the cycle of existence, [he says]: "Bhikkhus, the preceding point of ignorance is not evident, such that one could say, 'Before this, ignorance did not exist, but afterwards it came to be.' Yet, bhikkhus, it is said thus, and it is evident that 'Ignorance is conditioned by this.'" Thus, either with ignorance as the head, or [as he says], "Bhikkhus, the preceding..."
116:
The prior limit of craving for existence is not evident... 'Because of this cause, craving for existence arises'—thus He taught, making craving the head. Or, 'Monks, the prior limit of the view of existence is not evident... Because of this cause, the view of existence arises'—thus He taught, making wrong view the head. However, in this Brahmajāla Sutta, while teaching with wrong view as the head, He taught the wrong views that arise due to attachment to feeling, and then He taught the dependent origination rooted in feeling. By teaching thus, He showed that those with such wrong views, holding onto this view, wander and circulate from this existence to that, and from that existence to this, within the three realms, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings. Like an ox yoked to a mill, like a dog bound to a post, or like a boat wrecked by the wind, they merely revolve within the suffering of the cycle and are unable to lift their heads above the suffering of the cycle.

## Explanation of the Discourse on the Cessation of the Cycle, etc.

Having thus taught the cycle (vaṭṭa) which is the standing place of those with wrong views, He now spoke the words beginning with, 'Monks, when a monk...' desiring to show the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) by making the monk who practices meditation the standing place. Therein, 'yato' means 'when'. 'Of the six bases of contact' refers to those same six bases of contact by which those with wrong views, through contacting and experiencing, continue to revolve in the cycle. Regarding the terms such as 'arising' (samudaya), the arising and so forth of the bases of contact should be understood according to the method already mentioned in the meditation on feeling (vedanākammaṭṭhāna), such as 'with the arising of ignorance, the eye arises'. However, unlike what was said in that meditation on feeling as 'with the arising of contact, with the cessation of contact', here, in the case of the eye and so forth, it should be understood as 'with the arising of nutriment, with the cessation of nutriment'. In the case of the mind base (manāyatana), it should be understood as 'with the arising of name-and-form, with the cessation of name-and-form'.

'He knows further' means that a person with wrong view knows only the wrong view. This monk, however, knows the wrong view and also knows that which is further than the wrong view—virtue, concentration, wisdom, and liberation—up until Arahatship. Who knows in this way? An Arahat knows, a Non-returner, a Once-returner, a Stream-enterer, a monk who is learned and a bearer of the scriptures knows, and a person who has begun insight meditation (vipassanā) knows. This teaching, however, is concluded at the summit of Arahatship.
117:
Having thus taught the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa), He began again, saying, 'Monks, those who...' in order to show that 'there is no one with wrong views who escapes from the net of the teaching.' In that passage, 'antojālီkatā' means they are made to be within this net of my teaching (they are included). 'Ettha sitā vā' means they are dependent on, clinging to, or remaining within this net of my teaching. 'Ummuzzamānā ummuzzanti' (emerging, they emerge)—what does this mean? Whether those with wrong views sink down or rise up, they do so while being dependent on the net of my teaching. Being included in this net of the teaching, connected to this net, and remaining within the net, they emerge. There is no one with wrong views who is not included in this teaching.

'Sukhuma-acchikena' means with a net that has subtle and small meshes (holes). The Blessed One is like a fisherman; the teaching is like a net; the ten-thousandfold world system is like a small amount of water; the sixty-two types of wrong views are like large creatures such as fish and turtles. Just as a fisherman standing on the shore sees the large creatures caught within the net, the Blessed One sees all those with wrong views included within the net of His teaching. Thus should the comparison with the simile be understood.

Having thus shown how all those with wrong views are included in this net of the teaching because all views are encompassed by these sixty-two views, He now spoke the words beginning with, 'Monks, the body of the Tathāgata has the cord of existence cut,' desiring to show that He Himself is not included in any existence or mode of birth. In that passage, 'netti' is so called because one is led or pulled by it. It is a name for a rope that pulls after being tied to the neck. Here, however, craving for existence is intended as 'netti' because it is like a rope. That craving is called 'bhavanetti' (the cord of existence) because it ties the multitude of beings by the neck and leads them to various existences. He is called 'ucchinnabhavanettika' because He has the cord of existence cut by the weapon of the path of Arahatship.

'After the breaking up of the body' means after death. 'With the exhaustion of life' means because the life-faculty is entirely exhausted and finished, or it means the state of not taking rebirth again. 'They will not see Him' means that neither gods nor humans will see that Tathāgata; it means He will reach a state that cannot be designated (apaṇṇattikabhāva).
118:
"Bhikkhus, for example," in this statement, the comparison is as follows: The body of the Tathāgata is like a mango tree; the craving that occurred in previous lives, depending on which this body exists, is like the large stalk produced on the tree. Just as a cluster of mangoes—numbering five, twelve, or eighteen—is attached to that stalk, so too, when there is craving, being bound by craving, the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements that will arise in the future (are attached to that stalk of craving). When that stalk is cut, all those mangoes follow the fate of the stalk; that is to say, they are cut off because the stalk is cut. In the same way, as long as the stalk of craving for existence (bhavanetti) is not yet cut, the five aggregates, twelve bases, and eighteen elements that would arise in the future follow the course of that craving for existence; when that craving for existence is cut, all those phenomena are indeed cut off. 

Just as on that very tree, due to the touch of the venom of a frog-thorn, it gradually withers and dies, and there remains only the mere expression, "In this place, there used to be such a tree," but no one can see that tree anymore; in the same way, due to the touch of the Noble Path, the sap of craving is exhausted, and like something that has gradually withered, when this body breaks up, after the breaking up of the body and the exhaustion of the life-faculty, gods and humans will no longer see the Tathāgata. There will only be the mere expression, "Such was the teaching of a Teacher of such a nature." Thus, the Buddha concluded the discourse, leading it to the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbāna-dhātu).

When the Blessed One had spoken this discourse, the Venerable Ānanda, having reflected on the entire sutta from beginning to end, thought: "The Blessed One has preached this sutta demonstrating the power of the Buddha's knowledge, but he has not yet given a name to the sutta. Now, I shall ask him to give it a name." Thinking thus, he addressed the Blessed One.

In the words beginning with "Tasmātiha tvaṃ" (Therefore, you...), the connection of the meaning is: "Ānanda, because in this Dhamma-discourse (Dhamma-pariyāya), the benefit of this life and the benefit of the future life are distinguished, therefore, you should remember this Dhamma-discourse as the 'Net of Advantage' (Atthajāla). Because many doctrines (Dhamma) are preached in this sutta, you should also remember it as the 'Net of Dhamma' (Dhammajāla). Because the supreme Omniscient Knowledge is distinguished here in its noble sense, you should also remember it as the 'Net of the Supreme' (Brahmajāla). Because the sixty-two wrong views are distinguished here, you should also remember it as the 'Net of Views' (Diṭṭhijāla). Because, having heard this Dhamma-discourse, even the Māra of the gods (Devaputta-māra), the Māra of the aggregates (Khandha-māra), and the Māra of death (Maccu-māra)..."
119:
"...and even the Māra of defilements (Kilesa-māra) can be subdued, therefore, you should also remember it as the 'Incomparable Victory in Battle' (Anuttara Saṅgāmavijaya)."

"The Blessed One said this" means the entire sutta from the end of the introduction (nidāna) to the end where it says, "You should also remember it as the Incomparable Victory in Battle." The Blessed One spoke, revealing the extremely profound Omniscient Knowledge, which has a foundation unattainable by the wisdom of others, destroying the great darkness of wrong views just as the sun dispels the darkness.

"Those bhikkhus were delighted" means those bhikkhus were satisfied in their own minds; it means they had uplifted minds due to the joy directed towards the Buddha. "The words spoken by the Blessed One" refers to the words of the Blessed One who was speaking with a Brahma-voice (brahmassara), which is pleasant and agreeable to the ear like the song of the Karavīka bird, and which is like a sprinkling of nectar upon the hearts of wise people—this sutta being endowed with such a variety of methods and beauty of teaching. "They rejoiced (abhinanduṃ)" means they both rejoiced repeatedly and accepted it. This word "abhinanda" appears in the sense of craving in passages such as "abhinandati abhivadati" (he rejoices and welcomes). It appears in the sense of approaching (upagamana) in passages such as "Both gods and humans approach (abhinandanti) only food."

"When a man who has been long absent returns safely from afar,
his kinsmen, friends, and well-wishers rejoice (abhinandanti) at his arrival."

In such passages, it appears in the sense of accepting (sampaṭicchana). In passages such as "having rejoiced and appreciated (abhinanditvā anumoditvā)," it appears in the sense of repeated rejoicing (anumodana). Here, it is appropriate in the senses of both repeated rejoicing and accepting. Therefore, it is said: "'They rejoiced' means they both rejoiced repeatedly and accepted it."

The bhikkhus, appreciating the well-spoken words
of the One of such a nature (Tādi), who is unshaken by the eight worldly conditions,
accepted them with their heads bowed,
saying, "Sādhu, Sādhu."

"In this exposition (veyyākaraṇa)" means in this sutta which is without verses. Because it is without verses, this sutta is called an exposition (veyyākaraṇa).

"The ten thousandfold world system" means the world system with the extent of ten thousand universes (cakkavāḷa). "It shook" means it should be understood that it did not shake only at the conclusion of the sutta. It is said, "while it was being spoken." Therefore, while the sixty-two wrong views were being dismantled...
120:
It should be understood that the earth shook sixty-two times at the conclusion of each of those specific views as they were being taught.

Regarding that earthquake, it should be known to occur due to eight causes: due to the disturbance of the elements, due to the power of one possessing psychic power, due to the Bodhisatta’s descent into the mother’s womb, due to his birth from the mother’s womb, due to his attainment of supreme enlightenment, due to his setting in motion the Wheel of Dhamma, due to his relinquishing the life-principle, and due to his final passing away (Parinibbāna). The decision regarding these causes will be stated at the time of explaining the text from the Mahā-Parinibbāna Sutta: "Ānanda, these eight causes and eight conditions lead to the manifestation of a great earthquake."

However, this great earth also shook on eight other occasions: during the Great Renunciation, when approaching the seat of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), when taking up the rag-robe, when washing the rag-robe, during the teaching of the Kāḷakārāma Sutta, during the teaching of the Gotamaka Sutta, in the Vessantara Jātaka, and in this Brahmajāla Sutta. Among these, it shook due to the power of effort during the Great Renunciation and when approaching the seat of enlightenment. When taking up the rag-robe, it shook struck by the force of amazement, thinking, "The Blessed One, having renounced the four great islands with their two thousand surrounding small islands and become a monk, has gone to the cemetery and is taking up a rag-robe—how difficult a task he performs!" During the washing of the rag-robe and in the Vessantara Jātaka, it shook with an untimely shaking. In the Kāḷakārāma Sutta and the Gotamaka Sutta, it shook as a witness, as if saying, "I am the witness, O Blessed One." In this Brahmajāla Sutta, however, it should be understood that it shook by the power of the applause (Sādhukāra) while the sixty-two views were being untangled and taught without confusion.

Not only on these occasions did the earth shake, but it also shook during the three Councils, and on the day when the Elder Mahā-Mahinda arrived at this island, sat in the Jotivana, and taught the Dhamma. Also, at the Kalyāṇī Vihāra, when the Elder Piṇḍapātiya swept the courtyard of the shrine, sat there, and while experiencing joy with the Buddha as the object, practiced this Sutta; at the conclusion of the Sutta, the earth shook as far as the water's edge. Also, at the place called Eastern Ambalaṭṭhika of the Lohapāsāda, the Dīghabhāṇaka (Reciters of the Long Discourses) elders began the Brahmajāla Sutta, and at the conclusion of their recitation, the earth shook as far as the water's edge.
121:
Thus, by whose power the earth shook many times when this Brahmajāla Sutta, the most excellent of discourses, was being preached by the Self-Enlightened One.

Let the wise ones in this Dispensation, having respectfully learned the Dhamma and the meaning of that Brahmajāla Sutta, practice it thoroughly and correctly.

## Thus, in the Dīgha Nikāya Commentary named Sumaṅgalavilāsinī,
## the Commentary on the Brahmajāla Sutta is concluded.
122:
## 2. Commentary on the Sāmaññaphala Sutta
## Commentary on the Account of the King’s Ministers

From "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" up to "Rājagahe" is the Sāmaññaphala Sutta. Herein, this is the sequential commentary on the new terms (not previously mentioned): "Rājagahe" means in the city of that name. For that city is called Rājagaha because it was occupied and ruled by such personages as King Mandhātu and the chaplain Mahāgovinda. Others also explain various details here, but what is the use of those details? This is merely the name of that city. Furthermore, that city exists as a city during the time of Buddhas and during the time of Cakkavatti (Universal) kings; at other times, it is empty of humans and occupied by Yakkhas, remaining as their playground forest.

The word "viharati" (dwells) indicates, without distinction, being endowed with one of the dwellings such as the dwelling in postures (iriyāpatha-vihara), the divine dwelling (dibba-vihara), the brahma dwelling (brahma-vihara), or the noble dwelling (ariya-vihara). Here, however, it indicates being engaged in one of the postures among the varieties of standing, walking, sitting, and lying down. Therefore, whether standing, walking, sitting, or lying down, the Blessed One should be understood as "viharati" (dwelling). For the Blessed One carries on and maintains the physical body without it falling by interrupting the discomfort of one posture with another posture; therefore, he is said to "dwell" (viharati).

"Jīvakassa komārabhaccassa ambavane" (in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove) indicates the place of residence near the alms-resort village (gocaragāma) where he dwells. Therefore, the meaning should be understood as: he dwells in Jīvaka Komārabhacca’s mango grove near Rājagaha. For here, the locative case (bhummavacana) expresses the sense of proximity. In that context, he is called "Jīvaka" because he lives (jīvati), and "Komārabhacca" because he was nourished by the prince (kumārena bhata).

As stated in the Mahāvagga: "I say, what is this surrounded by crows?" "It is a baby boy, your majesty." "I say, does he live?" "He lives, your majesty." "In that case, I say, take that boy to our inner palace and give him to the nurses to nourish." They named him "Jīvaka" because he lived. They named him "Komārabhacca" because he was caused to be nourished by the prince. This is just a summary here. The full account, however, has already appeared in the Jīvaka-vatthu of the Khandhaka. The explanatory discussion on this has also been stated in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya commentary.
123:
On one occasion, this Jīvaka, having treated the Blessed One’s body which was congested with humors by administering a purgative, offered a pair of Siveyyaka cloths. At the conclusion of the thanksgiving for the offering of cloth, he was established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpatti-phala) and thought: "I should go to attend upon the Buddha two or three times a day. This Veḷuvana monastery is very far, but my Mango Grove (Ambavana) park is much closer. What if I were to have a monastery built for the Blessed One in this Mango Grove?" In that Mango Grove, he provided night quarters, day quarters, caves, cells, pavilions, and so forth, and had a Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) suitable for the Blessed One built. He also had the Mango Grove enclosed by a wall eighteen cubits high and the color of copper plates. Having satisfied the Saṅgha of monks headed by the Buddha with robes and food, he poured the water of dedication and handed over the monastery. It was in reference to that monastery that it was said, "In the Mango Grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca."

"With twelve hundred and fifty monks" means together with thirteen hundred monks minus fifty. In the words such as "King" (Rājā), he is called a "King" because he shines with the fulfillment of his own sovereignty and wealth, and because he pleases and prospers the great multitude with the four bases of sympathy (saṅgahavatthu). He is called "Māgadha" because he is the lord of the Magadhans. He is called "Ajātasattu" because he was pointed out by soothsayers as one who would be the king's enemy even before he was born.

While he was in the womb, a pregnancy craving (dohala) arose in the Queen: "O, that I might drink the blood from the King's right arm!" The Queen thought, "This craving has arisen in a difficult situation; it is impossible to tell anyone." Being unable to speak of it, she became thin and pale. Then the King asked, "Lady, your appearance is not as usual. What is the reason?" Although she said, "Do not ask, Great King," he urged her repeatedly, saying, "Lady, if you do not tell your desire to me, to whom will you tell it?" and made her speak. Having heard her, he said, "Foolish woman, why did you think this was difficult?" He then summoned a physician, had the arm opened with a small golden knife, took the blood in a golden bowl, mixed it with water, and gave it to her to drink. When the soothsayers heard of this, they prophesied: "This fetus will be the King's enemy; this person will kill the King." When the Queen heard this, she thought, "The one who comes out of my womb will kill the King," and desiring to abort the fetus, she went to the garden and had her belly pressed, but the fetus did not fall. She went again and again and did the same. The King, for what purpose...
124:
Investigating why she went to the garden so often, the King heard the reason and said: "Lady, it is not yet known whether it is a son or a daughter in your womb. If you do this to a child born of your own womb, a great mass of demerit will become manifest for us in the land of Jambudīpa. Do not do this," and he provided her with protection. At the time of birth, she thought, "I will kill him," but even then, the guards took the child away. Later, at another time, they showed the grown prince to the Queen. As soon as she saw him, motherly love arose, and she was no longer able to kill him. The King also gradually gave the prince the position of viceroy (oparajja).

Then, on one occasion, Devadatta went into seclusion and thought: "The Venerable Sāriputta has a following, the Venerable Mahāmoggallāna has a following, the Venerable Mahākassapa has a following; thus they are each leaders. I too will take up a leadership role." He thought, "It is impossible to produce a following without gain. Now, I will generate gain." Having thought thus, following the method found in the Khandhaka, he inspired Prince Ajātasattu with a feat of psychic power. Knowing the prince was very trusting, coming to attend upon him with five hundred chariots evening and morning, he approached him one day and said: "Prince, in the past, humans were long-lived; now they are short-lived. Therefore, Prince, you kill your father and become King; I will kill the Blessed One and become the Buddha." Thus he urged the prince to kill his father.

The prince thought, "Venerable Devadatta is of great power; there is nothing unknown to this venerable one." He strapped a dagger to his thigh and, even in broad daylight, entered the inner palace, fearful, agitated, suspicious, and trembling, and committed the aforementioned perverted act. Then the ministers seized and interrogated him, and having consulted together saying, "The Prince should be killed, Devadatta should be killed, and all the monks should be killed," they informed the King, saying they would act according to the King's command.

The King stripped the ministers who wanted to kill of their positions and placed those who did not want to kill in high positions. He then asked the prince, "Prince, why do you want to kill me?" When he replied, "Sire, I desire the kingdom," the King gave him the kingdom.
125:
Prince Ajātasattu informed Devadatta, "My heart's desire has been fulfilled." Then Devadatta said to him, "You think you have accomplished your task like a man who covers a drum with skin while keeping a jackal inside. Within a few days, your father will reflect on the insult you have committed and will become king himself again."

Then he asked, "Venerable sir, if that is so, what should I do?" "Kill him by uprooting him (mūlaghaccaṃ)," Devadatta replied. "Venerable sir, is my father not one who should not be killed by a weapon?" he asked again. "Then kill him by deprivation of food," Devadatta instructed.

King Ajātasattu then had his father placed in a heating house (tāpanageha). A heating house is a smoke-house built for the purpose of torture. He also gave an order, "Do not allow anyone to see him except for my mother."

The Queen placed rice in a golden bowl, hid it in her lap, and entered. The King sustained himself by eating that rice. When Ajātasattu asked, "How is my father sustaining himself?" and learned the truth, he ordered, "Do not allow my mother to enter with anything in her lap."

From then on, the Queen hid rice within her hair-knot and entered. Hearing of this also, he said, "Do not allow her to enter with her hair tied in a knot." Subsequently, she placed rice in golden sandals, sealed them, and entered wearing the sandals. The King sustained himself with that rice. Again, when he asked, "How is he sustaining himself?" and learned the truth, he ordered, "Do not allow her to enter even wearing sandals."

From then on, the Queen bathed in scented water, smeared her body with the four sweet delicacies (catumadhura), wrapped herself in a cloak, and entered. The King sustained himself by licking her body. Again, after inquiring and learning the truth, Ajātasattu ordered, "From today onwards, forbid my mother from entering."

The Queen stood at the prison door and cried out, "Lord Bimbisāra, when this son was young, you did not allow him to be killed; you yourself raised your own enemy. Now, this is the last time I shall see you. From now on, I shall not have the opportunity to see you, Great King. If I have any fault, please forgive me, my Lord." After weeping and lamenting, she departed.

From that time on, the King had no food. The King sustained himself through the bliss of the Paths and Fruits (magga-phala) and by walking meditation (caṅkama). His physical radiance was exceedingly bright. Ajātasattu asked, "I say, how is my father surviving?" When he heard, "Great King, he sustains himself by walking meditation, and his physical radiance is exceedingly bright," he thought, "I will now destroy his walking meditation." He then sent barbers, saying, "Go, slit my father's soles with a razor, smear them with salt and oil, and roast them over smokeless embers of khadira wood."

When the King saw them, he thought, "Surely my son must have been prompted by someone; these men have come to..."
126:
(When King Bimbisāra saw the barbers,) he thought, "They must have come to trim my beard." The barbers went, paid homage, and stood there. When asked, "Why have you come?" they informed him of the order. When told, "Do as your king desires," they said, "Sit down, Great King," and after paying homage to the King, they said, "Great King, we are carrying out the King's command; please do not be angry with us. This act is not worthy of a righteous king (dhammarāja) like you." Then, holding his ankles with their left hands and a razor with their right hands, they slit his soles, smeared them with salt and oil, and roasted them over smokeless embers of khadira wood.

It is said that in the past, the King had walked upon a pagoda courtyard (cetiyaṅgaṇa) wearing sandals, and had stepped on a mat spread for the monks to sit on with unwashed feet; this was the consequence of that deed. Intense pain arose in the King. While recollecting, "Oh, the Buddha! Oh, the Dhamma! Oh, the Saṅgha!", he withered away like a discarded flower on a pagoda courtyard and was reborn in the realm of the Four Great Kings (Cātumahārājikā) as a Yakkha named Janavasabha, an attendant of King Vessavaṇa.

On that very day, a son was born to Ajātasattu. Two letters arrived at the same moment: one to announce the birth of his son and the other to announce the death of his father. The ministers thought, "We will first announce the birth of the son," and placed that letter in the King's hand. At that moment, love for his son arose in the King, shaking his entire body and piercing through to the marrow of his bones. In that instant, he understood the gratitude due to a father, thinking, "When I was born, such love must have surely arisen in my father as well."

The King said, "Go, friends, and release my father." They replied, "What should we release, Great King?" and placed the other letter in his hand.

Upon hearing the news, he went to his mother weeping and asked, "Mother, did my father have love for me when I was born?" She replied, "Foolish son, what are you saying? When you were young, an abscess developed on your finger. When they could not stop your crying, they took you to your father who was sitting in the hall of judgment. Your father put your finger in his mouth. The abscess burst right in his mouth. Then, out of love for you, your father swallowed the pus mixed with blood without even spitting it out. Such was your father's love for you." He wept and lamented, and then performed the funeral rites for his father.
127:
Devadatta also approached Ajātasattu and said, "Great King, give the command and send men who can deprive the ascetic Gotama of life." He then sent the men provided by the king. Furthermore, he himself climbed Gijjhakūṭa Hill and rolled down a stone using a machine, and also released the Nālāgiri elephant. However, being unable to kill the Blessed One by any means, and with his gains and honor declining, he requested the five points. When he did not obtain those points, he thought, "I will win over the people with these points (showing that my practice is superior)," and thus he committed a schism in the Saṅgha. When the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna took the assembly and departed, Devadatta, due to intense grief, vomited hot blood and remained lying on a sickbed for nine months. Feeling remorse, he asked, "Where is the Teacher residing now?" Upon hearing, "He is residing at Jetavana Monastery," he said, "Carry me on a small couch and let me have the opportunity to pay homage to the Teacher." While being carried, because he had not performed the kamma worthy of seeing the Blessed One, he entered the earth which split into two near the pond of Jetavana Monastery and was established in the great Avīci hell. This is a brief summary here. The detailed account appears in the Khandhaka (Cūḷavagga, Saṅghabhedaka-khandhaka). Since it has already appeared in detail there, it is not fully recounted here. Thus, because the omen-readers pointed out even before he was born that he would be the king's enemy, he is called Ajātasattu (one who was an enemy even before birth).

'Vedehiputta' means he is the son of the daughter of the King of Kosala, not the son of the daughter of the King of Videha. 'Vedehī' is a designation for a wise woman. This is as stated: "Vedehikā, the housewife (the housewife who strives with wisdom)," and "The Venerable Ānanda, the Vedeha-sage (the monk Ānanda who strives with wisdom)." The word-definition (vacanattha) in that term is: they know by means of this wisdom, therefore that wisdom is called 'Veda'; it is a name for wisdom. Because she strives or endeavors with wisdom, she is called 'Vedehī'. Because he is the son of Vedehī (the wise woman), he is called 'Vedehiputta'.

'Tadahu' means it happened on that day; it means 'on that day'. They dwell on this day being endowed (with virtue, etc.), therefore it is called 'Uposatha'. It means they dwell being endowed either with virtue or by fasting. The extraction of meanings (atthuddhāra) here is: in such places as "Come, friend Kappina, let us go to the Uposatha," the recitation of the Pātimokkha is called 'Uposatha'. In such places as "Visākhā, the Uposatha endowed with these eight factors should be observed," virtue (sīla) is called 'Uposatha'. In such places as "For the pure, it is always the Phaggu festival; for the pure, it is always the Uposatha," fasting (upavāsa) is called 'Uposatha'. In such places as "The Naga king named Uposatha"...
128:
Prescription (paññatti) refers to the day to be observed, as in the Pali passages such as, "Monks, in those residences (āvāsa) where there are monks on that Uposatha day..." Here too, that very day is intended. That Uposatha day is of three kinds: the eighth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth. Therefore, to exclude the other two, it is said, "the fifteenth" (pannarasī). For that reason, it is said, "They observe (upavasanti) on this day, therefore it is called Uposatha."

'Komudiyā' means the night of the white water-lilies (kumuda). At that time, it is said, the white water-lilies are in full bloom; because those lilies are present there, it is called 'Komudī'. 'Cātumāsiniyā' means the Cātumāsī; that night is called 'Cātumāsī' because it is the conclusion of the four months of the rainy season. In this Pali, however, it is called 'Cātumāsinī'. It is called 'Puṇṇā' (full) because of the fullness of the month, the fullness of the season, and the fullness of the year. The moon is called 'Mā'; because that moon is full on this night, it is called 'Puṇṇamā'. Thus, the meaning of these two words 'Puṇṇāya Puṇṇamāya' should be understood.

'Rājāmaccaparivuto' means surrounded by royal ministers on a night that is beautiful with the radiance of the full moon free from the four defilements (upakkilesa), as if the quarters were being washed by streams of milk flowing from a silver jar, and as if surrounded by clusters of pearls, jasmine garlands, white cloth, and white water-lilies fallen from a silver celestial mansion. 'Uparipāsādavaragato' means he had gone to the upper floor of the noble palace. That king was sitting on a golden throne under a costly, well-raised white parasol. Why was he sitting? To dispel sleep. For this king, from the day he endeavored to kill his father, as soon as he closed his eyes thinking, "I will fall asleep," he would wake up screaming as if struck by a hundred spears. When asked, "What is this?" he would say, "It is nothing." Therefore, sleep was unpleasant for him, and thus he sat to dispel sleep. Furthermore, on that day, a constellation festival (nakkhatta) had been proclaimed. The entire city was sprinkled and swept, white sand was scattered, and house doors were decorated with five-colored flowers, parched rice, and full jars. All quarters were adorned with raised banners and flags and rows of brilliantly lit lamps, and the city was crowded with people enjoying the constellation festival in the main streets and alleys. They say he was also sitting because it was a festival day. However, even after saying this, the conclusion is made: "For royalty, it is always a festival; he was sitting only for the purpose of dispelling sleep."
129:
Regarding the phrase 'uttered an inspired utterance' (udānaṃ udānesi), it means he spoke words that were expressed with joy and delight. For example, just as oil overflows when it cannot be contained in a measuring cup, or water overflows when it cannot be contained in a tank, so too, words born of rapture (pīti) that cannot be contained in the heart and cannot remain within, break out externally; this is called an 'inspired utterance' (udāna). It means he emitted such words consisting of rapture.

'Dosinā' means being free from the five impurities: clouds, mist, smoke, dust, and Rāhu. Therefore, the five words of praise beginning with 'Ramaṇīyā' are used. Because it delights the minds of the people, it is called 'Ramaṇīyā' (delightful). Because it is illuminated by moonlight free from the five defects and is exceedingly beautiful, it is 'Abhirūpā' (beautiful). Because it is fit to be seen, it is 'Dassanīyā' (lovely). Because it gladdens the mind, it is 'Pāsādikā' (pleasant). Because it is worthy of being a mark of the day, month, etc., it is called 'Lakkhaññā' (auspicious).

Regarding 'To which recluse (samaṇa) or brahmin (brāhmaṇa) should we approach today?'—'Samaṇa' means one who has calmed evil; 'Brāhmaṇa' means one who has discarded evil. In saying 'one who will gladden our minds when we approach,' although there is a grammatical variation (vacanabyattaya), the meaning is that one's mind would be gladdened by hearing the sweet Dhamma from him while approaching to ask questions. With all these words, the King made an opening sign to Jīvaka for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One. Why did he do this to Jīvaka? It was for the purpose of seeing the Blessed One. If asked, 'Is the King himself unable to go see the Blessed One?'—Yes, he is unable. Why? Because of his great offense.

Because he killed his own father, a noble disciple (ariya-sāvaka) and a supporter of the Blessed One, and because he caused much harm to the Blessed One by relying on Devadatta, he has such a great offense that he does not dare to go himself. Since Jīvaka is a supporter of the Blessed One, the King made the opening sign, thinking, 'I will see the Blessed One under his shadow (protection).' If asked, 'Does Jīvaka know that this opening sign is for him?'—Yes, he knows. Then why did he remain silent? It was to cut off distraction.

In that assembly, many supporters of the other six teachers had gathered; having attended upon unskilled teachers, they themselves were unskilled. They, regarding the Blessed One's...
130:
Jīvaka thought: "If I begin to speak of the virtues of the Blessed One, these ministers will stand up from time to time and speak of the virtues of their own teachers. If they speak thus, the talk on the virtues of my teacher, the Blessed One, will not reach its conclusion. However, this King has approached the teachers of these ministers before and, knowing their lack of essence, will not be pleased with the talk of their virtues and will ask me again. Only then, without distraction, will I speak of the virtues of the Blessed One and take the King to the presence of the Blessed One." Knowing this, he remained silent for the sake of cutting off distraction.

Those ministers also thought: "Today the King praises the night with five terms. Surely he wishes to approach some recluse or brahmin, ask questions, and hear the Dhamma. If he becomes devoted after hearing someone's Dhamma, he will pay great honor to that person. If the recluse who is the teacher of a certain minister becomes the King's teacher, it will be good for that minister."

151-152. Having thought thus, they each strove to speak of the virtues of their own teachers, saying, "I will speak of the virtues of my own teacher and take the King; I will go." Therefore, the Venerable Ānanda said, "When this was said, a certain royal minister..." and so on. In that passage, 'Pūraṇa' is the name of that teacher who claimed to be a Buddha. 'Kassapa' is his clan name. It is said that he was born as the one who completed a hundred slaves in a certain family, so they named him 'Pūraṇa' (The Completer). Being an auspicious slave, there was no one to say "It is badly done," nor was there anyone to say "It is not done" regarding his duties. He thought, "Why should I live here?" and fled. Then thieves stripped him of his clothes. Not even knowing how to cover himself with leaves or grass, he entered a village naked. When people saw him, they approached him with cakes, rice, etc., saying, "This recluse is an Arahant who has few desires; there is no one like him." He thought, "These gains and honors have arisen because I am not wearing clothes." From then on, even when he obtained clothes, he did not wear them and took up that nakedness as his monkhood. Five hundred other men also went forth under him. Referring to him, it is said "Pūraṇa Kassapa."

He is called 'Saṅghī' because he has a community (saṅgha) known as a group of monks. He is called 'Gaṇီ' because he has that very group. He is called 'Gaṇācariya' because he is the teacher of that group by way of teaching conduct and training. He is called 'Ñāta' because he is well-known and famous.
131:
He is content. Because he has few desires, he does not even wear clothes; thus, having such fame, he is called 'famous' (yasassī). Because he creates a doctrine, he is called a 'sect-founder' (titthakara). Because he is regarded as a good man, a virtuous person, he is called 'regarded as good' (sādhusammata). The 'multitude' refers to the uninstructed, blind worldlings. Because he knows many nights passed since his ordination, he is called 'of long standing' (rattaññū). Because it has been a long time since he was ordained, he is 'long ordained' (cirapabbajita). The words of one recently ordained are not reliable; therefore, it is said 'long ordained'. 'One who has gone a long way' (addhagata) means one who has lived through two or three reigns of kings. 'One who has reached old age' (vayoanuppatta) means one who has reached the final stage of life. Both these terms are used to imply that 'the words of a young person are not reliable'.

'He remained silent' means it is like a man who, wishing to eat a sweet, golden-colored ripe mango, sees a ripe kāraja fruit placed in his hand. Although he wished to hear a sweet Dhamma discourse, endowed with qualities such as jhāna and higher knowledge (abhiññā) and marked with the three characteristics, he was displeased even by the sight of Pūraṇa Kassapa earlier; now, hearing false praise of his qualities, he became even more displeased and remained silent. Even though he was displeased, he thought, 'If I threaten this minister and have him removed by the neck, others will be afraid that the King does this to whoever speaks, and no one else will say anything.' Thus, enduring those unpleasant words, he remained silent. Then another minister thought, 'I will speak of the virtues of my own teacher,' and began to speak. Therefore, it is said, 'Then another [minister]...' and so on. All of this should be understood in the manner already described.

In this context, Makkhali is his name. Because he was born in a cowshed, he received the second name Gosāla. It is said that while he was walking on muddy ground carrying a pot of oil, his master said, 'Dear man, do not slip (mā khalī).' Out of negligence, he slipped and fell, and then began to run out of fear of his master. The master chased him and grabbed the edge of his garment. He abandoned the garment and fled naked (acelaka). The rest is similar to Pūraṇa Kassapa.

Ajita is his name. Because he wears a blanket made of human hair, he is called Kesakambala. Combining these two names, he is called Ajita Kesakambala.
132:
Among them, Kesakambala refers to a blanket made of human hair. There is no garment more inferior than that blanket made of human hair. As the Blessed One said: 'Monks, of all woven garments, the hair-blanket is said to be the worst. Monks, a hair-blanket is cold in the cold, hot in the heat, ugly in color, foul-smelling, and unpleasant to the touch (rough).'

Pakudha is the name of that teacher, and Kaccāyana is his clan (gotta). Combining the name and clan, he is called Pakudha Kaccāyana. He is one who rejects and does not use cold water. Even after defecating, he does not perform the duty of washing with water. He only washes when he obtains hot water or sour gruel (kañjiya). If he happens to cross a river or a puddle on the road, he thinks, 'My virtue is broken,' and after making a stupa of sand and re-undertaking his precepts, he continues his journey. He is one who holds such an inglorious doctrine.

Sañjaya is the name of that teacher, and because he is the son of Belaṭṭha, he is called Belaṭṭhaputta.

'We have no fetters of defilements that bind us (in saṃsāra), we are free from the knots of defilements.' Because of his doctrine of speaking thus, he is called Nigaṇṭha (fetterless) by way of the name he received. Because he is the son of Nāṭa, he is called Nātaputta.

## The Account of Jīvaka Komārabhacca

'Then the King...' means that when the King heard the words of those ministers, he thought: 'I do not wish to hear the words of those who have spoken, yet they are the ones who spoke. But the one whose words I wish to hear (Jīvaka) remains silent like a king of Garuḍas (Supaṇṇa) that has drunk Naga-fat; it is of no benefit to me.' Then this thought occurred to the King: 'Jīvaka is an attendant to the Blessed One, the Buddha, who is peaceful; he himself is also peaceful. Therefore, he sits silently like a monk endowed with proper conduct. He will not speak unless I ask him. Just as when being trampled by an elephant, one must grab the elephant's own foot (one must address Jīvaka directly),' he endeavored to consult with Jīvaka himself. Therefore, it is said, 'Then the King...' In that passage, 'Why are you silent?' means for what reason are you silent? These ministers' mouths are not enough to speak the praises of their own respective teachers. Do you not have a teacher to revere like them? Are you poor? Did my father not give you wealth and possessions? Or are you one who lacks faith? Thus he asks.
133: Then Jīvaka had this thought: "This King wishes me to speak of the virtues of my teacher. Now is not the time for me to remain silent. Just as these ministers, having paid homage to the King, spoke of the virtues of their own teachers while remaining seated, it is not proper for me to speak of the virtues of my teacher, the Blessed One, in such a manner." Jīvaka rose from his seat, faced the monastery where the Blessed One was residing, and paid homage with the fivefold prostration. Raising his joined palms, which shone with the radiance of his ten fingernails, to his head, he said: "Great King, do not think of me in this way, that I approach just any monk. For at the descent of my teacher into his mother's womb, at his birth from his mother's womb, at his Great Renunciation, at his Enlightenment, and at his turning of the Wheel of Dhamma, the ten-thousandfold world system shook. In this way, he performed the Twin Miracle; in this way, he performed the descent from the celestial realm. Great King, I shall speak of the virtues of my teacher; listen with a concentrated mind." Having said this, he spoke: "Great King, that Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One..." and so forth. In that passage, "taṃ kho pana bhagavantaṃ" uses the accusative case in the sense of itthambhūtākhyāna (state of being such), meaning "of that Blessed One." "Kalyāṇo" means endowed with beautiful qualities, meaning noble. "Kittisaddo" means a reputation of fame or the sound of praise. "Abbhuggato" means having spread and risen above the entire world including the devas. How? "For such reasons, that Blessed One is an Arahant, a Perfectly Enlightened One... the Blessed One." The connection of the words here is: That Blessed One is an Arahant for this reason, a Perfectly Enlightened One for this reason... a Blessed One for this reason. It means "due to this and that cause." Among those virtues, he is to be known as "Arahant" because he is remote from defilements, because he has killed the enemies (the defilements), because he has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra, because he is worthy of requisites and such, and because he does no evil even in secret. Having laid down this matrix (mātikā) in this manner, as all these terms are explained in detail in the Buddhānussati-niddesa of the Visuddhimagga, the detailed explanation should be taken from that text. Jīvaka, having concluded the meaning of each term, said: "In this way, Great King, my teacher is an Arahant; in this way, he is a Perfectly Enlightened One... in this way, he is the Blessed One." Then he said: "Your Majesty, please attend upon that Blessed One. Perhaps, as Your Majesty attends upon that Blessed One, your mind may become clear." In this context, while saying "Your Majesty, please attend upon him," he said: "Great King, for those like you, even by the hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands..."
134: "...my teacher, when questioned, possesses the power of the knowledge of teaching and the ten powers to answer by grasping the minds of all. Great King, approach and question him with confidence." As the King listened to the discourse on the virtues of the Blessed One, his entire body was suffused without interval by the five kinds of joy (pīti). At that very moment, desiring to go, he thought: "At this time, if I wish to go to the presence of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala), no one else but Jīvaka will be able to prepare the vehicles quickly." Then he said: "Friend Jīvaka, if that is so, have the elephant vehicles prepared." In that passage, "tena hi" is a particle used in the sense of urging. It means, "Go, friend Jīvaka." Regarding "hatthiyānāni" (elephant vehicles), although there were many vehicles such as horse-carriages and chariots, the elephant vehicle is the most noble. He thought that one should go to a noble person only by a noble vehicle. Furthermore, horse-carriages and chariots are noisy; their sound can be heard from afar. But even those following closely behind the footsteps of an elephant vehicle do not hear any sound. Thinking that one should go to the presence of the Blessed One, who is peaceful, only with peaceful vehicles, he said "elephant vehicles." "Pañcamattāni hatthinikasatāni" means five hundred she-elephants. "Kappāpetvā" means having them prepared and ready for riding. "Ārohaṇīyaṃ" means suitable for riding, meaning "opaguyhaṃ" (a secure royal mount). If it is asked whether Jīvaka did exactly as the King commanded or did what was not commanded, he did what was not commanded. Why? Because of his wisdom. For Jīvaka had this thought: "The King says he will go at this time, and kings have many enemies. If any danger should occur on the way, they will blame me, saying: 'What was Jīvaka thinking regarding our King? He took the King out even at an improper time.' They might also blame the Blessed One, saying: 'The ascetic Gotama, thinking "My discourse is proceeding," preaches the Dhamma without even considering the time.' Therefore, I will arrange it so that no blame arises for me or for the Blessed One, and the King's safety is well-provided." Then, considering that there is no danger for men when they rely on women, and thinking "I will go comfortably surrounded by women," he had five hundred she-elephants prepared. He had five hundred women dress in male attire and instructed them: "Surround the King, holding swords and spears." Then he thought again: "For this King, in this life..."
135:
(In this King's current existence), there is no longer a strong supporting condition (upanissaya) for the Paths and Fruits; the Buddhas only preach the Dhamma when they see such a strong supporting condition. Jīvaka thought: 'Now I will gather a great multitude. If the people are thus assembled, the Teacher will preach the Dhamma based on the supporting condition of someone, and that Dhamma will be of benefit to the great multitude.' That Jīvaka sent messages to various places and had the drums beaten, announcing: 'Today the King goes to the presence of the Blessed One; let everyone, according to their own wealth and power, take up the protection of the King.'

Then the people thought: 'It is said the King is going to see the Teacher. Friends, what will the Dhamma teaching be like? What benefit is there for us in the festival of the stars? Let us go to that very place.' All of them, taking perfumes, flowers, and so on, stood waiting on the road, expecting the King's arrival. Jīvaka also reported to the King: 'Great King, the elephant vehicles are prepared for you; now, go at the time you deem suitable.' In that speech, 'the time you deem suitable' is merely a conventional worldly expression. The meaning is: 'I have done whatever you commanded; now, make the time for going or not going according to your own desire.'

'Pacceka itthiyo' means individual women; it means one woman was placed on each elephant. 'Ukkāsu dhāriyamānāsu' means while torches were being held. 'Mahacca rājānubhāvena' means by the great majesty of the King. The Pali word 'mahaccā' has the meaning of 'mahatiyā' (great), and here the gender has been transformed. Royal majesty (rājānubhāva) refers to royal power (rājiddhi). What is that royal power? It is the glory of sovereignty over two great kingdoms spanning three hundred yojanas. Although the King had not made prior arrangements saying, 'On such and such a day I will approach the Tathāgata,' at that very moment, five hundred women took the appearance of men, wearing turbans, with swords slung over their shoulders, and holding gem-studded spears, and came forth. With reference to this, it is said: 'having mounted the women individually.'

Another sixteen thousand royal dancers surrounded the King. On their periphery were hunchbacks, dwarfs, Kirātas, and others. On their periphery were trusted palace guards. On their periphery were about sixty thousand ministers in various splendid costumes. On their periphery, adorned with various ornaments...
136:
About ninety thousand sons of the country (or local chiefs), like young Vidyādharas holding various weapons in their hands, followed in the retinue. On their periphery, about ten thousand Brahmins—clothed in garments worth a hundred, with garments worth five hundred draped over one shoulder, well-bathed and anointed, and beautified with various ornaments such as golden garlands—went raising their right hands and shouting the cry of victory, 'May the King be victorious!' On their periphery were musicians with five-fold instruments. On their periphery was a protective line of archers. On their periphery were herds of elephants. On their periphery was a line of horses so close that their necks touched. On their periphery were chariots so close they brushed against each other. On their periphery were soldiers so close their shoulders touched. On their periphery were eighteen guilds (seni) shining with the excellence of ornaments suitable to each.

In this way, Jīvaka Komārabhacca arranged the King's retinue so that an arrow shot from the periphery could not reach the King, and he himself followed very close to the King, thinking: 'If any danger arises, I will give the gift of my life for the King before anyone else.' As for the torches, there was no limit, whether they were in the hundreds or thousands. Referring to such royal majesty, it is said: 'With great royal majesty, he approached the mango grove of Jīvaka Komārabhacca.'

In the phrase 'fear (bhaya) arose,' there are four kinds of fear: mental terror (cittutrāsabhaya), fear through knowledge (ñāṇabhaya), fear due to an object (ārammaṇabhaya), and moral dread (ottappabhaya). Among these, the fear described in such ways as 'fear and dread born of birth' is called cittutrāsabhaya. The fear mentioned in 'Those deities, having heard the Dhamma teaching of the Tathāgata, for the most part, fall into fear, urgency, and terror' is called ñāṇabhaya. The fear mentioned in 'Surely that fear and horror is coming' is called ārammaṇabhaya.

'The wise praise one who is afraid; they do not praise the brave in that context.
For the virtuous, out of fear (of evil), do not commit sin.'

This is called ottappabhaya. Among these four, cittutrāsabhaya is intended here. 'Ahu' means 'ahosi' (occurred). 'Chambhitattaṃ' means the state of being paralyzed, the shaking of the whole body. 'Lomahaṃso' means horripilation, the standing up of the body hairs. That horripilation also occurs due to rapture (pīti) at the time of hearing the Dhamma and so on...
137:
Horripilation (lomahaṃsa) can occur when one experiences joy during the hearing of the Dhamma and so forth. For those of a fearful nature, it can also occur due to fear when seeing a battle or spirits, ghosts, and the like. In this context, it should be understood as horripilation caused by fear (bhaya-lomahaṃsa). If one asks why this King was afraid, some (teachers of the Uttaravihāra) say he was afraid because of the darkness. In the city of Rājagaha, there are 32 main gates and 64 small gates. Jīvaka’s mango grove is located between the city wall and Mount Gijjhakūṭa. It is said that the King exited through the eastern gate and entered the shadow of the mountain; there, the mountain peak obscured the moon, and the shadows of the mountain and trees created darkness. However, that is not the actual reason. This is because at that time, there were hundreds of thousands of torches, so there was no limit to the light.

In truth, this King became suspicious of Jīvaka and afraid because of the extreme silence. Jīvaka had told him even at the upper palace, "Great King, the Blessed One desires silence; one should approach in silence." Therefore, the King stopped the sound of musical instruments. The instruments were merely carried without being played; they moved using finger-snapping signals without letting even a loud word escape. Within the mango grove, not even the sound of someone sneezing could be heard. Kings, by nature, delight in sound. Because of that extreme silence, the King felt uneasy and developed suspicion toward Jīvaka. He thought: "This Jīvaka said there are twelve hundred and fifty monks in my mango grove. Now, not even the sound of a sneeze is heard in this grove; it must be a lie. This Jīvaka might be deceiving me, leading me out of the city, placing an army in front to capture me, and wanting to raise the umbrella of sovereignty for himself. This Jīvaka possesses the strength of five elephants. He is walking right near me, and there is not even a single man armed with a weapon near me. Alas, I am ruined!"

Although he was afraid like this, he could no longer pretend not to be afraid and clearly showed his fear to Jīvaka. Therefore, it is said: "Then the King... there is no sound." In that passage, "Samma" is a term for addressing a friend; it means calling him "Friend Jīvaka." "Do not deceive me (na palambhesi)" means "Do not trick me by saying what is not there is there." "Nigghosa" means the sound of conversation. Jīvaka said, "Do not be afraid, Great King." He thought, "This King does not yet know that 'This person will not take my life'; if I do not reassure the King..."
138:
"...he will be ruined," so he strengthened his mind and, to provide relief, said, "Do not be afraid, Great King," and spoke the words beginning with "Na taṃ devā." "Abhikkama" means go forward; "pavisa" means enter. Since saying it once might not be firm enough, he said it twice in haste. "Great King, the lamps are burning in this pavilion circle (maṇḍalamāḷa). A band of thieves does not stay with lamps lit. In this pavilion circle, the lamps are burning. Go by the sign of these lamps, Great King," he submitted.

## Sāmaññaphala-pucchā-vaṇṇanā

"Nāgassa bhūmi" refers to a place where one can go while riding an elephant. "Nāgā paccorohitvā" means having dismounted from the elephant at the outer gatehouse of the monastery. At the very moment he set foot on the ground, the power and majesty (teja) of the Blessed One pervaded the King's body. At that moment, sweat poured from the King's entire body, to the point where his royal robes had to be wrung out and removed. Remembering his own crime, great fear arose. Being unable to go directly to the Blessed One, he held Jīvaka's hand and, as if strolling through the park, praised the monastery, saying, "Friend Jīvaka, you have built and offered this monastery very well," and gradually approached the entrance of the pavilion circle.

Why did he ask, "Friend (Jīvaka), where is the Blessed One?" First, some teachers say, "He asked because he did not know." It is said that although the King had seen the Blessed One before when he came with his father in his youth, later, due to associating with evil friends, he committed the great crimes of killing his father, sending assassins, and releasing the elephant Dhanapāla; thus, he had not faced the Blessed One for a long time and asked because he did not recognize Him. That argument is illogical. This is because the Blessed One, graced with the great and minor marks and illuminating the entire monastery with six-colored rays, was seated in the middle of the pavilion circle surrounded by the assembly of monks, like the full moon surrounded by a host of stars. Who would not know such a Blessed One? In reality, this King asked only in the manner of kings. It is the nature of royalty to ask as if they do not know even when they do. When Jīvaka heard those words, he thought, "This King, while standing on the earth, asks 'Where is the earth?', or while looking up at the sky, asks 'Where are the sun and moon?', or at the foot of Mount Sineru..."
139:
Jīvaka, standing on the ground, was like one asking, 'Where is the ground?'; or like one looking up at the sky and asking, 'Where are the moon and the sun?'; or like one standing at the foot of Mount Sineru and asking, 'Where is Mount Sineru?'. Standing before the Possessor of Ten Powers, he thought, 'Now I will show the Blessed One to the King,' and raising his hands in anjali towards the Blessed One, he said, 'Great King, this is [the Blessed One],' and so forth. 'Surrounded' (purakkhato) means sitting in front of the Saṅgha of monks who were sitting around Him.

'Approached where the Blessed One was' means going to the place where the Blessed One was and arriving in the presence of the Blessed One. 'Stood at a respectful distance' (ekamantaṃ aṭṭhāsi) means paying homage to the Blessed One and standing alone in a place suitable for himself to stand, without disturbing either the Blessed One or the Saṅgha of monks. 'Silent' (tuṇhībhūtaṃ) means that wherever he looked, there was only silence. Among those monks, not even a single monk showed any restlessness of hands or feet, nor was there even the sound of a sneeze. Not even a single monk looked at the King or the royal retinue, who were adorned with all ornaments and accompanied by dancers, standing before the Blessed One. All the monks sat looking only at the Blessed One.

The King, being inspired by their tranquility, looked repeatedly at the Saṅgha of monks, who were as clear as a lake free from mud and possessed calmed faculties, and then uttered an inspired utterance (udāna). In that inspired utterance, 'by this tranquility' indicates that the Saṅgha of monks is peaceful due to the tranquility of virtue (sīla) through body, speech, and mind. In that inspired utterance, it was not said with the intention, 'Oh, would that my son might go forth and be as peaceful as these monks.' Rather, this King, seeing the Saṅgha and being inspired, remembered his son. This is because it is the nature of the world to remember beloved relatives, friends, and others when obtaining something rare or seeing something wonderful. Thus, seeing the Saṅgha and remembering his son, he said these words.

Alternatively, he said this because he had suspicions about his son and desired his tranquility. This thought occurred to him: 'My son is still young. He will ask, "My father is young. Where is my grandfather?" When he hears, "He was killed by your father," he will think, "I too will kill my father and rule the kingdom."' Thus, suspecting his son and desiring his tranquility, he said this. Although the King said this, his son would definitely kill him. For in that dynasty, the killing of the father occurred for five generations. Ajātasattu killed Bimbisāra, Udaya...
140:
(Prince Udaya killed) King Ajātasattu. That Udaya's son, the prince named Mahāmuṇḍika, killed King Udaya. That Mahāmuṇḍika's son, the prince named Anuruddha, killed King Mahāmuṇḍika. That Anuruddha's son, the prince named Nāgadāsa, killed King Anuruddha. Specifically, regarding King Nāgadāsa—the citizens of the country, becoming angry, thinking, 'These kings are destroyers of the lineage; what is the use of these kings?', killed him.

Why did He say, 'You have gone'? It is said that even before the King spoke, the Blessed One thought: 'This King has come and stands silently; what could he be thinking?' Then, knowing his mind: 'This King, unable to converse with me, is looking at the Saṅgha of monks in order and remembering his son. If I do not speak, this King will not be able to say anything. I will engage in conversation with him.' Therefore, immediately after the King's inspired utterance, He said, 'Great King, you have gone according to your love (yathāpemaṃ).' The meaning is: Great King, just as rain falling on high ground flows to the low ground, even so, after looking at the Saṅgha of monks in order, your mind has gone to where your love is (towards your son).

Then the King thought: 'How wonderful are the Buddha's qualities! There is no one who has offended the Blessed One as much as I have. I killed the Blessed One's noble attendant (his father), I followed Devadatta's words and sent archers, I released the elephant Nāḷāgiri, and because of me, Devadatta rolled down a rock. The Blessed One's mouth is not enough (to express His grace) in being the first to speak to me, who has such great offenses. Oh, the Blessed One is well-established in the quality of Tādi (equanimity) through five factors. I will not leave such a teacher to search outside.' Being filled with joy, he addressed the Blessed One, saying, 'Venerable Sir, [my son] is dear to me,' and so forth.

'Raising his hands in homage to the Saṅgha of monks' means—it is said he thought that if he went here and there to pay homage to the Saṅgha after paying homage to the Blessed One, he would have to turn his back on the Blessed One, and that would not be respectful. Just as one who pays homage to the sub-king after paying homage to the King shows disrespect to the King. Therefore, after paying homage to the Blessed One, while standing in the same place, he raised his hands in homage to the Saṅgha of monks and sat down at a respectful distance. 'A certain place' means a certain spot.
141:
Then, the Blessed One, encouraging the King to ask questions, said: "Ask, Great King, whatever you desire." The meaning of this is: "Ask if you desire; there is no heavy burden for me in answering questions." Or else, he extended the invitation of an Omniscient One (sabbaññupavāraṇā), which is not shared by Paccekabuddhas, Chief Disciples, or Great Disciples, saying: "Ask whatever you desire; I shall answer all your questions." For those individuals do not say, "Ask whatever you desire," but rather say, "Having heard it, we shall know (whether we can answer or not)."

But the Buddhas say:
"Friend, ask whatever you desire,"
Or, "Great King, ask whatever you desire,"
Or, "Vāsava, ask me any question that you wish in your mind;
To each and every question, I shall bring an end for you."
Or, "Therefore, bhikkhu, sitting in your own seat, ask whatever you desire,"
Or, "Regarding all the doubts of the teacher Bāvarī and of yours,
Permission is granted to all of you to ask whatever you wish in your mind."
Or, "Sabhiya, ask me any question that you wish in your mind;
To each and every question, I shall bring an end for you."
In this manner, they extend the invitation of an Omniscient One to various yakkhas, kings, devas, ascetics, brahmins, and wanderers. It is not surprising that the Blessed One, having reached the stage of a Buddha (buddhabhūmi), would extend such an invitation. Even when he stood in the stage of a Bodhisatta with partial knowledge (padesañāṇa)—

"Koṇḍañña, explain the questions;
The sages who are virtuous entreat you.
Koṇḍañña, this is the nature among men,
That this burden comes to the one who is great."
Thus, when entreated by the sages for the sake of Sakka and others, he once said:

"Sirs, permission is granted to ask;
Ask any question that is desired by the mind.
For I, having personally known this world and the world beyond,
Shall answer each of those questions for you."
142:
Thus it was at the time when he was the great hermit Sarabhaṅga, and also in the Sambhava Jātaka (he extended the invitation of an Omniscient One). In the Sambhava Jātaka, when the brahmin named Sucirata had wandered through the entire Jambudīpa three times without finding anyone who could bring an end to his questions, he requested the opportunity to ask questions. Then the youth Sambhava, who was only seven years old from birth, while playing with dust on the road, sat down in a cross-legged posture in the middle of the street and said:

"Indeed, I shall explain to you, just as a skilled wise man would;
Your King will surely know that, whether he acts upon it or not."
(Thus he extended the invitation of an Omniscient One.)

## He extended the invitation of an Omniscient One.

When the Blessed One had thus extended the invitation of an Omniscient One, King Ajātasattu, being delighted, asked the question beginning with: "Venerable Sir, just as these various crafts..." In that context, the craft itself is called 'sippāyatana'. 'Puthusippāyatanāni' means there are many crafts. 'Seyyathidaṃ' is an inquiry into what those crafts are. He intends to show those persons who live depending on various crafts such as elephant-riding and so on. This was the King's intention: "Just as for those who live by a craft, the fruit of the craft (sippaphala) is personally visible by depending on that craft; is it possible to point out a similarly personally visible fruit of recluseship (sāmaññaphala)?" Therefore, he mentions the branches of craft and shows those who live by them.

Among those terms (such as hatthārohā), by the term 'hatthārohā' (elephant riders), he shows all persons such as elephant-trainers, elephant-warriors, elephant-doctors, and elephant-grooms. By 'assārohā' (horsemen), all horse-trainers, horse-warriors, horse-doctors, and horse-grooms. By 'rathikā' (charioteers), all chariot-trainers, chariot-warriors, and chariot-guards. By 'dhanuggahā' (archers), the teachers of archery and the bowmen. By 'celakā' (standard-bearers), those warriors who go at the very front holding the victory flag in battle. By 'calakā' (camp-marshals), those warriors who arrange the army, saying, "The King shall stay here, such and such a great minister shall stay here." By 'piṇḍadāyakā' (lump-givers), he means the fierce great warriors. It is said they are so called because they enter the enemy army and cut off the enemies' heads like lumps of food (piṇḍa), and then leap up and exit. Or else, this is the name for those who carry and serve trays of food to the warriors in the midst of battle. 'Uggā rājaputtā' (noble princes) refers to the very prominent princes who frequent the battlefield. 'Pakkhandino' (leapers) refers to those who say, "Whose head or weapon..."
143:
Saying 'I will bring it,' and when ordered 'Bring the (head or weapon) of such a person,' they rush into the battlefield and bring that very thing; therefore they are called 'Pakkhandī' (those who rush in). 

'Mahānāga' (Great Naga) is so called because they are like great elephants; it is a designation for warriors who do not retreat even when facing elephants and such. Those who are singularly brave, able to cross even the ocean with their armor and leather shields, are called 'Sūra' (Heroes). Those who fight wearing leather tunics or holding leather shields are called 'Cammayodhī' (Leather-clad warriors). Household slave-soldiers who have great affection for their masters are called 'Dāsikaputta' (Sons of bondwomen). 

'Āḷārika' refers to confectioners. 'Kappaka' refers to barbers. 'Nhāpaka' refers to bath-attendants. 'Sūda' refers to cooks. Garland-makers and others are well-known. 'Gaṇaka' refers to those skilled in the science of calculation. 'Muddika' refers to those who make a living by the art of finger-accounting.
