'Yāni vā panaññānipi' refers to other craftsmen such as blacksmiths, sculptors, and painters. 'Evaṅgatāni' means such crafts as these. Those persons, such as the elephant-riders, demonstrate those various craft-foundations, receive great wealth from the royal family, and subsist on the visible fruit of their craft in this very life. 

'Sukhenti' means they make themselves happy. 'Pīṇenti' means they make themselves satisfied and strong. 

Among the terms such as 'Uddhaggikā,' it is called 'Uddhaggikā' (an offering with upward-tending fruit) because it produces results in the higher celestial realms. It is called 'Sovaggikā' because it is worthy of heaven. It is called 'Sukhavipākā' because it has happy results. It is called 'Saggasaṃvattanikā' because it leads to or produces the ten things: the excellent sights, sounds, smells, tastes, and touches, as well as life, beauty, happiness, retinue, and power. The meaning is that they establish such a gift. 

In this context of 'Sāmaññaphala' (Fruit of Recluseship), in the ultimate sense, the Path is called 'Sāmañña' (Recluseship). The Noble Fruit is called 'Sāmaññaphala.' As it is taught (in the Saṃyutta Nikāya): 'And what, monks, is recluseship? It is this Noble Eightfold Path. Namely, Right View ... Right Concentration. This, monks, is called recluseship. And what, monks, are the fruits of recluseship? The fruit of Stream-entry ... the fruit of Arahantship.' 

This King does not know that matter. He asks with reference to the example of the slave and the farmer that will come later. 

Then the Blessed One, without answering the question immediately, thought: 'Many royal ministers who are disciples of other sectarians have come here. While the dark side (unwholesome) and the bright side (wholesome) are being explained and taught to them, our King came here with great effort. From the time the King arrived, the Ascetic Gotama [has been talking about] the clamor of ascetics...'
144:
'...and the disputes of ascetics,' and they will not listen to the Dhamma respectfully. However, if the King speaks, they will not be able to complain and will only follow the King. For the world follows the powerful, does it not? 'Now, I will place the burden on the King,' and wishing to place the burden on the King, He said, 'Great King, do you remember?' and so on. 

In the phrase 'Abhijānāsi no tvaṃ,' it means 'Abhijānāsi nu tvaṃ' (Do you remember?). This word 'no' should be connected with the subsequent word 'pucchitā.' This is what is meant: 'Great King, have you questioned other ascetics and brahmins about this problem, and do you remember that you questioned them, or have you not forgotten?' 

'Sace te agaru' means if it is not a burden for you to speak here as they answered you, if there is no discomfort, then please speak. 

Why did he say, 'Venerable Sir, it is not a burden for me'? It is difficult to speak in the presence of those who only appear to be wise; they find fault in every word and every letter. But truly wise people, upon hearing a speech, praise what is well-spoken; and if there are errors in the Pali words, meanings, or phrasing in what is poorly spoken, they straighten and correct those points. There is no truly wise person equal to the Blessed One. Therefore, he said, 'Venerable Sir, it is not a burden for me in this place where the Blessed One or a wise person like the Blessed One is present.' 

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Pūraṇa Kassapa 

'Ekamidāhaṃ' should be analyzed as 'Ekaṃ idaṃ ahaṃ' (Once, here, I). 'Sammodanīyaṃ kathaṃ sāraṇīyaṃ vītisāretvā' means having concluded the conversation that is pleasant and worthy of remembrance. 

'Great King, for one who acts, for one who causes to act,' and so on: 'Karoto' refers to one who acts with his own hands. 'Kārayato' refers to one who causes to act by command. 'Chindato' refers to one who cuts the hands, feet, etc., of others. 'Pacato' refers to one who oppresses others with sticks or clubs. 'Socayato' refers to one who causes others to worry by stealing their property and so on. 'Socāpayato' means just as one causes sorrow oneself, so through others...
145:
Even for the one who causes [another] to do [it] (there is an effect). 'The one who is weary' means one who is weary themselves or causes others to be weary through the cutting off of food, imprisonment, and so forth. 'The one who trembles, the one who causes to tremble' means one who trembles themselves or causes others to tremble at the time when others are trembling. 'The one who kills, the one who causes to kill' means one who kills themselves or causes others to kill. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances through the power of doing and causing to do.

'House wall' means the joint (wall) of a house. 'Great looting' means a major plunder leaving nothing behind. 'Looting a single house' means surrounding and looting only one house. 'On the road' means waiting on the road to rob those who come and go. 'Even if one acts, no evil is done' means that even if one acts with the perception 'I am doing some evil,' no evil is done; it means there is no evil. It shows that only beings have such a perception as 'We are doing evil.' 'With a circular weapon with an edge as sharp as a razor' means with a razor-rimmed wheel or a wheel with an edge like a razor's blade. 'A single mass of meat' means a single heap of flesh. 'Heap of meat' (puñja) is just a synonym for that word 'khala'. 'Because of making that heap of meat' means due to the cause of making a single mass of meat.

'The Southern bank' refers to the people living on the southern bank of the Ganges who are harsh and cruel; referring to them, it is said 'one who kills' and so forth. The beings (people) living on the northern bank have faith, are confident in the Triple Gem, and cherish the Buddha, the Dhamma, and the Saṅgha; referring to them, it is said 'one who gives' and so forth. In that context, 'one who sacrifices' means one who performs a great sacrifice (mahāyāga). 'By restraint of the senses' means by taming the senses or by observing the Uposatha. 'By restraint' means by restraint of virtue (sīla). 'By truthful speech' means by speaking the truth. 'Coming' (āgama) means arrival; the meaning is 'occurrence'. In every way, it is the rejection of the performance (kiriya) of evil and merit.

'When asked about a mango, he answers about a breadfruit' is like when asked, 'What is a mango tree like? What are the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits of a mango tree like?' and one answers, 'A breadfruit tree is like this; the trunk, leaves, flowers, and fruits of a breadfruit tree are like this.' 'In the region where his authority extends' means in the territory where his command prevails. 'Should be harassed' means should be oppressed (or expelled). 'Without rejoicing' means without praising as 'Sādhu, Sādhu'. 'Without disparaging' means without rejecting or prohibiting by saying 'You have spoken the words of a fool.' 'Not accepting' means not accepting as the essence. 'Not taking to heart' means not placing in the heart as the essence, thinking 'This is the way to liberation, this is the ultimate truth.' As for the syllable (word), it is both learned and taken to heart by that person.
146:
## Description of the Doctrine of Makkhali Gosāla
167-169. In the doctrine of Makkhali, the word 'paccaya' (condition) is just a synonym for the word 'hetu' (cause). By both these words, he rejects the cause of corruption for bodily misconduct and so forth, which actually exists, and the cause of purification for bodily good conduct and so forth. 'Attakāre' refers to self-agency (kamma performed by oneself). He rejects that kamma by which beings attain the state of a deva, a Māra, a Brahma, the enlightenment of a disciple (sāvaka-bodhi), the enlightenment of a private Buddha (pacceka-bodhi), or even omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). By the second term, 'parakāra' (agency of others), he rejects the effort of others which is the cause for beings (excluding the Great Being, the Bodhisatta) to attain everything from human prosperity to the fruit of Arahantship, based on the advice and instruction of others. In this way, this fool is said to strike at the Wheel of Authority of the Buddha. 'Natthi purisakāre' means he also rejects human effort, by which beings attain the aforementioned attainments (sampatti). 'Natthi balaṃ' means he rejects strength, by which beings, established in their own strength, exert energy and reach those attainments. 'Natthi vīriyaṃ' and all such words are just synonyms for human agency (purisakāra). These terms are taken separately to reject such statements as 'This result is due to our energy, this result is due to human strength, this result is due to human effort.'

By the phrase 'all beings' (sabba sattā), he includes all beings without exception, such as camels, oxen, and donkeys. He speaks of 'all breathing things' (sabba pāṇā) in terms of beings with one sense-faculty, two sense-faculties, and so forth. He speaks of 'all creatures' (sabba bhūtā) referring to beings born from eggs or a womb. He speaks of 'all souls' (sabba jīvā) referring to plants such as hill paddy, barley, and wheat. Regarding those plants, that teacher Makkhali has the perception that they have life because of their nature of growth. For those beings, there is no power, strength, or energy of their own. In the phrase 'transformed by destiny, coincidence, and nature' (niyati-saṅgati-bhāva-pariṇatā), 'niyati' means fixed destiny (fate). 'Saṅgati' means the wandering into various states among the six classes of birth. 'Bhāva' is just nature (inherent property). Thus, they are transformed and reach various states through destiny, coincidence, and nature. He shows that whatever one is destined to be, that they become; whatever one is not destined to be, that they do not become. 'Only in the six classes of birth' (chasvevābhijātīsu) means they experience pleasure and pain while remaining only in the six classes of birth. He shows that there is no other ground for experiencing pleasure and pain. 'One million four hundred thousand principal modes of birth' (yonipamukha-satasahassāni) means fourteen hundred thousand of the foremost or best modes of birth, and another sixty hundred, and another six hundred, and five...
147: (Makkhali) intends five hundred kammas by the phrase 'kammuno satāni'. This is merely an illustration of a baseless doctrine through mere speculation. The same method should be understood in passages such as 'pañca ca kammāni tīṇi ca kammāni' (five kammas and three kammas). However, some teachers say that 'pañca ca kammāni' refers to the division of the five faculties, and 'tīṇi' refers to the division of the three kammas, such as bodily kamma and so on. In the context of 'kamme ca upaddhakamme ca', his (Makkhali's) view is that bodily kamma and verbal kamma are considered 'kamma', while mental kamma is considered 'half-kamma' (upaddhakamma). 'Dvatthipaṭipadā' refers to the sixty-two practices. 'Dvatthantarākappā' refers to sixty-two intermediate eons; although there are sixty-four intermediate eons in one kappa, this (Makkhali) says so because he does not know the other two eons. ## 'Chaḷābhijātiyo' refers to these six classes of birth: the black birth (kaṇhābhijāti), the blue birth (nīlābhijāti), the red birth (lohitābhijāti), the yellow birth (haliddābhijāti), the white birth (sukkābhijāti), and the purest white birth (paramasukkābhijāti). Among these six, he says that sheep-butchers, bird-slayers, hunters, pig-killers, forest-hunters, fish-slayers, thieves, executioners, jailers, or any others who have cruel occupations, belong to the 'black birth'. He says that monks (bhikkhus) belong to the 'blue birth'. He considers that these monks use the four requisites while being pricked by the thorns of desire. 'Monks are those who live with thorns' is his very text. Alternatively, it refers to certain ascetics who practice extreme self-mortification (attakilamathanuyoga) as if practicing on thorns. He says that the Nigaṇṭhas who wear a single cloth belong to the 'red birth'. This implies they are purer than the previous two. He says that white-robed lay followers of the Acelakas belong to the 'yellow birth'. In this way, he makes his own supporters even more noble than the Nigaṇṭhas. He says that Ājīvaka men and women belong to the 'white birth'. This implies they are purer than the previous four. He says that Nanda, Vaccha, Kisa, Saṅkicca, and Makkhali Gosāla belong to the 'purest white birth'. This implies they are the purest of all. ## 'Aṭṭha purisabhūmiyo' refers to these eight stages of man: manda-bhūmi, khiḍḍā-bhūmi, padavīmaṃsa-bhūmi, ujugata-bhūmi, sekkha-bhūmi, samaṇa-bhūmi, jina-bhūmi, and panna-bhūmi. Among these eight, from the day of birth up to seven days, because they have just emerged from the mother's womb, beings are tender and deluded; he calls this stage 'manda-bhūmi' (the stage of dullness). Those who come from a state of misery (duggati) constantly cry and wail, while those who come from a happy state (sugati) laugh as they remember that life; this stage is called 'khiḍḍā-bhūmi' (the stage of play). The stage of trying to walk on the ground while holding the hands or feet of parents, or a bed or a bench, is called 'padavīmaṃsa-bhūmi' (the stage of investigating the feet). The time when one is able to walk on foot is called 'ujugata-bhūmi' (the upright stage). When learning the arts...
148: The time of learning the arts is called 'sekkha-bhūmi' (the stage of the learner). The time of leaving home and becoming a monk is called 'samaṇa-bhūmi' (the stage of the recluse). The time of knowing right and wrong practices by serving a teacher is called 'jina-bhūmi' (the stage of the conqueror). "Neither the monk nor the aged (or the conqueror) says anything"; according to this text of theirs, a monk who receives no alms-food is called 'panna-bhūmi' (the stage of the fallen). ## 'Ekūnapaññāsa ājīvakasata' refers to four thousand nine hundred (4900) varieties of Ājīvaka livelihoods. 'Paribbājakasata' refers to four thousand nine hundred (4900) types of wanderer ordinations. 'Nāgāvāsasata' refers to four thousand nine hundred (4900) abodes of dragons (Nāga realms). 'Vīse indriyasate' refers to two thousand (2000) faculties. 'Tiṃse nirayasate' refers to three thousand (3000) hells. 'Rajo-dhātuyo' (dust elements) refers to the backs of the hands, the backs of the feet, etc., which are places where dust accumulates. 'Seven sentient births (saññīgabbha)' refers to camels, oxen, donkeys, goats, sheep, wild animals (deer, etc.), and buffaloes. 'Seven non-sentient births (asaññīgabbha)' refers to hill paddy, rice, barley, wheat, millet, beans, and rye. 'Nigaṇṭhigabbha' (births at the joints) refers to sugarcane, bamboo, reeds, etc., which have "wombs" or growth at their joints. 'Seven gods' means that although there are many gods, that teacher Makkhali says there are only seven. Although humans are infinite, he says there are only seven. 'Seven types of pisāca demons' means that although pisācas are very numerous, he says there are only seven. 'Lakes' refers to the seven great lakes: Kaṇṇamuṇḍa, Rathakāra, Anotatta, Sīhappapāta, Chaddanta, Mandākinī, and Kunāla. ## 'Pavuṭa' refers to things with knots or joints. 'Papāta' refers to great precipices. 'Papātasata' refers to seven hundred minor precipices. 'Supina' refers to great dreams. 'Supinasata' refers to seven hundred minor dreams. 'Mahākappino' refers to the number of great eons (mahākappa). The duration of these great eons is as follows: if one were to take a single drop of water with the tip of a blade of kusa grass from a great lake once every hundred years, the time it takes to empty that lake seven times is called one great eon (mahākappa). His doctrine is that after passing through eight million four hundred thousand (8,400,000) such great eons, both the foolish and the wise will make an end of suffering. It is said that even a wise man cannot become pure in the interval, and a fool cannot go beyond that limit. ## 'By virtue' means by the virtue of an ascetic (acelaka-sīla) or by any other kind of virtue. 'By vows (vata)' means by such vows. 'By penance (tapa)' means by the practice of austerities (tapokamma). 'Maturing the immature' refers to one who tries to become pure in the interval, saying, "I am wise." 'Exhausting the matured by repeated contact' refers to one who goes beyond the prescribed time, saying, "I am a fool." 'There is no such thing' means there is no such thing as becoming pure in the interval. Both of those are not...
149:
It shows that one is able to do so. "Doṇamite" means as if measured by a doṇa measure. "Sukhadukkhe" refers to pleasure and pain. "Pariyantakate" means having a limit made by the aforementioned duration of time. "Natthi hāyanavaḍḍhane" means there is no decrease or increase. The meaning is that the saṃsāra of the wise does not decrease, and the saṃsāra of the fool does not increase. "Ukkaṃsāvakaṃse" means excess and deficiency. This is just another name for decrease and increase.

Now, wishing to establish that meaning with a simile, he said "Seyyathāpi nāma" and so on. In that passage, "Suttaguḷe" refers to a ball of string that has been wound. "Nibbeṭhiyamānameva paleti" means that a ball of string thrown while standing on a mountain or a treetop goes only as far as it is unwound by the length of the string; when the string is exhausted, it stops right there and goes no further. Similarly, it shows that it does not go beyond the stated time.

## Explanation of the View of Ajita Kesakambala

170-172. In Ajita's view, "natthi dinnaṃ" refers to the absence of the fruit of giving. "Yiṭṭhaṃ" refers to a great sacrifice (mahāyāga). "Hutaṃ" refers to offerings made as hospitality (pahaṇakasakkāra). He rejects both of these, referring to the absence of fruit. "Sukatadukkaṭānaṃ" refers to the meaning of wholesome and unwholesome kamma, well-done or ill-done. "Phalaṃ vipāko" means that what is called the root fruit or the resultant fruit does not exist. "Natthi ayံ loko" means that for one established in the other world, this world does not exist; "natthi paro loko" means that for one established in this world, the other world does not exist. It intends to show that all beings are annihilated right in those respective existences. "Natthi mātā natthi pitā" refers to the absence of the fruit of good or bad conduct toward those parents. "Natthi sattā opapātikā" means there are no beings who, having passed away, are reborn [spontaneously].

"Cātumahābhūtiko" means one who is composed of the four great elements. "Pathavī pathavikāyaṃ" means the internal earth element goes to the external earth element. "Anupeti" means it follows. "Anupagacchati" is a synonym for the same. "Anugacchati" is also the meaning. It shows that it approaches through both. The same method applies to the liquid element (āpo), etc. "Indriyāni" means the six faculties, beginning with the mind, pass into space. "Āsandipañcamā" means with the bier as the fifth; the four men who carry the bier and its four legs...
150:
"Cātumahābhūtiko" means it is composed of the four great elements. "Yāvāဠāhanā" means as far as the cemetery. "Padāni" refers to the collection of virtues and faults that arise in such a way as 'This person was thus virtuous, thus immoral,' etc. Or else, in this context, "padāni" refers to the body itself. "Kāpotakāni" means having the color of a dove, like the color of a pigeon's wing. "Bhassantā" means ending in ashes (bhasmantā), or this "bhasmantā" is the original Pali text itself. "Āhutiyo" means all the various offerings and sacrifices brought from afar; they all end only in ashes and do not go on to become givers of fruit beyond that. "Dattupaññattaṃ" means that which is prescribed by fools and ignorant people. The meaning is: 'This giving is prescribed only by fools without wisdom, not by the wise. Fools give, and the wise receive.'

Among those three teachers, the teacher Pūraṇa, saying 'In acting, no evil is done,' denies kamma. The teacher Ajita, saying 'With the breakup of the body, one is annihilated,' denies the result (vipāka). The teacher Makkhali, saying 'There is no cause,' denies both. In that denial, one who denies kamma also denies the result, and one who denies the result also denies kamma. Thus, all of them, in essence, are deniers of both, being proponents of non-causality (ahetukavāda), non-action (akiriyavāda), and nihilism (natthikavāda).

Furthermore, those who take up their views and sit in their night-quarters or day-quarters, reciting and investigating them—for those who investigate thus: 'In acting, no evil is done; there is no cause, no condition; when dead, one is annihilated'—in that object, wrong mindfulness (micchā-sati) becomes well-established, the mind becomes one-pointed, and the javanas (impulse moments) run. In the first javana, it is still remediable; likewise in the second and so on. But in the seventh javana, even the Buddhas cannot remedy it; they become those who do not turn back from wrong view, like the monk Ariṭṭha and the novice Kaṇḍaka. Among them, some fall into one view, some into two, and some into all three. Whether one falls into one, two, or three, one becomes a person of fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi). One reaches the obstruction of the path to heaven and the obstruction of the path to liberation. In the existence immediately following that life, one is not even fit to go to heaven, let alone to liberation. This being is called a 'stump in the cycle of rebirth' (vaṭṭakhāṇu) and a 'guardian of the earth' (pathavīgopaka). Generally, for such a person, there is no emergence from the cycle of rebirth.

Therefore, an evil person, like a venomous snake,
The wise man desiring prosperity should avoid from afar.
151:
## Explanation of the Doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana
173-175. In the doctrine of Pakudha Kaccāyana, 'akaṭā' means things that are not made and cannot be made. 'Akaṭavidhā' means things for which there is no creation or arrangement. It means that even if someone orders, 'Do it this way,' they are not caused to be done. 'Animmitā' means they are not created even by psychic power. 'Animmātā' means they are not caused to be created; some teachers say the word is 'animmātabbā,' but that word is found neither in the Pāḷi nor in the Commentary (Aṭṭhakathā). The three terms beginning with 'vañjhā' (barren) have the same meanings as previously stated.

'Na iñjanti' means they do not move because they stand firm like a gatepost. 'Na vipariṇamanti' means they do not abandon their original nature. 'Na aññamaññaṃ byābādhenti' means they do not oppress one another. 'Nālaṃ' means they are not capable. In the terms beginning with 'pathavikāyo,' the earth element itself is the earth-group or the earth-aggregate. 'Tattha' means among those seven bodies/groups, with the soul (jīva) as the seventh. 'Sattannaṃ tveva kāyānaṃ' means that just as a weapon struck into a heap of beans enters between the beans, so a weapon enters through the gaps, holes, or interstices between these seven bodies. It is shown that in such an entry, saying 'I deprive this person of life' is merely a notion or perception.

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Nigaṇṭha Nāṭaputta
176-178. In the doctrine of Nāṭaputta, 'cātuyāmasaṃvarasaṃvuto' means one whose doors of body, speech, and mind are restrained by the fourfold restraint. 'Sabbavārivārito ca' means one who is prohibited from using all cold water. It is said that because Nāṭaputta perceives living beings in cold water, he does not use it. 'Sabbavāriyutto' means one who is endowed with the restraint of all evil. 'Sabbavāridhuto' means one who has shaken off evil by the restraint of all evil. 'Sabbavāriphuṭṭho' means one who is pervaded by the restraint of all evil. 'Gatatto' means one whose mind has reached the summit. 'Yatatto' means one whose mind is restrained. 'Ṭhitatto' means one whose mind is well-established. In this doctrine of Nāṭaputta, although there are some points that align with the Dispensation (Sāsana), because it is not a pure belief, the entire view has become wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi).

## Explanation of the Doctrine of Sañjaya Belaṭṭhaputta
179-181. The doctrine of Sañjaya follows the same method as stated in the doctrine of the Eel-wrigglers (Amarāvikkhepavāda).
152:
## Explanation of the First Visible Fruit of Recluseship
"Sohaṃ bhante" means "Venerable Sir, I, that person, like one who squeezes sand and gets no oil, found no essence in the doctrines of the sectarians and thus ask the Blessed One." "Yathā te khameyya" means "as it may please you" (answer in that way). "Dāsa" (slave) refers to one of four types: one born in the house, one bought with wealth, a prisoner of war, or one who has become a slave of one's own accord. "Kammakāra" (laborer) refers to one who is not lazy but has the habit of working. One who rises first upon seeing the master from afar, even before he arrives, is called "pubbuṭṭhāyī." One who sits down only after rising first in this way and performing duties such as preparing the seat and washing the feet for the master is called "pacchānipātī." Alternatively, one who rises before the master wakes from sleep is "pubbuṭṭhāyī." One who performs all duties from dawn until the master falls asleep at night and only then goes to sleep is "pacchānipātī." One who goes about listening for what is to be done, asking "What shall I do? What shall I do?" is called "kiṃkārapaṭissāvī." One who acts only in a pleasing manner is "manāpacārī." One who speaks only endearing words is "piyavါဒီ" (piyavādī). One who goes about looking up at the master's happy and joyful face is "mukhullokako."

"Devo manye" means "like a god." "So vatassāhaṃ puṇyāni kareyyaṃ" means "If I were to perform meritorious deeds, I would become such a person like that king." Although there is a variant reading "so vatassassa," the meaning is the same. By the words "yannūnāhaṃ," he shows his enthusiastic thought for monkhood: "If I were to give gifts, I would not be able to give even a hundredth part of what the king gives in a single day throughout my whole life; therefore, I shall go forth as a monk."

"Kāyena saṃvuto" means being restrained by the body, thus closing the door through which unwholesome states enter. The same method applies to the other two terms (restraint by speech and mind). "Ghāsacchādanaparamatāya" means being content with the supreme practice of effacement (sallekha), which is the utmost limit in food and clothing, abandoning improper search for the sake of these items. "Abhirato paviveke" means delighting in the three kinds of seclusion known as physical seclusion (kāya-viveka), mental seclusion (citta-viveka), and seclusion from acquisitions (upadhi-viveka).
153:
Abandoning the company of the group, one dwells alone physically. Abandoning the company of mental defilements, one dwells alone by the power of the eight attainments. Or, having entered the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti) or the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) and reaching Nibbāna, one dwells—this is the meaning. The word 'yagghe' is a particle used in the sense of urging.

'One might also invite him with a seat' means shaking out a sitting place and saying, 'Please sit here.' 'One might also invite him by bringing [requisites] before him' means inviting him by bringing requisites forward. In that context, bringing forward (abhihāra) is of two kinds: by word and by body. A lay follower who says, 'Venerable sir, at any moment you desire, I shall fulfill your needs with robes and other requisites; please tell me whatever you need,' is said to invite by bringing forward by word. A lay follower who, noticing a lack of robes or other requisites, gives them saying, 'Please accept this,' is said to invite by bringing forward by body. Referring to both of these, it is said, 'One might also invite him by bringing [requisites] before him.' Here, 'medicinal requisites for the sick' refers to any medicine suitable for a sick person. Its etymological meaning has been stated in the Visuddhimagga. 'Protection, ward, and guard' refers to guarding (gutti) in the form of protection (rakkhā) before danger arises and warding (āvaraṇa) when danger appears. Such guarding is not called 'righteous protection' by stationing men with weapons in their hands. Rather, it is called 'righteous protection' when arrangements are made so that wood-gatherers, leaf-gatherers, and others do not enter the monastery at improper times, and hunters and others do not catch animals or fish within the monastery precincts. Referring to such protection, it says 'righteous' (dhammika).

'If it be so' means: if your majesty's slave were to receive benefits such as salutation from your majesty, if it be so (is there a benefit of recluseship?). The word 'addhā' expresses the sense of certainty. By saying 'first,' it shows that there are other benefits as well. For that very reason, the King asked, 'Venerable sir, is it possible to point out another benefit?' and so forth.

## Commentary on the Second Visible Fruit of Recluseship

186-188. He is called a farmer (kassaka) because he plows. He is called a householder (gahapatika) because he is the master of a house, or the head of a single household. He is called a taxpayer (karakāraka) because he pays the tax known as tribute (bali). He is called an increaser of wealth (rāsivaḍḍhaka) because he increases the heap of grain and the heap of wealth.
154:
'Appaṃ vā' means a small amount of wealth. At the minimum, it means a mass of wealth even as small as a single measure of rice. 'Bhogakkhandhaṃ' means a mass of wealth. 'Mahantaṃ vā' means an abundant or great mass of wealth. Why are both mentioned? To show that just as it is difficult to renounce great wealth and go forth, it is also difficult to renounce even a small amount of wealth. In the section concerning the slave (dāsavāra), however, since a slave is not even master of himself, let alone of wealth—for whatever wealth he has belongs only to his masters—the word 'bhoga' (wealth) was not used in the slave's section. 'Ñātiparivaṭṭa' refers to the circle of relatives.

## Commentary on the More Excellent Fruit of Recluseship

In asking, 'Venerable sir, is it possible to point out another visible fruit of recluseship in this very life?', the phrase 'just so' (evam-eva) was not used here. Why? Because if he had said 'just so,' the Blessed One would have been able to demonstrate the fruit of recluseship with such similes for a whole day and night, or even longer. In that case, although there is no end to hearing the words of the Blessed One, the meaning would be the same as the previously shown sections on the slave and the farmer. Thinking thus, and wishing to ask about a higher distinction in the fruit of recluseship, he did not say 'just so' but said 'more pleasing and more excellent.'

In that context, 'abhikkantatara' means more pleasing, more superior. 'Paṇီtatara' means more sublime. The phrase 'tena hi' is a particle in the sense of urging (uyyojana). The Blessed One, urging him to listen, spoke to the King thus. 'Suṇohi' means 'listen to the more pleasing and more excellent fruit of recluseship.'

In the phrase 'sādhukaṃ manasikarohi,' the two words 'sādhukaṃ' and 'sādhu' have the same meaning. This word 'sādhu' is seen in the senses of request (āyācana), acceptance (sampaṭicchana), appreciation (sampahaṃsana), goodness (sundara), making firm (daḷhီkamma), and so on.

'Venerable sir, may the Blessed One teach me the Dhamma in brief'—in such passages, it is found in the sense of request (āyācana). 'Very well, venerable sir'—when that monk, having delighted in and appreciated the words of the Blessed One, accepts them, it is found in the sense of acceptance (sampaṭicchana). 'Sādhu, sādhu, Sāriputta'—in such passages, it is found in the sense of appreciation (sampahaṃsana).

'A king who delights in the Dhamma is good (sādhu); a man who possesses wisdom is good;
Sādhu mittānamaddubbho, pāpassākaraṇaṃ sukhan-ti.
One who does not betray friends is good; the non-doing of evil is happiness.'

In such verses, it is found in the sense of goodness (sundara). In such passages as 'Therefore, Brahmin, listen, attend carefully (sādhukaṃ),' the word 'sādhuka' is found in the sense of making firm (daḷhီkamma) or command (āṇatti).
155:
In this Sāmaññaphala Sutta, the word 'sādhukaṃ' (well/carefully) should be understood in the sense of making firm (daḷhīkamma) and in the sense of a command (āṇatti). It is also appropriate in the sense of 'excellent' (sundara). Indeed, by the sense of daḷhīkamma, it indicates: 'Listen to this Dhamma firmly, grasping it well.' By the sense of āṇatti, it indicates: 'Listen by my command.' By the sense of sundara, it indicates: 'Listen to this excellent and good Dhamma.'

'Manasi karohi' means to reflect or to take well into the heart. The intention is: 'Listen attentively without a distracted mind; keep it in the mind.' Furthermore, the word 'suṇāhi' (listen) is for preventing the distraction of the faculty of hearing (sotindriya). 'Sādhukaṃ manasi karohi' (pay attention well) is for preventing the distraction of the faculty of mind (manindriya) by urging firmness in attention. The former prevents the wrong grasp of the phrasing (byañjanavipallāsa), while the latter prevents the wrong grasp of the meaning (atthavipallāsa). By the former, he encourages the listening to the Dhamma; by the latter, he encourages the retention and investigation of the Dhamma that has been heard. By the former, he shows that 'This Dhamma is complete in phrasing, therefore it is worth hearing.' By the latter, he shows that 'This Dhamma is complete in meaning, therefore it should be well attended to.'

Alternatively, connecting the word 'sādhukaṃ' with both: 'Because this Dhamma is profound in its nature (dhamma) and profound in its teaching (desanā), listen well'; and 'Because it is profound in its meaning (attha) and profound in its penetration (paṭivedha), pay attention well.' This is how the construction (yojanā) should be understood. 'Bhāsissāmi' (I will speak) means 'I will speak in detail the Sāmaññaphala teaching which I have promised, saying "It is possible, Great King."' For the word 'desessāmi' (I will teach) indicates a brief explanation, while 'bhāsissāmi' indicates a detailed explanation. Thus the Elder Vangīsa said:

'He teaches in brief, and speaks in detail;
His voice is like that of a myna bird,
Bringing forth inspired eloquence (paṭibhāna).'

When this was said, King Ajātasattu of Magadha, the son of the Videhan princess, became enthusiastic and respectfully accepted the Buddha's words, saying, 'Even so, Bhante.' Then the Blessed One said this to him: 'Here, Great King...' and spoke the entire sutta. In that passage, 'idha' (here) is an indeclinable (nipāta) indicating a place; in some places, it is used in reference to the world, as in: 'Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world.' In some places, it refers to the Dispensation (sāsana).
156:
For example: 'Monks, only here in this Dispensation is there the first recluse (samaṇa), only here is there the second recluse.' (Here 'idha' refers to the Dispensation). In some places, it is used to indicate a location. For example: 'Sirs, know this: while staying right here (in the Indasāla cave), being a deva, I have regained my life-span.' (Here it refers to a place). In some places, it is merely a verse-filler. For example: 'Monks, here I have finished my meal and refused more.' (Here it is just a filler). In this (Sāmaññaphala Sutta), however, it should be understood as being said in reference to the world. The address 'Great King' is used again to preach the discourse as promised. The meaning is: 'Great King, in this world, a Tathāgata arises, an Arahant... a Buddha, a Blessed One.'

Therein, the word 'Tathāgata' was explained in the Brahmajāla Sutta. The qualities beginning with 'Arahant' were explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. In the phrase 'arises in the world,' the 'world' (loka) is threefold: the world of space (okāsaloka), the world of beings (sattaloka), and the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). Here, the world of beings is intended. Even when arising in the world of beings, a Tathāgata does not arise in the deva worlds or the brahma worlds, but only in the human world. Even in the human world, he does not arise in other world-systems, but only in this world-system.

Even in this world-system, he does not arise everywhere, but only in the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa), which is defined as follows: 'To the east is the market town named Gajaṅgala, and beyond it is Mahāsāla, and then the border regions; on this side (inward) is the Middle Country. To the south-east is the river named Salalavatī, beyond which are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country. To the south is the market town named Setakaṇṇika, beyond which are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country. To the west is the brahmin village named Thūṇa, beyond which are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country. To the north is the mountain named Usīraddhaja, beyond which are the border regions, and on this side is the Middle Country.' In this Middle Country, which is three hundred yojanas in length, two hundred and fifty yojanas in breadth, and nine hundred yojanas in circumference, he arises. Not only the Tathāgata, but also Pacceka-Buddhas, the Chief Disciples (Aggasāvaka), the Eighty Great Elders (Asītimahāthera), the Buddha's mother, the Buddha's father, the Universal Monarch (Cakkavatti), and other eminent brahmins and householders arise only here.
157:
In that passage (the phrase "Tathāgato loke uppajjati"), the Tathāgata, the Blessed One, is said to be "arising" (appearing) during the period from the time he partook of the honeyed milk-rice offered by Sujātā until the Path of Arahatship (Arahattamagga); he is said to have "arisen" (appeared) at the Fruit of Arahatship (Arahattaphala). Alternatively, he is "arising" from the time of the Great Renunciation until the Path of Arahatship. Or, from the Tusita heaven until the Path of Arahatship. Or, from the time at the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara until the Path of Arahatship, he is "arising"; and at the Fruit of Arahatship, he has "arisen." In this discourse, the word "uppajjati" (arises) is spoken with reference to the very first instance of having arisen among all instances of arising. The meaning here is that the Tathāgata has appeared in the world.

"So imaṃ lokaṃ" means that the Blessed One (knows) this world. Now, he points out the world to be described. "Sadevakaṃ" means the world together with the devas. In the same manner, "Samārakaṃ" means with Māra, "Sabrahmakaṃ" means with Brahmā, and "Sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ" means with ascetics and brahmins. Because they are produced diversely by kamma and defilements, they are called "pajā" (beings/generation); it refers to that mass of beings. "Sadevamanussaṃ" means with devas and humans. Among those terms, by the word "sadevaka," the devas of the five sensual-realm heavens should be understood. By the word "samāraka," the devas of the sixth sensual-realm heaven (Vasavatti) should be understood. By the word "sabrahmaka," the Brahmās such as those of the Brahmakāyika realm should be understood. By the word "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇī," one should understand the ascetics and brahmins who are enemies and opponents of the Dispensation, as well as the ascetics who have calmed evil and the brahmins who have barred evil. By the word "pajā," the world of beings (sattaloka) should be understood. By the word "sadevamanussa," conventional gods (kings) and the remaining humans should be understood. Thus, in this context, by the first three terms, the world of beings is taken together with the world of locations (okāsaloka). By the two terms regarding "pajā," it should be understood that only the world of beings is taken.

Another method: by the inclusion of "sadevaka," the formless-realm (arūpāvacara) deva world is taken. By the inclusion of "samāraka," the six sensual-realm deva worlds are taken. By the inclusion of "sabrahmaka," the fine-material (rūpa) Brahma world is taken. By the inclusion of "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇa" etc., either the human world together with conventional gods by way of the fourfold assembly is taken, or the entire remaining world of beings is taken.

Furthermore, in this context, by the word "sadevaka," he speaks of the state of having realized the entire world by way of the highest limit. Then, for those who thought, "Māra is of great power, the lord of the six sensual-realm heavens, the Vasavatti; has even he been realized by this Blessed One?", he said "samārakaṃ" to dispel their doubt. Then, for those who thought, "Brahmā is of great power, he can spread light over a thousand world systems with a single finger..."
158:
...with two fingers... up to ten fingers, he can spread light over ten thousand world systems. He also experiences the incomparable bliss of meditative attainments (jhānasamāpattisukha). "Has even that Great Brahmā been realized (by the Blessed One)?"—to dispel the doubt of those who so wondered, he said "sabrahmakaṃ." Then, to dispel the doubt of those who thought, "There are many ascetics and brahmins who are enemies of the Dispensation; have they also been realized?", he said "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajā." Having thus declared the state of having realized the most eminent individuals, he then said "sadevamanussaṃ," desiring to show the realization of the rest of the world of beings, including conventional gods (kings) and other humans, by way of the highest limit of the noble destination. This is the sequence of terms according to the inclination (of the listeners) in this context.

However, the ancient teachers (Porāṇā) say: "sadevakaṃ" means the rest of the world together with devas; "samārakaṃ" means the rest of the world together with Māra; "sabrahmakaṃ" means the rest of the world together with Brahmās. Thus, having included all beings belonging to the three planes of existence in three terms by three modes, he then said "sassamaṇabrāhmaṇiṃ pajā sadevamanussaṃ" desiring to encompass them again with two terms. Thus, by these five terms, the entire triple-element world (tedhātuka) is encompassed in various ways.

In the phrase "sayaṃ abhiññā sacchikatvā pavedeti," "sayaṃ" means by himself, without being led by others (through his own knowledge). "Abhiññā" means having known with higher knowledge, specifically the knowledge of omniscience. "Sacchikatvā" means having realized through direct experience; by saying this, the use of inference (anumāna) and so forth is rejected. "Pavedeti" means he makes it known, makes it understood, and declares it.

"He teaches the Dhamma, good in the beginning... (pe)... good in the end" means that the Blessed One, out of compassion for beings, gives up the incomparable bliss of seclusion (vivekasukha) and teaches the Dhamma. Whether he teaches a little or a lot, he teaches it only in the manner of being good in the beginning and so forth. It means that in the beginning, he teaches by making it good, auspicious, and faultless; in the middle and in the end as well, he teaches by making it good, auspicious, and faultless. In that context, there is a beginning, middle, and end of the teaching (desanā), and there is also that of the Dispensation (sāsana). Regarding the teaching, even in a four-line verse (gāthā), the first line is called the beginning, the next two lines are the middle, and the last line is the end. In a discourse with a single connection (ekānusandhika sutta), the introduction (nidāna) is the beginning, and the conclusion "this is what he said" is the end.
159:
The middle is the space between the beginning and the end. In a Sutta with many connections (anusaṇḍhi), the first connection is the beginning, the connection at the end is the end, and one, two, or many in the middle are simply the middle.

In the Dispensation (Sāsana), virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and insight (vipassanā) are called the beginning. It is also said: "What is the beginning of wholesome states? Well-purified virtue and straight view (diṭṭhi)." (Saṃ. Ni. 5.369). The Noble Path, spoken of as "Monks, there is a middle way (majjhimā paṭipadā) fully awakened to by the Tathāgata," is called the middle. Fruition (phala) and Nibbāna are called the end. For it is said: "Brahmin, this holy life (brahmacariya) has this (arahantship) as its purpose, this as its essence, and this as its end" (Ma. Ni. 1.324); here, fruition is called the end. "Friend Visākha, the holy life is immersed in Nibbāna, it has Nibbāna as its goal, Nibbāna as its end" (Ma. Ni. 1.466); here, Nibbāna is called the end.

In this context, the beginning, middle, and end of the teaching (desanā) are intended. When the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma, he shows virtue in the beginning, the path in the middle, and Nibbāna at the end. Therefore, it is said: "He teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning, good in the middle, and good in the end." Thus, another Dhamma-preacher, when teaching the Dhamma, should also:

"Show virtue in the beginning, clarify the path in the middle,
And show Nibbāna at the end; this is the established order for a preacher."

"Sātthaṃ sabyañjanaṃ" means: If one's teaching is based on elaborating and praising rice gruel, boiled rice, women, men, and so on, he is not said to be teaching the Dhamma that is meaningful (sāttha). The Blessed One, however, setting aside such teaching, teaches the Dhamma based on the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) and so forth. Therefore, he is said to teach the Dhamma that is meaningful (sāttha). If one's teaching consists of only a single syllable, or is entirely without labial sounds (oṭṭhaja), or is filled only with visarga and niggahīta sounds, his teaching is called "without phrasing" (abyañjana) because it lacks phonetic completeness, like the languages of barbarians such as the Damiḷa, Kirāta, and Savara. The Blessed One, however, teaches:

"Lax (sithila), aspirated (dhanita), long (dīgha), short (rassa),
Heavy (garu), light (lahu), nasal (niggahīta),
Connected (sambandha), delimited (vavatthita), and released (vimutta)—
Thus, there are ten divisions in the understanding of phrasing (byañjana)."
160:
Without destroying these ten kinds of phonetic phrasing mentioned above, he teaches the Dhamma by making the phrasing complete in every way; therefore, he is said to teach the Dhamma with phrasing (sabyañjana). In the term 'kevalaparipuṇṇa', 'kevala' is a word meaning 'entire' or 'all'. 'Paripuṇṇa' is a word meaning 'without deficiency or excess'. The meaning is that he teaches only the Dhamma that is entirely complete; there is not even a single portion of the teaching that is incomplete. It should be understood as 'kevalaparipuṇṇa' because there is no meaning to be added and no meaning to be removed. 'Parisuddha' means 'without defilements' (nirupakkilesa). If a Dhamma-preacher teaches with the thought, "By depending on this Dhamma-teaching, I shall obtain gain or honor," his teaching is an impure teaching. The Blessed One, however, being indifferent to worldly lures, has a tender heart through the development of loving-kindness that spreads welfare, and teaches with a mind established in the nature of lifting beings up (from suffering). Therefore, he is said to teach the Dhamma that is pure (parisuddha).

In the phrase 'brahmacariyaṃ pakāseti', this word 'brahmacariya' is seen in these meanings: giving (dāna), service (veyyāvacca), the five precepts (pañcasīla), the boundless states (appamaññā), abstinence from sexual intercourse (methunavirati), contentment with one's own wife (sadārasantosa), energy (vīriya), the factors of the observance day (uposathanga), the Noble Path (ariyamagga), and the Dispensation (sāsana).

"O King of Nagas, what is your vow? What is your holy life (brahmacariya)?
By the fruit of what well-practiced merit does this result occur?
Possession of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy,
And this great celestial mansion is also your reward.

When my wife and I were in the human world,
We were both faithful donors;
At that time, my house was like a well or a pond,
And recluses and brahmins were satisfied.

That vow is my vow, that holy life is my holy life,
By the fruit of that well-practiced merit does this result occur;
Possession of psychic power, splendor, strength, and energy,
O Wise One, this great celestial mansion is also my reward."
(Jā. 2.17.1595)

In this Puṇṇaka Jātaka, giving (dāna) is called the holy life (brahmacariya).

"Why does your palm give whatever is desired? Why does honey flow from your palm?
By what holy life of yours is the fruit of merit accomplished in your palm?"
161: Because of that merit, the hand can give whatever is desired; because of that merit, the hand pours forth sweet flavors. Through that holy life (brahmacariya), the fruit of merit is fulfilled in my hand. In this Aṅkura-petavatthu, service (veyyāvacca) is called the holy life. "Monks, thus there was that holy life called Tittiriya," in this Tittira-jātaka, the five precepts (pañcasīla) are called the holy life. "Pañcasikha, that holy life of mine does not lead to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation... it leads only to rebirth in the Brahma-world," in this Mahāgovinda-sutta, the four immeasurables (appamaññā) are called the holy life. "Others will be those who practice unholy conduct, but we here shall be those who practice the holy life," in this Sallekha-sutta, abstinence from sexual intercourse (methunavirati) is called the holy life. "We do not transgress against our wives, nor do our wives transgress against us; apart from them, we practice the holy life, therefore the young ones in our family do not die." In the Mahādhammapāla-jātaka, contentment with one's own wife (sadārasantosa) is called the holy life. "Sāriputta, I know that I have lived the holy life endowed with four factors, being one whose practice burns away defilements," in the Lomahaṃsana-sutta, energy (vīriya) is called the holy life. Hīnena brahmacariyena, khattiye upapajjati; majjhimena ca devattaṃ, uttamena visuddhatīti. Thus, in the Nimi-jātaka, the eight-factored observance (uposatha) performed by way of self-restraint is called the holy life. "Pañcasikha, this holy life of mine leads certainly to disenchantment, to dispassion, to cessation... this is indeed the Noble Eightfold Path," in the same Mahāgovinda-sutta, the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is called the holy life. "This holy life is successful, prosperous, widespread, known by many, become great, and well-proclaimed as far as there are gods and men," in the Pāsādika-sutta, the entire Dispensation (sāsana) comprised within the three trainings (sikkhattaya) is called the holy life. In this context as well, it is this [Dispensation] that is intended as the holy life. Therefore, "he makes known the holy life" means he teaches the Dhamma that is good in the beginning... pure. When teaching thus, [the holy life] comprised within the three trainings...
162:
In this context, the meaning should be understood as making known the holy life, which is the entire Dispensation. Brahmacariya means conduct that is noble (brahma) in the sense of being excellent. Or, it means the conduct of those who have become noble, such as the Buddhas.

'Taṃ dhammaṃ' means the Dhamma endowed with the qualities mentioned. In the phrase "A householder (gahapati) or a householder's son hears that Dhamma," why is the householder mentioned first? It is because their pride has been humbled and because they are numerous. Indeed, those who go forth from the Khattiya (warrior-noble) class often develop pride based on their birth. Those who go forth from the Brāhmaṇa (priestly) class develop pride based on the mantras. Those who go forth from low-born families are unable to remain established [in virtue] because of their own corrupted lineage. However, the sons of householders, having tilled the earth with sweat pouring from their armpits and salt [crystals] blooming on their backs, lack such pride and are thus ones whose pride and arrogance have been humbled. When they go forth, without showing pride or arrogance, they learn the entire word of the Buddha (Buddhavacana) according to their strength and, by practicing the work of insight (vipassanā), they are able to become established in the fruit of Arahantship. Those who have left other classes to go forth are not many; householders alone are numerous. Thus, because their pride is humbled and because they are numerous, the householder is mentioned first.

'Aññatarasmiṃ vā' means one born in any one of the other classes. 'Paccājāto' means one who is born [there]. "He gains faith in the Tathāgata" means that having heard the pure Dhamma, he gains faith in the Tathāgata, the Lord of Dhamma, thinking, "The Blessed One is indeed the Fully Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha)." "He reflects thus" means he contemplates in this manner. "Household life is crowded" (sambādho gharāvāso) means that even if a couple lives in a house sixty cubits wide or in a place a hundred leagues away, the household life is still crowded for them in the sense of having anxieties and obstacles. "It is a path of dust" (rajopatho) means it is the place where the dust of passion (rāga) and so forth arises; this is stated in the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā. Some also say it is the "path of arrival" [for defilements]. "The life of going forth is like the open air" (abbhokāsa) means it is like the open air in the sense of being unattached. For a monk, even if he lives in a gabled house, a jeweled palace, or a celestial mansion with doors and windows closed and well-sheltered, he is not attached, not stuck, and not bound. Therefore it is said, "Going forth is the open air." Furthermore, household life is crowded because there is no opportunity for performing wholesome deeds. It is a path of dust because it is a place where the dust of defilements (kilesa) accumulates, like a place of unrestrained activities. The life of going forth is the open air because there is the presence of opportunity to perform wholesome deeds as one pleases.
163:
"It is not easy to practice this holy life..." In this passage, the summary meaning is as follows: That holy life associated with the three trainings should be practiced perfectly and completely until reaching the final death-consciousness, without breaking it even for a single day. It should be practiced purely and completely until reaching the final death-consciousness, without being defiled by the stains of defilements even for a single day. "Saṅkhalikhitaṃ" means it should be practiced so as to be as pure as a polished and washed conch shell. It is not easy for one living in a house to practice this holy life perfectly and completely. Therefore, (he reflects), "What if I were to shave off my hair and beard, don the saffron-dyed robes (suitable for those practicing the holy life), and go forth from the home life into homelessness?" Here, the work of householders such as farming and trading is called "agāriya." Since such work does not exist in the state of a monk, the state of a monk should be known as "anagāriya" (homelessness). "Pabbajeyyaṃ" means "if I were to practice (such a life)" or "if I were to go forth."

192-193. "Appaṃ vā" (or small): A mass of wealth less than a thousand is called small; from a thousand upwards, it is called great. Because they bind with the bond of attachment, even one's own relatives on both the mother's and father's side are called "ñātiparivaṭṭa" (circle of relatives). Among relatives, less than twenty is called small; from twenty upwards, it is called great. "Pātimokkhasamvarasamvuto" means being endowed with the restraint of the Pātimokkha. "Ācāragocarasampanno" means being possessed of proper conduct and resort. "Aṇumattesu" means in the slightest measure; "vazzesu" means in unwholesome states; "bhayadassāvī" means one who habitually sees danger; "samādāya" means having properly (without deviation) undertaken; "sikkhati sikkhāpadesu" means having undertaken each of those training rules, he trains in them. This is the summary here; the detailed explanation has been given in the Visuddhimagga.

In the phrase "possessed of wholesome bodily and verbal action and having a pure livelihood," although wholesome bodily and verbal actions are already included by the mention of proper conduct (ācāra) and resort (gocara), this virtue of purity of livelihood (ājီvapārisuddhisīla) does not arise in the sky or at the tops of trees, but only at the doors of body and speech. Therefore, to show the doors where that virtue arises, it is said "possessed of wholesome bodily and verbal action." Because he is endowed with those, he is said to have a pure livelihood. Alternatively, this is stated according to the Samaṇamuṇḍikaputta Sutta. In that Sutta, it is asked, "Carpenter, what are wholesome virtues?"
164:
"Wholesome bodily action, wholesome verbal action, and pure livelihood—these, carpenter, I declare to be included in virtue," so it was said. Because he is endowed with these, he should be known as one who has a pure livelihood.

"Sīlasampanno" means being endowed with the three types of virtue taught in the Brahmajāla Sutta. "Indriyesu guttadvāro" means one whose doors are closed (one with guarded faculties) regarding the six faculties beginning with the mind-faculty. "Satisampajaññena samannāgato" means being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension in the seven situations such as going forward and returning. "Santuṭṭho" means being content with the four requisites through the three types of contentment.

## Commentary on the Minor Section on Virtue

194-211. Having thus laid down the table of contents (mātikā) and wishing to analyze it in sequence, the Buddha said, "And how, Great King, is a bhikkhu possessed of virtue?" and so forth. In that text, "idampissa hoti sīlasmiṃ" means that this restraint from taking life is also one virtue among the collection of virtues of that bhikkhu. Alternatively, this locative case (sattami) is in the sense of the nominative case (paṭhamā). In the Mahā-aṭṭhakathā also, this very meaning is stated: "This also is the virtue of that ascetic." The rest should be understood according to the method stated in the Brahmajāla Sutta. "Idamassa hoti sīlasmiṃ" means "this is his virtue."

"He sees no danger from any side due to his restraint in virtue" means that among the dangers that arise due to the lack of restraint, he does not see any danger that would arise from restraint, even from a single type of restraint. Why? Because when there is restraint, there is no danger rooted in the lack of restraint. "Muddhābhisitto" means a king who has been anointed on the head with the royal consecration performed according to the prescribed ritual. "Danger from an enemy" means he does not see any kind of danger that would arise from any single enemy. Why? Because he has conquered his enemies. "Ajjhattaṃ" means within his own internal continuity. "Anavajzasukha" (blameless happiness) means experiencing bodily and mental happiness that is blameless, not censurable, wholesome, and encompassed by the states of non-remorse, joy, rapture, and tranquility, which have virtue as their proximate cause. "Thus, Great King, a bhikkhu is possessed of virtue"—having thus explained in detail and without interruption, the Buddha concluded the talk on virtue by stating that a bhikkhu endowed with the three types of virtue shown is called one possessed of virtue.
165:
## Discussion on Restraint of the Faculties

In the section explaining the different aspects of being guarded at the doors of the faculties, the word "eye" (cakkhu) in the phrase "seeing a form with the eye" (cakkhunā rūpaṃ) refers in some scriptures to the "Buddha-eye" (the Buddha's eye of knowledge). For example, as stated (in the Mahāvagga): "He looked upon the world with the Buddha-eye." In some scriptures, it refers to the "all-seeing eye" (samanta-cakkhu), which is known as the knowledge of omniscience. For example, as stated (in the Mahāvagga): "O Wise One, having ascended the palace made of Dhamma, you possess the all-seeing eye." In some scriptures, it refers to the "eye of Dhamma" (dhamma-cakkhu). In the phrase "The dustless, stainless eye of Dhamma arose," this "eye of Dhamma" refers to the wisdom associated with the three lower paths. In the phrase "The eye arose, the knowledge arose," the "eye of wisdom" (paññā-cakkhu) refers here to knowledge such as the recollection of past lives. In passages such as "with the divine eye," it refers to the "divine eye" (dibba-cakkhu). In the phrase "dependent on the eye and forms," it refers to the "sensitive eye" (pasāda-cakkhu). However, in this context, the word "eye" refers to "eye-consciousness" (cakkhu-viññāṇa) by way of the term "sensitive eye." Therefore, the meaning here is "having seen a form with eye-consciousness." Whatever needs to be said regarding the remaining terms has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. "Unadulterated happiness" (abyāsekasukha) means that because it is free from the intrusion of defilements, one experiences the unmixed, pure happiness of the higher mind (the bliss of concentration).

## Discussion on Mindfulness and Clear Comprehension

In the section explaining the different aspects of mindfulness and clear comprehension, regarding the phrase "in going forward and returning" (abhikkante paṭikkante), "going forward" (abhikkanta) refers to moving ahead, and "returning" (paṭikkante) refers to turning back or retreating. Both of these can be found in all four postures. In walking, one who first moves the body forward is said to "go forward" (abhikkamati). One who turns back is said to "return" (paṭikkamati). In standing, even while remaining in place, one who leans the body forward is said to "go forward," and one who pulls back is said to "return." In sitting, even while seated, one who moves toward the front of the seat is said to "go forward," and one who moves back toward the rear of the seat is said to "return." The same principle applies to lying down.

"Acting with clear comprehension" (sampajānākārī) means one who performs all actions with clear comprehension. Or, it means one who practices clear comprehension itself. Such a monk indeed practices clear comprehension in going forward and so on. At no point is he devoid of clear comprehension. In this regard, there are four types of clear comprehension: clear comprehension of purpose (sātthaka-sampajañña), clear comprehension of suitability (sappāya-sampajañña), clear comprehension of the domain (gocara-sampajañña), and clear comprehension of non-delusion (asammoha-sampajañña). Among these four, when the thought to go forward arises, instead of going merely according to the mind's whim, one reflects on the benefit or lack thereof: "Is there a benefit for me in going here or not?" Discerning the benefit and choosing it is called "clear comprehension of purpose."
